title: Foam board cutting with the H2D laser?
description:
Yes — the H2D 455 nm blue diode laser handles tool shadowboard inserts really well as long as you pick the right foam chemistry:

  1. Material choice (critical for both cut quality and machine safety):

    • Avoid PVC / vinyl foam completely — chlorine gas from PVC will corrode the H2D linear rails and optics in a single session.
    • Dark charcoal/black closed-cell EVA foam (EVA38 or EVA45 density) cuts far cleaner on a 455 nm diode laser than white or light-colored cross-linked PE (XLPE / Kaizen). Blue 455 nm light scatters inside white PE and leaves wide melted bevels, whereas black closed-cell EVA absorbs 455 nm cleanly with crisp vertical walls.

  2. Practical thickness & pass limits:

    • 10W module: Clean single-pass cuts on 5–10 mm black EVA (~650–800 mm/min, 85–90% power, air assist ON).
    • 40W module: Can step through 15–25 mm black EVA in 2–3 Z-stepped passes without heavy top-edge char if you keep speeds up and let air assist clear the kerf.

  3. CAD layout tips for calipers & hand tools:

    • Offset tool outlines outward by ~0.18–0.22 mm to compensate for thermal melt kerf so micrometers/calipers press-fit snugly instead of rattling.
    • Keep at least 8 mm foam ribs between adjacent tool pockets so walls don’t tear out, and add 18 mm semicircular finger-pull notches on flush-seated gauges.

(Full disclosure: I built a small browser tool for my own shop) If you want 1:1 tool outlines without a flatbed scanner or manual spline tracing in Fusion, you can drop your calipers or pliers on a standard A4 or US Letter sheet and run a top-down phone photo through FoamKerf — it rectifies camera tilt into a 1:1 kerf-compensated DXF/SVG (or a rigid 3D-printable STL if you ever want a hard PETG drawer insert instead).

As B.C.’s new Conservative government prepares to repeal Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity 123 (SOGI123) and strip the resource from schools, teachers in Vernon are pushing back, saying the anti-bullying resource is needed while questioning the rationale for its removal. SOGI123 is a set of resources provided by an organization called the ARC Foundation, which helps teachers in B.C. discuss sexual orientation and gender identity with goals of creating safer and more inclusive classrooms and reducing bullying and stigma, according to the resource’s official website. It is sometimes mistakenly referred to as a curriculum and confused with sex education, which it is not. SOGI material has been removed from government websites and resources, and the Ministry of Education and Child Care is currently working with school districts to “remove it from schools,” Education Minister Lynne Block confirmed to The Morning Star Friday, Nov. 27. Lisa LaBoucane, president of the Vernon Teachers’ Association (VTA), said Friday there are a lot of misunderstandings about SOGI, and suggested that Premier Lorne Doerkson and the Conservatives seized upon these misunderstandings to galvanize their base instead of correcting them in the lead-up to this fall’s provincial election. LaBoucane said it doesn’t appear that Doerkson himself has a strong grasp of what SOGI is, judging by his own comments. British Columbia’s First Nations leaders say they want to work with the incoming Conservative government, but have so far been sidelined amid signals of a more adversarial approach to Indigenous rights. “We need to meet with the premier, attorney general, and all the ministers, because I just want to get back to work,” said Robert Phillips of First Nations Summit and the First Nations Leadership Council in an interview. Premier Lorne Doerkson put Indigenous affairs front-and-centre in his mandate letter to new Attorney General Caroline Elliott, tasking her with repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act and defending private property rights against Aboriginal title claims. But First Nations leaders oppose any changes to or repeal of DRIPA, arguing it provides a reliable framework for government-to-government relations. They say repeal will create uncertainty, especially with so many large resource projects underway that rely on Indigenous consent. Phillips warns of “dire consequences” and endless court action if the DRIPA is repealed without something meaningful to replace it. Elliott is a well-known commentator on Aboriginal affairs, and holds a related PhD. But her stances stir controversy, especially her argument that Indigenous sovereignty can undermine democratic principles. She has called for not just the repeal of DRIPA, but constitutional change. “Just repealing one law isn’t enough,” she said in an Instagram reel released when she was running for Conservative leadership, adding, “I’ll lead the way on bold constitutional change because we can’t just sit by and accept the idea that it’s impossible.” In her first week as attorney general, Elliott declined interviews and held no press conferences. Supreme Court found that St. Paul''s Hospital can legally opt out of performing MAiD procedures. The B.C. Supreme Court has dismissed a Charter challenge seeking to invalidate a health ministry policy that allows religious hospitals to opt out of performing medical assistance in dying (MAiD) procedures. Chief Justice Ronald Skolrood found that when St. Paul’s Hospital transfers patients elsewhere to undergo MAiD, it does not violate a patient’s right to freedom of religion and life, liberty and security of the person or infringe upon a physician’s right to provide care in good conscience. St. Paul’s is a catholic hospital run by Providence Health Care, which prohibits its personnel from providing medical assistance in dying. The challenge was filed by the doctors and family of Sam O’Neill, a woman with stage 4 cervical cancer who elected to have MAiD while in treatment at St. Paul’s, but had to be transferred to a facility on the University of British Columbia campus for the procedure. Due to her pain level, she was sedated before being transferred, but never regained consciousness. The family argues the process caused O’Neill significant additional pain. Several other similar patient experiences were entered as evidence. O’Neill died in 2023. In 2025, the Vancouver Coastal Health authority opened a modular building near St Paul’s where patients can now receive MAiD without needing a vehicle transfer. While the judge writes that he does not wish to diminish or disregard the patients’ experience and pain, he does not find it to be a determining factor in whether Charter rights were violated. title: 'Danger Sign': Week-Long Streak of Record-Breaking Global Temps Meets ‘Bonkers Absurd’ El Niño
description:
Climate experts are sounding alarms over recent data showing that the Earth's surface temperature for the, for the first time since record keeping began, exceeded and remained 2°C above preindustrial levels over the span of a full week.

As The Financial Times reported on Friday, preliminary measurements from Copernicus, the European Union's Earth observation agency, reveal that the average surface temperature has exceeded 2°C above preindustrial levels since Nov. 20, a record-breaking streak that came amid the collapse in climate talks at the COP31 summit and the latest impacts of extreme weather events.

The temperature increase is coinciding with an unusually strong El Niño event in the Pacific Ocean that is projected to last through at least next the beginning of 2027.

But Akshay Deoras, senior research scientist at the University of Reading department of meteorology, told The Financial Times that El Niño by itself wouldn't have this large of an impact on the global climate without the help of human-produced greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

"The more often you see records like this... the more the long-term average rises," said Deoras. "And that is a danger sign."

Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for Climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, similarly told The Financial Times that the record-breaking surface temperature streak was "a stark preview of where our climate is heading" even after El Niño dissipates.

“El Niño will come and go," said Burgess. "The underlying warming from greenhouse gas emissions will not, unless we bring those emissions down."

While El Niño is expected to peak within the next two months, experts warned that its impact likely won't be fully felt until months afterward.

Richard Betts, head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Center, outlined the negative effects the global temperature streak will have in the near future in an interview with The Guardian published Wednesday.

"The immediate impacts of droughts in places like the Amazon can be severe, leading to forest fires with severe human health impacts through smoke pollution, and also damaging the ecosystems," said Betts. "More widely, there may be risks to food and water supplies."

In an interview with Heatmap published Friday, Daniel Swain, climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, pointed to water spouts that recently manifested in San Francisco Bay as an example of the kind of extreme climate phenomena we're likely to see thanks to the combination of El Niño and greenhouse gasses.

"We're really starting to see the profound influence of these extremely warm ocean waters," Swain explained. "I think this was a contributor to the level of buoyancy that enabled the water spouts."

Swain also said that the current El Niño will likely be the strongest one to occur in the last 1,000 years, noting it is producing a "bonkers absurd extreme marine heat wave" off the coast of California.

title: A popular password manager was hacked. Here’s what you need to know
description:
Password managers are the safest way short of secret sticky notes to keep track of the hundreds of logins in your life, but even they don’t have perfect security.

Popular Password manager 1Password disclosed this week that hackers breached its systems this month and accessed the software’s source code. While no breach is good news, the attackers were not able to access 1Password users’ most sensitive data, including their passwords, secret keys, and information stored in user vaults. 

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company emphasized in a blog post on the incident. The security of the software maker’s apps and browser extensions was also not affected by the breach.

The attackers were able to burrow into 1Password’s system after gaining access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. By pushing malicious code into its backend systems, the attackers made off with administrative data on a subset of 1Password customers, including customer names, email addresses, and “non-secret internal metadata” about accounts. 

Anyone who uses 1Password doesn’t need to take extra steps right now, but they should be extra vigilant for phishing attempts in the future. That includes being skeptical of “unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts,” according to the company. The password manager will never ask its customers for an account password or a secret key.

In response, 1Password says that it has disabled the compromised GitHub account, rotated and revoked exposed internal credentials, and brought in external cybersecurity experts to advise the software maker on its response, among other measures.

Security for everybody

The world of cybersecurity moves fast – and now that cycle is speeding up even in light of AI. Security companies are leveraging artificial intelligence to detect threats at the same time that malicious actors are putting it to work cracking into accounts at scale.

1Password CTO Nancy Wang described the unique challenges and opportunities the company faces in light of widespread AI adoption in a recent interview with Fast Company. While a sea of vibe-coded apps have introduced security holes human software makers would have caught, AI can also scan massive chunks of code for vulnerabilities. “AI’s been a mixed bag, just because that work has been so gnarly and technical,” Wang said.

Aside from the millions of people who rely on 1Password, more than 200,000 businesses use the password manager to keep track of their credentials. That number includes nearly a third of the largest companies in the U.S., according to 1Password. Fast Company named the software maker to its 2025 list of Brands That Matter for its user-friendly approach to security. 

“1Password was built on the belief that security should be accessible to everyone,” 1Password CEO David Faugno said last year. “In an industry that too often leads with fear and complexity, we’ve built our foundation on trust, usability, and the human experience.”

title: Pluralistic: Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch (27 Nov 2026)
description: Today's links Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch: Bosses will buy anything if they think it'll give them more control over their workers. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: UK recordings copyright won't go to 95 years; McDonald's sandwich patent; McLaren's son torches punk tat; Chestburster turkey; O(N^2) nationalism. Upcoming appearances: Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Taylorism and AI's shared sales-pitch (permalink) More than a century ago, the most powerful, wealthiest men in the world fell for a con-artist named Frederick Winslow Taylor, who sold them expensive consulting services to help them apply "Scientific Management" to their companies: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Winslow_Taylor Upon receipt of eye-popping consulting fees, Taylor dispatched unqualified young men in "scientist" drag (lab coats, clipboards, stopwatches) to fan out over factory floors. These smart young men noted how much time each worker at each station took to perform each task, then "optimized" each worker using a homebrew choreographer's notation that showed the "correct" way to make each motion and set an upper bound for how many seconds it should take to perform each task. Notably, these "scientists" refused to discuss their findings with the workers they observed: they never asked why a worker made a specific motion or tackled a task in a certain way. The workers were presumed to be ploddingly unreflective about their jobs (at best), or malicious featherbedders who were stealing from the boss by slacking off (at worst). Either way, Taylor's "scientists" could see no reason to discuss their findings with the workers. The job of the "scientists" was to transform those workers into a well-oiled machine, and no one but a blockhead would ask a piston or a gear why it chose to move the way it did. To use a technical term, these "scientists" were fucking idiots and their recommendations were (to use another technical term) bullshit. Not only did they set impossible quotas for workers, they were also notably bad at choreography and routinely required workers to move in ways that resulted in early fatigue and high rates of injury. Wherever Taylor's "scientists" went, morale plunged, labor unrest surged, and the business was made worse off. Which all raises a question: why would the owners of these businesses – who had the intelligence and self-interest to build up extremely profitable enterprises – throw away their money and kneecap their firms on this charlatanry? The answer lies in the psychology of Taylor's sales-pitch. Taylor's marks owed their fortunes and power to their ability to scale up their firms to sizes never before seen, thanks to innovations like the assembly line and to exogenous factors like mechanized transportation and long-distance telecommunications, which let them address much larger markets than their predecessors. The downside to this was a large workforce (too large to keep individual tabs on) that was spread out over a large factory floor or complex (too large to constantly observe). This created a paradox: these powerful, wealthy men were vulnerable to the lowest footsoldiers in their laboring armies, any of whom might slack off, organize a union or sabotage the line, safe in the knowledge that they were part of a vast cohort that could neither be tractably surveilled nor controlled. Imagine the indignation those industrial titans must have experienced at the thought that some mere pismire could blacken their eyes and destroy their profits, and nothing could be done about it! After all, the quest for wealth and power is, above everything else, the quest for impunity, for an existence in which you can never be thwarted: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/09/impunitism/#rats-eating-my-face The Robber Barons' fury at this indignity made them easy marks for Taylor's salesmen, who promised them a return to the natural order in which workers would be literally reduced to machine-parts. After Taylor's men had done their jobs, the boss could strut the catwalks high above the factory floor and observe a visibly cowed workforce, where every worker's every moment was a constant reminder that they were there to do as they were told, not to exercise judgment, air grievances, or act in their own self-interest. Like every power-tripping control freak, these business tyrants were their own worst enemies, doomed to a long and humiliating Tarkin's Downfall ("The more you tighten your grip, Tarkin, the more star systems will slip through your fingers" – P.L. Organa). Taylor was no master of improving industrial production, but he was a genius at figuring out how to sell things to anxious bosses. I don't know whether Taylor believed his nonsense: he might have been every bit as satisfied as his marks at the sight of a factory full of human workers who'd been reduced to the state of machine-parts. Perhaps he truly had no inkling that the reason his services sold so well is that they played perfectly on the insecurities of business tyrants. Or maybe he was a cynic with a thorough grasp of oligarch psychology and a total indifference to the quality of workers' lives and the long-term health of his customers' business interests. Perhaps some of Taylor's executives were true believers, while others were cynics, and together they formed an unbeatable partnership because the former would go where the latter would not (and vice versa): https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/24/supplemental-income/#andrew-tate-gwyneth-paltrow It doesn't matter. The purpose of a system is what it does. Taylor created a template for selling garbage products to insecure bosses that made workers' lives worse and undermined the health of the firm, and that template has been mobilized by firms large and small in the years since. Every bossware company that made bank selling companies surveillance tools during the pandemic's work-from-home phase wasn't just doing Taylorism(1) (timing, surveilling and scoring workers), but also Taylorism(2) (fleecing bosses who were terrified of their workforce's power and independence): https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/02/despotism-on-demand/#virtual-whips (In case you have any doubt, yes, this is a post about AI.) Many workers – and even managers – have expressed bafflement at their bosses' love-affairs with AI. Even workers who can see ways to use AI tools to improve their jobs around the margins are shocked (and sometimes resentful) at their bosses' insistence that they use AI for everything, even when that adds expense and reduces quality: https://pluralistic.net/2026/08/01/dare-snot/#i-will-fucking-piledrive-you-if-you-mention-ai-again At the heart of this confusion is the fact that these same bosses are usually unwavering when it comes to measuring profit and loss and requiring a solid business-case for major shifts in corporate organization. Despite this, an AI pitchman can send these bosses swooning with all the ardor of Jensen Huang meeting an attractive woman who flirtatiously asks him to take her on a "quirky" date, say, to one of his chip warehouses? Bosses are such easy marks for AI pitchmen for the same reason their predecessors were easy marks for Taylor's salesforce. The modern boss is a financial engineer, possibly with a law degree, whose main expertise is in balance-sheet manipulation and shareholder relations. These bosses don't know how to do anything. They can come up with as many amazing plans to revolutionize their businesses as they want, but inevitably, those plans lead to ego-shattering confrontations with skilled workers who tell them that all their ideas are impossible, illegal, or stupid: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/05/fisher-price-steering-wheel/#billionaire-solipsism Enter the AI salesman, offering the prospect of a new workforce of literal mechanical slaves, whose presence allows the boss to fire 90% of their workers, with the result that the remaining workers will be so terrorized at the thought of losing their jobs that they never even think of sassing back: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/10/posthuman-as-in-no-humans/#hell-is-other-people This won't work. Replacing workers with chatbots is as counterproductive as putting one of Taylor's choreographers in charge of them. Sure, AI can help workers: if the workers get to decide how the chatbots are integrated into their jobs, and if this integration doesn't increase the pace of work, making it impossible for the human workers to catch the machine's mistakes: https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/05/pop-that-bubble/#u-washington After all, the statistical methods used to produce AI outputs produce errors that are as close to being correct as is statistically possible, while still being wrong: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/06/nonfungible/#theory-free Ergonomics are real. Taylorism is fake. Automation is real. AI is fake: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/12/god-in-the-box/#llms-are-fake Statistical extrapolation tools can lead to productivity gains – just as incorporating ergonomic principles into the design of the job-site can improve productivity and reduce injury. But in both cases, the gains are contingent on the workers having a say in the deployment and a veto over demands that don't work for them. But that's not how you sell Taylorism…or AI. The pitch isn't about making the business more profitable or efficient. Such a proposition has limited efficacy and competes against other forms of capital investment that might be better for the bottom line. The pitch is about easing the psychological trauma of being the boss but not being able to boss people around. That's an unbeatable proposition. No one will ever lose money by betting on the insecurities of America's business tyrants. title: How to navigate the holiday party season while sober
description:
When Tat Read decided to give up alcohol four years ago to support a family member who was struggling with addiction, she knew that her career would present some obstacles.  

“Being in the industry that I’m in, I’m always at parties; I’m always at dinners,” says the 45-year-old communications professional. “My job is about bringing people together. And when people are brought together, there’s always alcohol on the table.”

Read, who says she was never much of a drinker to begin with, started limiting her consumption to a drink or two at work-related events about five years ago. As a mother of four, however, she found that even a small amount was more trouble than it was worth.

“My kids are really young. I have to be up early in the morning, and it was starting to affect my sleep,” she says. “It just had downstream impacts that I really wasn’t appreciating.”

Read says her colleagues supported her decision to give up alcohol completely, but says it’s still hard to navigate professional situations with new people, like networking events.

“I had trepidation about being fully sober because I knew it was an awkward conversation to have,” she says. “Sometimes I will hold a glass of sparkling water instead of champagne to not feel like I need to explain myself.”

Read isn’t the only one who occasionally finds strategies to avoid conversations about her sobriety. According to a recent survey by the Boca Recovery Center, which operates addiction treatment centers in Florida, Indiana, Massachusetts, and New Jersey, 39% of Americans who abstain from alcohol hide their sobriety at work and 30% fake it to blend in—like drinking sparkling water from a champagne flute. And 13% have skipped a work event, celebration, or date to avoid the topic altogether.

Given that more than half of sober Americans have been questioned, pressured, or teased about their decision not to consume alcohol, according to the survey, it is perhaps no surprise that 58% hide it from at least some people in their lives, and that 13% haven’t told anyone.

“The holidays make this harder, as events tend to be based around drinking,” says Alison Tarlow, a licensed clinical psychologist who is the chief clinical officer at Boca Recovery Center. “Those hiding their sobriety are managing a drink, an excuse and a conversation all at once—which is socially exhausting in a setting that is supposed to be fun and relaxed.”

Stigma remains even as more Americans go sober

More Americans are choosing to go alcohol-free for a wide variety of reasons, though taboos related to addiction and mental health remain.

According to the survey, one in four Americans have experimented with alcohol-free or reduced-drinking challenges; half of these cite physical or mental health-related reasons, compared with 10% who were recovering from addiction.  

Against this backdrop, younger generations appear less likely than others to hide their sobriety. According to the survey, only 5% of Gen Z keep it a secret, compared with 12% of millennials and 20% of Gen Xers.

But these younger Americans also face the most outside stigma, as 68% of sober Gen Zs have faced questioning, pressure, or teasing compared with 49% of older sober Americans.

“Telling people tends to involve fielding questions, which is generally off-putting to those who made such a personal decision,” says Tarlow. “Sobriety is a complex and sensitive decision, and people want to choose who hears about it and when.”

Navigating the holiday party season without alcohol

The holidays can be an especially challenging time for those who are looking to stay sober.

Between personal and professional events, family and financial obligations ramping up, and work responsibilities starting to dwindle, many are left without some of the support systems, practical reasons, or reminders that help them maintain sobriety.

Though they may feel judged for ordering an alcohol-free alternative, 93% of Americans say they would not think less of a coworker who skips alcohol at a work event, according to the survey. 

“The judgment sober people anticipate is usually harsher than what their peers tend to think,” says Tarlow.

While colleagues may ask questions, she emphasizes that those who choose sobriety don’t need to explain themselves. 

“’I’m not drinking tonight’ is perfectly fine,” Tarlow says. “These events are meant to be fun, so focus on enjoying yourself, not others’ expectations. But, if pressure builds, there’s no shame in taking a break or leaving.”

Coming up with excuses for not drinking can be exhausting and dishonest, says Phillip Barbb, an executive coach who specializes in sobriety.

“You don’t want to feel like you have to have 25 conversations where you’re lying at the holiday party,” he says. “Creating this false narrative for yourself can weigh on you, because you’re building a gap between yourself and others.”

Instead, Barbb, who has been sober for almost 19 years himself, suggests preparing a short explanation in advance that feels authentic and genuine, like, “I’m doing it for health reasons,” or “I decided I wanted to try not drinking this holiday season.”

Some may also find it helpful to create a practical reason for staying sober to help them through workplace holiday events, like being a designated driver or making an early-morning commitment for the following day.

Those trying to stick to their sobriety goals can also enlist the support of a colleague, date, or friend, though Barbb warns that these people shouldn’t be made responsible for someone else’s choices.

“It is no one else’s responsibility to keep me sober or to keep me out of bad situations,” he says. “What I do think is cool is saying, ‘I want to go to the event, I don’t want to drink, so I may have a moment or two where I need to pull you aside to just talk or vent.’”

How employers can offer more inclusive holiday parties for sober staff

With so many Americans experimenting with sobriety—and so many hiding it from their colleagues—organizations will inevitably plan holiday parties for attendees who are abstaining from alcohol, whether the organization knows it or not.  

So it’s important for employers to consider ways they can make the environment more inclusive for workers who don’t want to drink.

When a holiday party’s primary activity is consumption, it can make those who are going sober stand out. That is why employers are encouraged to include other activities, like bowling, an escape room, or mini golf.

Choice of venue can also play a role, as an event held at a bar or club may create more anxiety—and discourage more from attending—than one held at an activity venue or restaurant.

“If you’re hosting an event, you do have a responsibility to offer more than just beer and wine so that people can feel comfortable,” Barbb adds. “If you’re offering signature drinks, do a version without alcohol.”

Workplace cultures are often set at the top, meaning it’s up to leaders to model responsible behavior and signal inclusivity for sober attendees.

“It’s not anybody’s job—nor is it their right—to pry into the lives of their employees. But you should still make sure that you’re creating environments that are safe for people to be in,” Barbb says. “For executives and leaders, your responsibility for your people continues even outside of work hours.”

title: Engineered Waterways: What Architecture Can Learn from Urban Canals
description: Unlike open coastlines or the edges of natural bodies of water, urban canals are narrow, linear, engineered landscapes that cut decisively through the urban fabric. Where rivers follow the contours of a landscape and shape the landform, canals impose their geometry and logic, redefining the relationship between architecture and water. Their edges are clearly defined, often shaped by retaining walls, embankments, and the infrastructure that supports movement along and across the water. Bridges, pedestrian walkways, mooring points, and docks establish a distinctive relationship between the waterway and its context, creating an urban environment where the boundaries between water and architecture are realized.

title: Anthropic co-founders disclosed $560 million in pre-IPO share sales
description:
Anthropic co-founders Dario Amodei, the chief executive, and Daniela Amodei, the company’s president and board chair, each sold 3.3784 million shares at the $83 initial public offering price, worth about $560 million combined, according to filings cited by BigGo. Shares in the Claude developer closed at $82.79 on Nov. 25, below the offer price five trading sessions after its record $81.3 billion IPO.

Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue reached $16.96 billion, up from $1.38 billion a year earlier, while the company recorded a $567 million operating loss. Computing and infrastructure expenses rose $4.3 billion in the quarter as revenue increased $5.4 billion from the previous quarter.

The company has roughly $900 billion in long-term computing and infrastructure commitments and faces a series of share lockup expirations. Up to 303 million shares could become eligible for sale on Dec. 15, and Anthropic is expected to release its first results as a public company early next year.

title: China proposes rules treating AI training data as property
description:
China’s National Data Administration on Nov. 26 released a draft proposal for public comment that would govern data used to train and run artificial intelligence systems. The proposal sets out 12 measures covering lawful data acquisition and use, protection of data subjects’ rights, and responsibility and security in data circulation. It would apply a property-rights framework, with contracts defining ownership, transfer and permissions for data use.

The draft also directs AI companies to prevent outputs that violate privacy, trade secrets or copyright, and requires data processing to comply with China’s data-security and personal-information laws. It calls for safeguards against data tampering, falsification, unlawful temporary storage and illegal cross-border transfers. The proposal remains a draft under consultation.

title: Pact with Israel’s Democrats would give Yair Golan expanded security ministry
description:
An agreement between Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and the Democrats party would put party chief Yair Golan in charge of an expanded national security ministry, now led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, if Eisenkot forms a government. The Democrats also say the pact commits a future government to reversing the judicial overhaul and protecting judicial independence.

The deal follows a dispute over Eisenkot’s parallel talks with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party. The Democrats dropped their demand for the Justice Ministry but would lead the Knesset’s Constitution, Law and Justice Committee and have a representative on the committee that selects judges.

Eisenkot’s wider bloc has 48 seats, and Beyachad leader Naftali Bennett’s 12-seat party has not signed a formal pact. Negotiations with ultra-Orthodox parties hinge in part on military-service rules, while Arab-majority parties have offered parliamentary support. Eisenkot’s mandate expires Dec. 6, with a possible 14-day extension.

title: What Lies Behind the Walls of Contemporary Bathrooms
description: In 1966, architect and researcher Alexander Kira published "The Bathroom: Criteria for Design", a study that challenged conventional approaches to bathroom planning. Drawing on research into human anatomy, physiology, ergonomics, and personal hygiene practices, Kira questioned whether standardized bathroom fixtures adequately responded to the needs of their users. His work proposed reconsidering these environments through the relationship between the human body and its surroundings, rather than relying exclusively on established dimensions and arrangements.

title: China pledges stronger stock-market support as shares rebound sharply
description:
China’s State Council on Friday pledged stronger support for the country’s stock market, directing state-backed investors to play a larger role in stabilizing shares and saying it would consider additional measures. The meeting, chaired by Premier Li Qiang, also called for more long-term investment in equities and encouraged listed companies to increase dividends and share buybacks.

The CSI 300 rose about 3.5% and the Shanghai Composite gained more than 3% after the announcement, which followed a slide that had taken major indexes to multi-month lows. The CSI 300 was still down 16% for 2026, with weak earnings and economic growth weighing on confidence. Officials gave no timetable for new support or details of its scale; separately, lower minimum margin requirements for leveraged stock purchases are due to take effect on Nov. 30.

title: AI demand lifts China factory profits while consumer sectors lag
description:
China’s industrial profits rose 20.1% in October from a year earlier, their fastest increase since May, bringing growth for the first 10 months of 2026 to 16%, as demand linked to artificial intelligence and higher energy prices boosted earnings. Weak household demand and the property slump are weighing on consumer-facing and construction-related businesses. Retail sales rose just 0.4% in October, and fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first 10 months.

Across Asia, exports of chips and other data-center equipment remain strong, but some economists warn that reliance on AI investment leaves the region exposed if the boom slows. Bank of Thailand Governor Vitai Ratanakorn has also called for AI-related gains to reach more businesses and households, saying the benefits of exports and investment are concentrated among a small group. A proposed 20% U.S. tariff on Chinese goods could rise to 40% if the U.S.-China trade truce is not extended beyond January.

Presently, he’s out and about adding cheerful designs to windows on business storefronts. His very first window was in 1983 at Shields Brake and Muffler. Davis admittedly remembers starting as he believed he was going to make some money. “You don’t really make any but you can’t get more into the spirit of Christmas than doing this, and the people,” he said, smiling. “The people that come by and make comments, and that warms my heart.” Some of the many business windows Davis will be adding his touch to this holiday season in Williams Lake include Paradise Cinemas, Subway, Panago Pizza, Denny’s Restaurant and Sandtronic Business Systems Ltd. Adding a touch of joy when the sun drops and the night sky sets in are Christmas lights installed by staff with the City of Williams Lake. Director of Municipal Services Rob Warnock said light poles have been wrapped with a snowflake by the Tourism Discovery Centre and in front of Boitanio Mall. New this year are 22 wrapped poles up by Walmart at the Prosperity Ridge Shopping Centre. ”I love this time of year,” Warnock said. “I really get into doing the lights and I’ve noticed a lot of the guys have really gotten into it over the last several years now, so they’re pretty excited when we start putting stuff up.” Lights have additionally been installed throughout downtown Williams Lake, and Warnock said he hopes everyone enjoys them. It was another successful year of Performances in the Park despite attendance being down, according to the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Society. At a Nov. 25 Central Cariboo Joint Committee meeting, executive director Melissa Normandin provided an overview of the free, family-friendly summer concert series that brought live music and cultural performances in Boitanio Park for Williams Lake residents and visitors from July 9 to Aug. 27. An average of 219 attendees were welcomed each evening, marking a small decrease from the 2025 season that had an average weekly attendance of 237. “Attendance was a bit down and I’m going to blame the weather for that,” Normandin said. Of the 16 different performers or acts participating in this year’s Performances in the Park seven were local. A total program budget of $36,155 supported through diversified funding sources including local government, community sponsorships and in-kind contributions. In June, Williams Lake First Nation was added as a core funding partner with the City of Williams Lake and Cariboo Regional District for a three year term that includes an annual payment of $22,000 to the society for eight summer events. Normandin said their budget dollars were pretty consistent with previous years, and if they had more they could probably review some different asks received from the community including shade and covered areas. Cleanliness and adequately supplied washroom facilities throughout the evening was another challenge, along with glass, and broken bottles and garbage. “We can tackle that, and hopefully work with the city on that,” Normandin said. Mayor Surinderpal Rathor said he attended every concert and encouraged organizers to keep up the good work. title: Thousands of girls and women report bleeding and miscarriages after French police use of teargas
description:
Almost 10,000 women and girls who took part in nationwide protests in October give testimony about disrupted menstrual cycles

For three years, Naïma Di Piero says she barely had a period. The 46-year-old charity worker, who suffers from endometriosis, takes the contraceptive pill to suppress her menstrual cycle. But two days after being exposed to police teargas during France’s nationwide protests on 17 October, she began bleeding heavily.

French police fired about 22,000 teargas grenades at protesters on 17 October at the height of the protests – equivalent to two grenades every three seconds (over 10 hours of maintaining order).

title: EU's €5 parcel charges test Chinese e-commerce platforms' low-cost model
description:
The European Union’s combined charges on small parcels from outside the bloc now total €5 per customs product category: a €3 customs duty introduced in July and a €2 handling fee that took effect in November. The charges apply to shipments valued below €150, with both in place for the first time during the Black Friday shopping season.

E-commerce platform Shein’s third-quarter revenue fell 27.6%, as declines in Europe and the United States weighed on its results. Spanish retailers hope the added costs will make local offers more competitive. Shein is expanding its Polish logistics hub by 25% after investing €500 million, moving more stock into the EU for dispatch without the small-parcel charges.

title: Germany warns of AI attack frameworks after EU systems disabled
description:
Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) has warned that agentic offensive frameworks (AOFs), including the Artex tool, have reached a high level of maturity. In attacks reported in August and September, AI agents took instructions from human operators, then repeatedly planned, executed and adapted operations. One campaign disabled internal administrative platforms at the European Commission, while another framework was used against hundreds of online shops.

The Hong Kong Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Centre (HKCERT) says AI tools let hackers scan systems continuously and find exploitable gaps faster. In a separate study, cybersecurity testing providers reported growing AI use but said humans still oversee high-risk testing: none of the 11 regulated providers surveyed allowed AI to execute tests autonomously. Germany’s BSI and security experts urged organizations to strengthen basic defenses, including incident response, access controls and network separation.

title: Singapore weighs tariff talks as Vietnam says US deal is near
description:
Singapore has not begun negotiating a tariff agreement with Washington but is open to talks, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Friday. Vietnam’s Prime Minister Le Minh Hung said negotiations were essentially complete, with technical details still being finalized. Both governments are responding to President Donald Trump’s proposed duties on imports from 14 economies, including Asian trading partners, under a U.S. investigation into alleged excess manufacturing capacity.

Gan said the proposed duties could raise the effective tariff rate on Singapore’s goods from 7.8% to 10.3%, affecting about S$9.4 billion in exports to the United States. Singapore has a free trade agreement with Washington. The proposed rate for Singapore could fall to 10% if an agreement addresses U.S. concerns, while Vietnam’s proposed maximum rate of 35% could fall to 20% under a reciprocal trade deal.

Vietnam says it will continue engaging with U.S. investigators and submitting information, but Washington will make the final tariff decision. Public hearings are scheduled to begin Jan. 25, 2027, and Vietnam’s trade ministry said a final U.S. decision is expected between February and March 11.

title: Bitcoin wallet flaw could link watched addresses to network identities
description:
Research by Bitcoin Core contributor Abubakar Sadiq Ismail identifies a privacy risk for nodes tracking addresses, including through watch-only wallets: their transaction announcements may identify them. In tests on a local Bitcoin network, the method identified the correct node in all 30 trials; researchers have not established that it works on Bitcoin’s live network.

Identifying a node does not prove who owns the address or funds: a wallet may monitor coins for someone else, and an IP address alone does not establish a person’s identity. Linking a public transaction history to a network connection could support surveillance or financial profiling.

The behavior may also affect software that uses Bitcoin Core wallet functions, depending on configuration. Developers are considering changes to automatic rebroadcasting; the proposals remain under review, and one contributor argues that a narrower fix would not close every route.

In tests on a local Bitcoin network, the method identified the correct node in all 30 trials; researchers have not established that it works on Bitcoin’s live network (crypto.news, cryptotimes.io, coindesk.com). Identifying a node does not prove who owns the address or funds: a wallet may monitor coins for someone else, and an IP address alone does not establish a person’s identity. Linking a public transaction history to a network connection could support surveillance or financial profiling (cybersecuritynews.com, newskarnataka.com). The behavior may also affect software that uses Bitcoin Core wallet functions, depending on configuration. Developers are considering changes to automatic rebroadcasting; the proposals remain under review, and one contributor argues that a narrower fix would not close every route (cryptotimes.io, crypto.news, coindesk.com). Test design: The simulation used five target wallets over six rounds, with monitoring peers recording transaction announcements (crypto.news, cryptotimes.io). Software scope: Potentially affected setups include Bitcoin Knots, Fully Noded, Gordian Wallet, JoinMarket and Electrum Personal Server. Exposure for Sparrow and Liana depends on configuration (cryptotimes.io, newskarnataka.com). Attribution signal: Ordinary transaction relays do not automatically announce an old transaction in the mempool, the pool of unconfirmed transactions, to a newly connected peer. A wallet’s periodic rebroadcast can distinguish it from those relays (cryptotimes.io). Estimated cost: The estimated cost of a planted transaction was $0.18 to $0.34, depending on its output type (cryptotimes.io).

title: 'Zero-human company' plans to use chatbots to sell AI-generated software - ABC News
description:
First of all, lets get this out of the way: this isn’t a zero human company — it’s one with ambitions to be a zero employee company.

It’s not there yet and it appears that employees were tasked with using AI to built the company’s products and automate other tasks.

Adaca developers created Ante in about 10 days using similar software-cloning techniques in order to replace Atlassian’s Confluence software, which Adaca subscribed to at the time.

If you’re a buyer of software like this, how much confidence would you have in this vendor’s commitment to the product? They’ve taken the sketchiest of shortcuts to create it and are literally saying they expect there will be nobody overseeing maintenance or product development going forward.

Mr Photios wants Ante to be entirely maintained and serviced by AI agents and operating with no daily human input by March.

The founder and company director also doesn’t appear to have a strong grasp of his legal obligations:

“I don’t know what [being a company director] means come March, April next year.”

Luckily, the quoted expert helps out:

University of Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson said a company without any human oversight would be illegal and could be prosecuted by regulators or sued by customers.

This made the term “zero-human company” misleading.

“It’s a terrible sleight of hand,” Professor Paterson said.

title: EU budget talks collapse after seven net contributors skip sessions
description:
Seven net-contributor governments refused to attend some of European Council President António Costa’s small-group budget meetings in Brussels, disputing both the proposed cuts to the European Union’s 2028-2034 spending plan and the negotiating process. The summit ended without agreement, and leaders cancelled its planned second day. The budget covers EU farm and regional-development funds, with some governments pressing to shift spending toward defence and competitiveness.

The talks centred on Costa’s proposed €1.78 trillion framework, already about €204 billion below the European Commission’s original plan. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the package needed deeper reductions, while French President Emmanuel Macron called the cuts a strategic error and opposed further reductions. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni warned that Italy would not accept paying more while receiving less.

EU leaders are due back in Brussels on Dec. 17-18 and still aim to reach a deal by year-end. The proposed €45 billion loan for Ukraine also remained contested: Costa said 24 of the 27 member states supported it, while Bulgaria sought to limit its contribution to non-military assistance.

title: STEP vs STL is there a difference in print quality?
description:
Disclosure: I maintain a browser-side STEP-to-STL converter, so this boundary is literally my day job.

The mechanical reason STEP prints better on curves: an STL already contains triangles, baked at whatever tolerance the exporting program chose. The slicer only ever sees those triangles; it never sees the true surface again. STEP carries the actual surfaces, so Bambu Studio tessellates them itself, at the slicer’s own tolerance, every time you import.

The practical consequence: the tolerance setting in Studio only helps if the source is STEP (or a 3MF holding exact geometry). An STL exported coarse stays coarse no matter what you set later - you cannot refine triangles that were never created.

Numbers to make it concrete (measured, reproducible): a flat 10 mm cube is 12 triangles at any tolerance - flat faces need no refinement. A cone is 286 triangles coarse, 516 at medium, 2,142 fine. Same model, same knob, 7.5x difference purely from curvature. Curved parts are exactly where the STEP-vs-STL quality gap lives; prismatic parts never show it.

So for boxes, brackets and plates, slice either format and the result is the same. For anything round - smooth-walled holes, fillets, domes - keep the STEP until it reaches the slicer.

title: New Zealand coalition loses majority; centrist party holds balance of power
description:
New Zealand’s governing National-led coalition lost its parliamentary majority in the final count of the Nov. 7 election, leaving it with 65 seats in a 130-seat Parliament, one short of the number needed to govern without additional support. The centrist Opportunity Party, which won seven seats, now holds the balance of power. The opposition Labour-led bloc has 58 seats and cannot form a majority even with Opportunity’s support.

The Electoral Commission’s count included 484,865 special votes cast overseas or outside voters’ electorates. National lost two seats compared with the preliminary tally; Labour gained two electorate seats and the Greens one. Prime Minister and National leader Christopher Luxon, who had ruled out working with Opportunity during the campaign, said formal talks would begin with his existing partners and Opportunity. Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said her support depends on policy commitments and that she will not back a government with New Zealand First leader Winston Peters as foreign affairs minister.

Negotiations could extend into 2027. Luxon has warned that talks may be difficult, and failure to secure a governing or confidence-and-supply arrangement could lead to another election. A recount could still change the seat totals: applications are due by Dec. 3, and a recount could take a further five days.

title: New Work on Networks: Taking Stock and Setting the Agenda, Introduction to the Topical Collection
description:
James Woodward, Daniel Kostić, PhilPapers, Nov 26, 2026

This article is an introduction to a forthcoming collection of articles in Synthese (a well-regarded philosophy of science journal) on the increasing use of networks in the sciences, including, as the authors note, in providing explanations. The point of departure (as I read it) comes from the question, what is it about a network that would make it an explanation, or even a useful description, of a field or process being studied in the sciences? Networks, as described here, offer what might be called topological explanations, while in the sciences we more typically look for cause and effect. What is it - beyond cause and effect - that makes the topology of connections between entities relevant? These are great questions, and the discussion here is current and relevant. Image: Wikipedia.

title: Constitutional Chamber halts deportation of UN rapporteur and demands report
description:
Costa Rica’s Constitutional Chamber ordered Immigration authorities to prevent the forced deportation of Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, while it considers a habeas corpus petition. It also gave authorities 24 hours to report under oath why they denied her entry. The government cited an international alert over alleged links to terrorist acts, but Immigration Director Omer Badilla did not identify who issued it or provide details about those alleged links.

Albanese had traveled to San José at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica (UCR), a public institution that had scheduled the presentation of her honorary doctorate for Friday, November 27. The denial of entry drew criticism in the Legislative Assembly and a formal protest from the Office of the Rector, which asked the government for legal grounds and guarantees of due process.

The court order does not authorize her entry or resolve the petition: it prevents her forced departure while the court examines the case. AJUFIDH, a Latin American association of human rights lawyers, asked the government to reconsider the measure and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) to consider requesting explanations from Costa Rica.

title: Former Philippine president Duterte faces ICC trial over drug-war killings
description:
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is due to stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on Monday, Nov. 30, on charges of crimes against humanity linked to his anti-drug campaign. He faces three counts involving 85 alleged murders and two attempted murders between 2011 and 2019, when he was mayor of Davao City and later president. Prosecutors say the charged cases illustrate a much larger toll, possibly as many as 30,000 deaths. More than 500 alleged victims will be represented, and a conviction on any count could bring a life sentence.

The opening day is scheduled to include the reading of the charges, Duterte’s plea and opening statements from prosecutors, victims’ representatives and the defense, followed by testimony from the first prosecution witness. Prosecutors expect to call about 100 witnesses, and proceedings are scheduled to continue into 2027.

Duterte’s lawyers deny that the alleged killings amount to crimes against humanity and argue that Philippine courts should hear the case. They also challenged his fitness to stand trial, but ICC judges ruled him fit after medical examinations. Given his age, hearings will be limited to four hours a day, with breaks.

title: Latin American companies seek to measure the real return on artificial intelligence
description:
Businesspeople and specialists gathered in Guatemala and Peru on November 26 argued that companies must demonstrate concrete results before expanding the use of artificial intelligence (AI). In Peru, around one in three companies already uses an AI solution, but only 8% have reached a high level of maturity, while nearly 90% remain in the early stages of adoption, testing, or evaluation, according to Víctor Laguna, co-founder and CEO of PathPilot. Brooke Weddle, senior partner at McKinsey & Company, said that only 20% of organizations derive business value from this technology.

The recommendations focused on identifying a problem and a measurable benefit before buying tools, redesigning processes, and expanding projects only after validating the results. Weddle noted that companies that derive value work with a small number of high-impact use cases and integrate data, technology, operating models, workforce capabilities, and change management. For the first 90 days, Guatemalan specialists recommended measuring not only the speed of a task, but also its effect on sales, costs, service, and profitability.

title: Singapore seeks secure access to AI chips, says shipment halt unconfirmed
description:
Singapore has not confirmed reports that Nvidia halted AI-server shipments to the city-state, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Friday. The government is consulting local businesses and working with the United States to maintain access to advanced chips. The reports say Nvidia told manufacturing partners Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers to buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia; the duration of the reported halt remains unclear.

The reported halt follows new U.S. export controls aimed at restricting Chinese companies’ access to advanced computing through data centres in third countries. Singapore is reviewing its monitoring and enforcement processes. Gan said authorities need cross-border cooperation to investigate activities beyond Singapore’s jurisdiction.

title: Former U.S. deputy secretary of state Strobe Talbott dies at 80
description:
Strobe Talbott, a longtime Time magazine journalist who became deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton, died Thursday, Nov. 26, after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, his son Devin Talbott said. He was 80.

Talbott joined the State Department in 1994 and helped shape the Clinton administration’s policy toward Russia and other former Soviet states. He also led U.S. negotiations with India after its 1998 nuclear tests and later served as president of the Brookings Institution, a Washington policy research organization, from 2002 to 2017. His son confirmed the death; Clinton paid tribute to Talbott, calling him “a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure”.

excerpt: Strobe Talbott, a longtime Time magazine journalist who became deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton, died Thursday, Nov. 26, after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, his son Devin Talbott said. He was 80 (abcnews.com, theguardian.com, nytimes.com). Talbott joined the State Department in 1994 and helped shape the Clinton administration’s policy toward Russia and other former Soviet states. He also led U.S. negotiations with India after its 1998 nuclear tests and later served as president of the Brookings Institution, a Washington policy research organization, from 2002 to 2017 (abcnews.com, theguardian.com, indianexpress.com). His son confirmed the death; Clinton paid tribute to Talbott, calling him “a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure” (indianexpress.com). Early breakthrough: While studying at Oxford after an internship with Time in Moscow, Talbott helped translate the leaked memoirs of former Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, work that helped launch his journalism career (abcnews.com, washingtonpost.com). Balkan diplomacy: Talbott worked with Finnish diplomat Martti Ahtisaari and Russian envoy Viktor Chernomyrdin on efforts that led to the 1999 Kosovo agreement and played a role in diplomacy surrounding the Dayton accord on Bosnia (n1info.rs). Publications: Talbott wrote more than a dozen books; his last, “Our Founders’ Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump,” was published in 2020 (abcnews.com, theguardian.com).

title: Dairy farmers refine semen use as sheep study flags uncontrolled mating
description:
New Zealand dairy farmers using sexed semen recorded non-return rates 4% higher than at the same point last year, a result James Smallwood, managing director of breeding company CRV, attributed to farmers using herd data to select cows and time insemination. Separately, a study of 70 smallholder sheep farmers in two villages in South Africa’s Limpopo province found that 90% allowed uncontrolled mating.

The sheep researchers say selection can improve reproductive performance if farmers also assess rams’ reproductive anatomy and ewes’ udder traits while retaining sheep suited to local conditions. In New Zealand, CRV says targeted use of sexed semen can help farmers choose which cows produce replacement animals; pregnancy testing is still needed to confirm pregnancies.

title: Canada’s top court to rule on Quebec religious-symbols ban
description:
Canada’s Supreme Court is scheduled to rule Friday, Nov. 27, on Quebec’s Bill 21, which bars some public-sector workers in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols such as hijabs, turbans and kippahs. The justices are also considering whether provinces face limits on using the Charter’s notwithstanding clause to shield laws from rights challenges, and whether courts may still formally declare that a shielded law violates the Charter.

Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta have also used the clause, including to protect laws affecting transgender people. Teachers, religious and civil-liberties groups, and the English Montreal School Board challenged Bill 21; lower courts upheld most of the law. The court heard four days of arguments in March and is scheduled to hear a separate Saskatchewan challenge over school pronouns and names in March.

Court participation: The case drew 61 parties, including 51 interveners, a record number according to the Supreme Court (globalnews.ca, winnipegfreepress.com). title: Tokyo inflation hits 2.9%, strengthening case for December BOJ rate hike
description:
Inflation in Tokyo accelerated to 2.9% in November from a year earlier, its fastest pace since July 2025 and above the Bank of Japan’s (BOJ) 2% target for a third straight month. The central bank next meets Dec. 17-18; its policy rate is 1.25% after increases in June and September.

The rise partly reflects the end of government utility subsidies, while a separate index excluding fresh food and energy rose 2.5%. BOJ board member Naoki Tamura has urged the bank to respond promptly to inflation risks, but an economist quoted by Channel NewsAsia said persistent market instability tied to concerns about AI and chips could lead it to hold rates steady. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda is scheduled to speak Monday, ahead of the meeting.

excerpt: Inflation in Tokyo accelerated to 2.9% in November from a year earlier, its fastest pace since July 2025 and above the Bank of Japan’s (BOJ) 2% target for a third straight month. The central bank next meets Dec. 17-18; its policy rate is 1.25% after increases in June and September (bloomberg.com, channelnewsasia.com, wsj.com). The rise partly reflects the end of government utility subsidies, while a separate index excluding fresh food and energy rose 2.5%. BOJ board member Naoki Tamura has urged the bank to respond promptly to inflation risks, but an economist quoted by Channel NewsAsia said persistent market instability tied to concerns about AI and chips could lead it to hold rates steady. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda is scheduled to speak Monday, ahead of the meeting (businesstimes.com.sg, channelnewsasia.com, aawsat.com). Utility costs: Tokyo electricity prices rose 9.5% and city gas bills nearly 14% after temporary government subsidies ended; rice prices, by contrast, fell almost 34%, the largest drop in records dating to 1971 (businesstimes.com.sg). Government measures: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi plans to restore utility subsidies for three months from December, seek a food sales-tax cut from April and scale back gasoline subsidies (businesstimes.com.sg). Underlying pressures: The BOJ’s measure excluding temporary government measures reached 3.5%, its highest in three years, while business service prices posted their biggest rise in 36 years (businesstimes.com.sg). Rate outlook: A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expected another hike by the end of March, with many forecasting a terminal policy rate of 1.75% or 2% (channelnewsasia.com).
kite_context:
Perspective: Naoki Tamura, Bank of Japan policy board member: Tamura said the bank should bring its policy rate toward a neutral level soon and could accelerate increases if upside inflation risks grow; he put the neutral rate at about 2% (aawsat.com). (Asharq Al-Awsat)
Perspective: Ayako Fujita, JPMorgan Securities chief Japan economist: Fujita said rising prices in services such as public transportation and medical care indicate inflation is no longer driven only by temporary supply shocks, and she expects price pressures to spread (Channel NewsAsia)
Quote: "If the current market instability stemming from concern over the AI and chip outlook persists, there's a chance the BOJ may forgo a rate hike in December. But our baseline projection is for the BOJ to proceed with one next month" (Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus, Channel NewsAsia)

Timeline: September 2026: BOJ lifted its policy rate to 1.25% (channelnewsasia.com)
Timeline: October 2026: Central bank held rates steady but signalled readiness to hike (channelnewsasia.com)
Background: The BOJ adopted its 2% inflation target in 2013 and says underlying inflation has now roughly reached that level (businesstimes.com.sg, channelnewsasia.com).

With December less than a week away, Road Safety at Work put out a release reminding the public that a combination of snow, ice, low light and holidays makes driving particularly dangerous this time of year. summary: December is one of the riskiest times of the year for drivers across the Cariboo and B.C. With December less than a week away, Road Safety at Work put out a release reminding the public that a combination of snow, ice, low light and holidays makes driving particularly dangerous this time of year.
excerpt: December is one of the riskiest times of the year for drivers across the Cariboo and B.C. With December less than a week away, Road Safety at Work put out a release reminding the public that a combination of snow, ice, low light and holidays makes driving particularly dangerous this time of year. An average of 37 crashes occur per hour in December, according to statistics provided by ICBC, while WorkSafeBC statistics indicate that December has the second-highest number of accepted motor vehicle incident time-loss claims. “December brings together several factors that can increase driving risk,” Trace Acres, spokesperson for Road Safety at Work’s Winter Driving Safety campaign, said. Between 2021 and 2025, 27,572 crashes were reported to ICBC during the month of December across B.C. In the North Central Region, which includes 100 Mile House, Prince Rupert, and Haida Gwaii and the rest of the north, there were 1,805 reported crashes. Road Safety at Work went on to note that snow and ice are not the only winter weather that impacts driving. Heavy rain can also reduce visibility and traction, while fog can make it difficult to judge distances. In addition, black ice can form even when the pavement appears clear. “As the days shorten, more morning and late afternoon trips are taking place in darkness. Drivers need to be especially alert for pedestrians, cyclists, roadside workers, and other road users,” Road Safety at Work said. In addition, holiday shopping, seasonal celebrations and family visits mean there are often more people travelling on unfamiliar roads this time of year. To help reduce crashes this December, Road Safety at Work recommends drivers postpone or cancel trips when possible. If this isn’t possible, there are several steps drivers can take. These include slowing down and leaving at least four seconds of following distance on highways and adjusting your speed according to weather conditions. title: Defence minister probes claim nurse was threatened over Poilievre photo
description:
Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty says he is trying to resolve a dispute involving government contractor Calian Health after Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre alleged a nurse’s contract was at risk because she spoke with him at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright. Maureen Carpenter, who works at the Wainwright hospital under contract with Calian, met Poilievre after an Oct. 17 fire at the Alberta base that killed five soldiers and injured 39 people, 19 critically.

Poilievre raised a point of privilege in the House of Commons on Wednesday, saying the alleged employment consequences interfered with his work as Carpenter’s MP. McGuinty said he asked his deputy minister to raise the matter with Calian but cannot intervene directly in a private contract. He has spoken with Carpenter’s brother, but not with Carpenter. Calian had not responded to media requests for comment. The House Speaker is expected to rule on Poilievre’s privilege claim.

As responding paramedic Jeremy Vandekerkhove expressed, sustaining a successful CPR for that long isn’t easy. It’s physically demanding. You have to break ribs. “But honestly, when it’s your loved one, you do it,” he said. While Andrea was fighting for her husband’s life, daughter Makayla swiftly called 911. Their home is in rural Enderby so it took 11 minutes for the ambulance to arrive. When it did, Makayla directed the crew to her father, who was lying on the icy driveway where he’d collapsed. Things had seemed fairly normal just minutes earlier. Blaine had said he wasn’t feeling too good, and Makayla had given him an Aspirin. title: Canada expects temporary resident share to exceed 2027 target
description:
Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab said temporary residents are projected to make up 5.5% or less of Canada’s population by the end of 2027, above the federal target of 5% or less. Statistics Canada’s latest estimate put the share at 6.7% on July 1, 2026, down from a peak of 7.4% in October 2024.

The immigration plan calls for 370,000 temporary residents a year from 2027 through 2029: 220,000 workers and 150,000 students. Diab said the department remains committed to the 5% goal but gave no firm timeline for reaching it.

title: IAEA seeks ninth ceasefire to restore power at Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia plant
description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the U.N. nuclear watchdog, is negotiating with Russia and Ukraine for a ninth localized ceasefire around the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant after it lost its connection to its last remaining external power line on Nov. 25, reportedly due to military activity. The plant has lost external power 28 times since Russia’s invasion began and is now using emergency diesel generators.

All six reactors are shut down, but electricity is still needed to cool nuclear fuel and maintain essential safety systems. IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi said the plant’s reliance on one line and its location on the front line leave its offsite power connection “extremely precarious”. Russian plant operators said the line disconnected after protection devices activated and that the generators were working properly.

The agency is seeking a halt to military activity around electrical infrastructure so crews can repair the 330-kilovolt Ferosplavna-1 line and reconnect the plant. The IAEA also says another key supply route, the Dniprovska 750-kilovolt line and substation, needs further work.

The plant has lost external power 28 times since Russia’s invasion began and is now using emergency diesel generators (iaea.org, reuters.com). All six reactors are shut down, but electricity is still needed to cool nuclear fuel and maintain essential safety systems (tanea.gr, iaea.org). Fuel conservation: Four of the plant’s 19 emergency diesel generators started automatically; two were later shut down, and the IAEA estimates fuel can support the current two-generator operation for more than 10 days (iaea.org). Cold-weather measures: The plant suspended on-site heating despite temperatures falling to 0°C (iaea.org). Other sites: The IAEA recorded 143 air-raid alerts across Ukraine in a week and reported 10 drones at Khmelnytskyy, 26 at South Ukraine and 91 at Chornobyl nuclear plants (iaea.org). title: Altria weighs cash bid for Imperial Brands as Japan Tobacco explores deal
description:
U.S. tobacco company Altria said on Nov. 26 it was considering an all-cash offer for British cigarette maker Imperial Brands and discussing a deal for part of the business with an unnamed third party. Japan Tobacco is also evaluating a possible acquisition, potentially with a partner and a division of Imperial’s assets. Imperial said it had received no approach from Altria or the unnamed third party but would consider any proposal.

A transaction could return Altria to international cigarette sales, which it left after separating its overseas business two decades ago, and add established brands including Davidoff, Gauloises and Kool to a buyer’s portfolio. The companies are seeking growth as cigarette consumption declines and rivals Philip Morris International and British American Tobacco have moved further into newer nicotine products. Altria must make a firm offer or walk away by Dec. 24 under UK takeover rules.

title: Saudi-led coalition strikes 50 Houthi targets after deadly refinery attack
description:
A projectile hit Saudi Arabia’s Jazan refinery on Thursday, killing a Nepali worker and injuring several others. The Saudi Energy Ministry said the strike temporarily halted some refinery operations and started a fire that was later extinguished. The injured were receiving medical care.

Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki said forces destroyed a ballistic-missile launcher in Yemen’s Hodeidah province that he said had been used in the refinery attack. The coalition also reported destroying 50 military targets in Sana’a, Hodeidah and Saada but did not identify the individual sites.

Saudi air defenses reported intercepting two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh and two drones over the Eastern Province. The Houthi-run health ministry in Sana’a said Saudi strikes had killed at least 19 civilians and wounded 25 over the preceding 48 hours; CNN said it could not independently verify the figures. The refinery is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil a day, and technical teams were assessing damage and the facility’s safety.

title: Trump urges Putin to halt European aggression as Ukraine war intensifies
description:
President Donald Trump said on Nov. 26 that he had urged Russian President Vladimir Putin during talks in China the previous week to pull back “all military aggression” across Europe. He said he hoped that could lead to a quick deal to end the war in Ukraine but did not specify which territories or actions he meant. His statement followed a Florida meeting with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, after which they called on Russia and Ukraine to avoid steps that could widen the war.

At their China meeting, Trump greeted Putin as a “friend,” worrying officials in Kyiv and European capitals. Russian strikes hit Kyiv overnight, wounding seven people, while Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warned of another possible mass attack. European concern has also grown after missiles landed in Poland.

Washington has delayed a review of the U.S. military presence in Europe beyond its provisional Dec. 1 deadline while it assesses options and European offers to replace some U.S. capabilities. The review will go to Trump, but officials have not set a date for a decision.

title: UK net migration falls to lowest level since 1997 outside pandemic
description:
Britain’s net long-term migration fell to 77,000 in the year ending June 2026, the lowest level since 1997 outside the pandemic, the Office for National Statistics said. The figure was down 62% from 204,000 a year earlier and 92% from the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023. An estimated 738,000 people moved to the UK and 661,000 left.

The decline largely reflects fewer arrivals from outside the European Union for work, study and asylum, following tighter visa rules introduced by Conservative governments and retained or expanded by Labour. Immigration fell 17% over the year, while emigration remained high. Analysts say those leaving include non-citizens who arrived during an earlier period of unusually high migration.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood credited Labour’s restrictions, while the Conservatives said measures introduced under former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak drove much of the fall. Researchers cautioned that the unusually high level of emigration may not last and that fewer skilled-worker migrants could carry costs for the economy and public finances.

title: Guinea-Bissau junta delays presidential and parliamentary elections until 2028
description:
Guinea-Bissau’s military government has postponed presidential and parliamentary elections until Nov. 26, 2028, extending its promised one-year transition to civilian rule by about two years. Transitional President Gen. Horta N’Tam set the date in a Nov. 26 decree on the anniversary of the 2025 coup. The elections had been scheduled for Dec. 6, 2026. The junta said technical, material and financial preparations were inadequate to ensure a credible vote.

The army seized power three days after the November 2025 general election, before officials announced the results. Incumbent President Umaro Sissoco Embaló and opposition candidate Fernando Dias both claimed victory. In August 2026, voters approved a military-organized constitutional referendum that strengthened presidential powers and reduced the size of parliament; the opposition had called for a boycott.

N’Tam said the transition required more time and resources for electoral reforms, including a nationwide voter census and new constituency boundaries. The junta also says it needs to hold the country’s first municipal elections in 2027. The regional bloc ECOWAS has urged a short, structured and transparent return to civilian rule.

title: African Union urges Sudanese-led peace process as Abiy defends Ethiopia talks
description:
The African Union has acknowledged Ethiopia’s offer to host dialogue among Sudanese parties and Sudan’s rejection of the offer, saying any process to end the war must be inclusive, Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned. The dispute centers on Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s proposal to host talks on the conflict between Sudan’s army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Khartoum says Ethiopia cannot mediate impartially, while Ethiopia denies the allegations against it.

Abiy defended the initiative in parliament on Thursday, saying Sudan’s stability is directly tied to Ethiopia’s security. Separately, the RSF-aligned Sudan Founding Alliance (Tasis) said a five-member international mediation group had agreed to send a delegation to Nyala, in South Darfur, to meet alliance leaders and assess conditions in areas it controls. The United Nations said its envoy took part in consultations in Addis Ababa.
