title: Alberta forecasts $8.5-billion surplus as oil prices surge
description:
Alberta now expects an $8.5-billion surplus for 2026-27, an $18-billion turnaround from the $9.4-billion deficit projected in February, as higher oil prices lift provincial revenue. The province raised its forecast for benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude to US$83.50 a barrel from US$60.50, citing supply disruptions linked to the U.S.-Iran conflict.

The update leaves about $3.9-billion in surplus cash to allocate; at least half must go to the Heritage Savings Trust Fund, while the government says it will use some of it for one-time infrastructure projects, including roads. Finance Minister Jason Nixon said the province would avoid treating higher oil revenue as permanent. title: Conservatives seek parliamentary testimony from Carney’s wife on ocean envoy role
description:
Conservative MPs are seeking parliamentary testimony from Diana Fox Carney, the wife of Prime Minister Mark Carney, about her unpaid appointment as Canada’s ocean envoy, citing questions about her mandate, travel costs and possible lobbying. On Thursday, Conservative MP Jonathan Rowe tabled a motion at the House environment committee asking her to appear; Liberal MPs adjourned debate. Conservatives say five earlier attempts to bring her before the House fisheries committee were also blocked.

A mandate letter obtained by The Globe and Mail describes Fox Carney’s role as voluntary, time-limited and focused on helping convene the Our Ocean Conference in Halifax in spring 2027. The letter does not identify who she reports to or set a travel budget. Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said Fox Carney does not manage the government’s $1.2-billion ocean-protection fund. The House ethics commissioner said last month he saw no conflict in her hosting the conference, while the commissioner’s office said an unpaid appointee without a cabinet order generally would not qualify as a public office holder under conflict-of-interest rules.

title: Britain’s grid operator issues record number of power alerts as wind bottlenecks persist
description:
Britain’s National Energy System Operator issued electricity margin notices on three consecutive days, Nov. 24-26, as transmission limits restricted wind power from Scotland and colder weather increased demand. On Nov. 26, notices cited a 1.3-gigawatt shortfall in the morning and nearly 2.8 gigawatts later in the day. The operator said the notices were precautionary and did not signal a risk of power cuts.

In Brazil, almost 22% of potential wind and solar output was curtailed between January and September. Wind utility Copel has paused new wind investments after curtailment cut its quarterly operating profit.

Britain’s notices followed maintenance that left the B4 transmission boundary, linking northern and southern Scotland, operating at about half its 3.4-gigawatt capacity. Brazil’s first battery-storage auction is scheduled for early December, with contracts due to begin in 2028.

title: Italy and Germany warn Ukraine against widening war after Libya strikes
description:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul warned Ukraine against widening its war with Russia after Ukrainian drones struck Russian vessels in and off Benghazi, Libya, on Nov. 22. Kyiv said the operation targeted Russian military assets; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed responsibility the following day. Ukraine said the corvette Merkury sank and a cargo ship used to carry military equipment was hit.

Meloni said Italy would continue helping Ukraine defend itself but must also protect its own citizens and borders. Wadephul also affirmed Ukraine’s right to self-defense while warning against escalation and risks to Baltic shipping and the environment. Rome’s concerns include Libya’s proximity, energy links and role in migration routes. Italy also said it had not been told about the operation in advance.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told his Libyan counterpart that Kyiv did not intend to extend the war to Libya or any other country. Libya’s internationally recognized government condemned the operation, while Italy is considering additional security measures for about 200 Italian troops there. Wadephul said Germany was in close talks on containing escalation and protecting maritime traffic.

title: EPA reports no airborne lead after Iowa blast; lab tests pending
description:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday its real-time monitors had detected no airborne lead after the U.S. Army detonated nearly 9,700 pounds of degraded lead azide on Nov. 25 at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The agency collected more than 1,000 post-detonation samples, and laboratory results could begin arriving Friday. Testing also covers other substances that might have been released.

The Army said the stockpile had become unstable and could explode accidentally as colder weather set in, making destruction in place the safest option. The EPA said it would continue monitoring while laboratories process the samples. Its pre-blast baseline included 1,591 samples, and officials said sampling covered homes, farms, parks and drinking-water sources.

title: Carney campaigns in Saskatchewan byelection, discusses trade and electricity
description:

The Liberals have never won the riding, where advance voting began Friday.

Moe said Saskatchewan could help expand the electricity grid to serve new projects, while Carney said Ottawa still needs to secure a new trade deal with the United States. Carney also credited Moe with helping extend a trade agreement with China that lowers tariffs on many Canadian agricultural and food exports; Moe said U.S. tariffs have hit Saskatchewan’s forestry, manufacturing and honey sectors.

title: Ontario e-bike rules raise delivery costs and classification questions
description:
Ontario’s new e-bike rules could raise delivery costs and leave some riders unsure whether their bicycles qualify as e-bikes, as the province moves to classify motorcycle- and scooter-style vehicles as motor vehicles. Food delivery workers Syed Ahmed and Shubham Nahra told CBC that licensing and insurance costs could make delivery work unaffordable. The requirements take effect May 1, 2027.

The rules define qualifying e-bikes by features including a bicycle-style frame, functional pedals, a maximum assisted speed of 32 km/h and motor output capped at 500 watts. Vehicles outside the definition face motorcycle or moped requirements. Canadian Cycling Magazine’s analysis says the power limit could put some commercially sold commuter, cargo and mountain e-bikes in a legal grey area, depending partly on how motor output is interpreted.

title: SAP targets product and engineering teams in AI overhaul
description:
SAP has asked teams in product development, engineering and sales to identify potential reductions as it reorganizes its enterprise software business around artificial intelligence. People familiar with the discussions said earlier attempts to introduce AI products faced problems. The plan under consideration would eliminate at least 10,000 jobs, but the final figure could change after labor negotiations.

At a May user conference, SAP introduced Joule Work, an interface intended to give employees a single point of access to its applications, along with Joule Assistants and Industry AI for sector-specific workflows. SAP said its assistants would use more than 200 subagents to automate repetitive business tasks.

SAP has not confirmed the proposed cuts. In the United States, employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, about 20% of the total, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. SAP is expected to provide more detail with its full-year results in January.

title: Governments and AI leaders press for human oversight as safety rules diverge
description:
Governments and technology leaders are pursuing AI safety measures ranging from voluntary international commitments to proposed inspections and mandatory incident reporting. The Paris Call, signed Nov. 9 by governments, AI companies and civil-society groups, is nonbinding, while the U.S. administration has favored industry-led safeguards and Congress has yet to pass proposed federal requirements. California’s transparency law took effect in January 2026; New York’s RAISE Act is due to take effect in January 2027, and Japan’s government aims to submit legislation requiring reports of serious AI failures to its 2027 ordinary parliamentary session.

At a Nov. 23 United Nations summit in Barbados, Finland’s Transport and Communications Minister Lulu Ranne said human interests and governance should be central to AI development. Experts at a Brookings Institution discussion urged the United States and China to cooperate on incident reporting, testing standards and researcher exchanges, even if their domestic regulations differ. In Russia, President Vladimir Putin called for clear limits on what AI agents can do without human approval.

AI safety expert Stuart Russell called for international standards and mandatory pre-release testing, while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued that regulators should use existing laws unless they identify a specific gap. Japan’s proposed bill would allow inspections when safeguards are inadequate and penalties of up to 100 million yen, according to Nikkei.

title: Qatar and Egypt align on Gaza ceasefire, regional de-escalation
description:
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi met in Cairo on Nov. 26 and agreed to continue diplomatic coordination on regional tensions and Gaza, where they backed efforts to implement the ceasefire. title: DXVK 3.2 adds Vulkan timing support to improve Linux game pacing
description:
DXVK 3.2, a Vulkan-based layer that runs Direct3D games on Linux, was released Nov. 26 with support for Vulkan’s VK_EXT_present_timing extension to improve frame pacing in supported setups. The feature requires vertical sync and a compatible compositor and graphics driver; on Wayland, users need a recent Gamescope build with support enabled or a compatible Proton build and compositor.

The release also updates NVIDIA Reflex handling to prevent certain games from getting stuck at 10 frames per second, improves video-memory management and Direct3D 11 uploads, and corrects HDR detection on devices including the ASUS ROG Ally. Users can download the source release, while those using distribution software repositories must wait for updated packages.

excerpt: DXVK 3.2, a Vulkan-based layer that runs Direct3D games on Linux, was released Nov. 26 with support for Vulkan’s VK_EXT_present_timing extension to improve frame pacing in supported setups (9to5linux.com, linuxiac.com, phoronix.com). The feature requires vertical sync and a compatible compositor and graphics driver; on Wayland, users need a recent Gamescope build with support enabled or a compatible Proton build and compositor (9to5linux.com, linuxiac.com). Game fixes: The update includes a workaround for NVIDIA GPU hangs in Deadlock, rendering fixes for Quantum Break, and support for multiple monitors in Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance using Direct3D 9 (linuxiac.com). AMD compatibility: On Windows, DXVK disables a descriptor-heap extension on AMD drivers because of compatibility problems; Linuxiac says the change can significantly reduce CPU-bound performance on RDNA 3 and RDNA 4 GPUs (linuxiac.com). Frame pacing setup: The timing feature addresses frame pacing during full-screen play at refresh rates below a display’s native rate and when using DXVK’s internal frame-rate limiter, but XWayland and Windows lack the timing support it requires (9to5linux.com, linuxiac.com).

title: Iraqi Kurds rally against Baghdad's oil and border takeover
description:
Thousands of people protested in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region on Nov. 26 against Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s orders to transfer control of oil operations and border crossings to federal authorities. The Federal Supreme Court backed Baghdad’s authority to secure international borders, oversee crossings and supervise oil and gas operations, including in areas administered by the region. Kurdish officials and parties called the measures unconstitutional, while Baghdad said they aim to curb oil smuggling.

Iraq’s four top state offices agreed to hold a national dialogue on Dec. 1, sponsored by Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zaidan, to seek a constitutional resolution. The Kurdistan Regional Government has said it is willing to work with federal authorities against corruption and smuggling, but rejected what it called military threats.

The Federal Supreme Court backed Baghdad’s authority to secure international borders, oversee crossings

title: Bank of England plans bank capital cuts, flags AI debt risks
description:
The Bank of England (BoE) said on Thursday it plans to reduce capital requirements tied to UK domestic lending risks by 0.27 percentage points of risk-weighted assets for major lenders. Together with other recent changes, the measures would lower overall requirements by about 0.5 percentage points and free roughly £175 billion in lending capacity. The central bank plans to consult on the proposals in the first half of 2027.

The BoE also warned that rapid borrowing in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector and increasingly complex, circular financing could spread losses across markets. Hyperscalers are expected to issue more than $305 billion in bonds this year. The central bank also urged financial firms to prepare for AI and quantum advances that could compromise encryption.

Mortgage pressure: Just over 1 million UK households with fixed-rate mortgages below 3% are due to refinance by the end of 2027, with monthly payments expected to rise by about £200 (ft.com). Encryption transition: Current guidance calls for banks to migrate high-priority systems to quantum-resistant cryptography by the end of 2031 and all remaining systems by the end of 2035 (yahoo.com). Cloud outages: The BoE cited a November Microsoft disruption and an October Google Cloud data-centre power failure, though neither caused a major interruption to vital UK financial services (inside.com.tw).

title: Poland lifts ASF restrictions in 254 municipalities, eases them in 63
description:
Poland lifted African swine fever (ASF) restrictions in 254 municipalities and eased them in 63 others effective Nov. 26, under a European Commission regulation published the previous day. The changes affect eight provinces and reduce restrictions on the movement of pigs, pork and pork products.

Pig prices remain low, and production costs at some farms exceed their returns. The agriculture ministry says it will continue removing restrictions where animal-health conditions allow.

title: Remus malware uses fake Chrome extension to steal Gmail messages
description:
Researchers say the Remus infostealer’s advertised Gmail “zero-day” is not a flaw in Google’s email service: the malware installs a Chrome extension disguised as Google Sheets to read messages from signed-in accounts. The extension remains on the infected computer after a password change or session revocation and resumes collecting mail when the user signs in again on that device.

The feature was promoted on underground forums beginning Nov. 8. Researchers at Gen Threat Labs and Invoke RE published analyses on Nov. 24 identifying the extension as the mechanism. Google told Cybernews that “there is no Gmail or Google vulnerability at play here”. Researchers advise users to check Chrome’s extensions page for an unrecognized Google Sheets add-on or Developer Mode they did not enable. Users who find signs of infection should remove the malware before changing passwords and revoking sessions.

title: Burnham’s EU reset bill advances as minister urges closer ties
description:
Britain’s government has introduced legislation to implement its new agreements with the European Union, while Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander has become the first senior cabinet minister to publicly argue that the deal should lead to closer ties. The package covers food and drink trade, links between carbon markets and a youth mobility scheme; lawmakers are due to debate the bill on Dec. 7.

The food agreement would reduce checks and paperwork but requires Britain to align with relevant EU rules without voting on them. Under a 10-year termination clause, either side that withdraws early must pay reasonable, proportionate costs to restore border-check infrastructure; disputes over those costs would go to an international tribunal. The government calls the package pragmatic, while opposition leaders Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch have threatened to undo it if they take power.

Alexander called the agreement “a floor — a proof of concept — not a ceiling on our ambitions” for future ties. The food deal is scheduled to take effect in 2028, but EU officials say implementation of the package depends on an agreement within six months over tuition fees for European students in Britain; the UK government disputes that linkage.

title: Italy moves to scrap plan to spread Superbonus credits over 10 years
description:
Italy’s government is preparing to remove a proposal from its 2027 budget that would spread the use of Superbonus tax credits over 10 years. Credits usable in 2027 would instead be spread through 2036. The change is not final: Parliament must amend the bill, now under review in the Chamber of Deputies. The government is also considering changes to pension indexation, an expanded building amnesty and a revised exit tax as parties submit priority amendments.

A proposal from the governing Brothers of Italy would narrow the exit tax to people moving their tax residence abroad under specified low-tax conditions, with a threshold of 2 million euros in financial gains. Coalition parties disagree over whether available pension funds should support early retirement or limit cuts to inflation adjustments. Lawmakers are due to begin voting on amendments on Dec. 3, and the government has until Dec. 10 to submit its amendments.

title: Dutch watchdog tests six smart glasses as Meta faces privacy case
description:
A Dutch privacy regulator’s tests of six smart-glasses models found risks to both wearers and bystanders, including an AI assistant that incorrectly told a user an ambulance was coming, South Korean broadcaster JTBC reported. Dutch consumer and digital-rights groups filed a privacy case in Amsterdam District Court on Nov. 26 against Meta Platforms, the U.S. technology company behind the glasses, and eyewear maker EssilorLuxottica.

At the hearing, Meta’s lawyer said images used by the glasses’ AI assistant to answer questions about a scene pass through company servers, with bystanders’ faces blurred; the consumer group the Consumers’ Association said its analysis found that personal data was sent to Meta. The court is due to rule by Dec. 24.

title: Home Assistant Beta enables camera recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home
description:
The second beta of the smart home software Home Assistant 2026.12 makes it possible for the first time to connect cameras via the HomeKit Bridge and save their recordings with HomeKit Secure Video in Apple Home. Until now, the Bridge only transmitted live video; additional software was needed for recordings. Requirements include an Apple home hub, an iCloud+ subscription, a motion sensor, and setting up the camera as a standalone HomeKit accessory. Recording must be enabled separately for each camera.

Recordings only start when motion is detected. As a result, the first few seconds may be missing. Home Assistant recommends H.264 streams, since conversion via FFmpeg uses processing power. In the developer test, an H.265 source failed to meet the Apple home hub’s time limit. The final version is planned for December 2, 2026; until then, beta features may still change.

title: Ireland awards 1,555 MW of renewables, mostly solar, in auction
description:
Ireland’s sixth Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (RESS) auction provisionally awarded 1,367.25 MW of solar and 188.05 MW of onshore wind across 28 projects, according to results published by grid operator EirGrid on Nov. 25. The solar awards total about 30% of the gap between Ireland’s nearly 3.5 GW of installed solar capacity and its 8 GW target.

Bidders can file notices of dissatisfaction through Nov. 27. EirGrid expects to publish final results, subject to ministerial approval, on Dec. 9, with award notices scheduled for Jan. 11, 2027.

title: French far-right chief Bardella denies newly published antisemitic messages
description:
Jordan Bardella, leader of France’s far-right National Rally, denied writing newly published antisemitic messages attributed to him in private Facebook conversations from 2013, when he was 17 or 18. Investigative outlet Mediapart and newspaper Le Monde published further excerpts on Nov. 26, including claims that Zionists controlled banks and that French ministers put Israeli and banking interests ahead of French interests.

Le Monde said it obtained the full conversation from the former schoolmate who supplied the material and had a judicial officer certify it as complete and unaltered. The publications cited details about Bardella’s teachers, family and past activities to link the messages to him; Bardella and his lawyer categorically denied that he wrote them.

Bardella called the reporting a “persecution” campaign and has filed complaints against Mediapart alleging defamation and forgery; his lawyer said he may file another complaint over the latest articles. Marine Le Pen, who has named Bardella as her choice for prime minister if elected president in 2027, did not respond to the latest publications.

title: Anthropic brings Claude-built desktop apps to free users, limits enterprise rollout
description:
Anthropic is rolling out its Claude Artifacts desktop-app beta across its plans, including the free tier, so users can turn interactive tools built in Claude chat into apps for Windows and macOS. The apps open in their own windows and can connect to Claude and linked services; some can also use operating-system features with users’ permission.

The beta requires users to sign in to Claude Desktop and have an internet connection. Building apps and sending requests to Claude through them count toward the account’s plan allowance. Enterprise administrators must enable installation, while organizations using hybrid deployment or HIPAA-ready settings are excluded. Anthropic says it does not review apps before installation, and full computer access can let them run programs or alter files without asking users to confirm each action.

title: EU Parliament approves drug reform to curb shortages and spur production
description:
The European Parliament approved an overhaul of the European Union’s pharmaceutical rules on Nov. 25, alongside the Critical Medicines Act, which aims to reduce shortages and reliance on suppliers outside Europe. The reform allows national authorities to monitor shortages more closely and require companies to supply enough medicine to meet patient needs. It also lets generic-drug makers carry out certain preparatory work before an original medicine’s market protection ends. New medicines retain eight years of data protection and one year of market protection, with conditional extensions that can bring the total to 11 years.

The Critical Medicines Act covers drugs including antibiotics, insulin, vaccines and treatments for chronic diseases, and gives supply security more weight in public purchasing. The Council of the EU still needs to give the act formal approval. Following publication and entry into force, most provisions are due to apply after two years, while shortage-notification and monitoring rules are scheduled to take effect after six months.

title: Spain secures ECB presidency in Franco-German leadership package
description:
Spain’s governing Socialists and opposition conservatives both backed former Bank of Spain governor Pablo Hernández de Cos, whom eurozone leaders agreed on Nov. 26 to recommend as the next European Central Bank president. He would be the first Spaniard to lead the bank. His selection was part of a package deal that gives France’s Laurence Boone the markets portfolio and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier the chief economist post.

The agreement ended the Netherlands’ bid for former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot after France and Germany rallied behind Hernández de Cos. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, campaigning ahead of Spain’s Nov. 29 election, missed the Brussels summit and asked French President Emmanuel Macron to represent him. Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also supported Hernández de Cos.

EU leaders will consult the European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council before making the formal appointments at their December summit. A European Parliament hearing is scheduled for Dec. 7, followed by a committee vote and plenary approval.

title: Engineered chromosome 'glue' cuts errors in aged mouse eggs
description:
Researchers have engineered TALhesin, a molecular tether that reduced premature chromosome separation in older mouse eggs, and adapted it to bind human chromosomes in donated eggs. In 17-month-old mice, the share of eggs without premature separation errors rose from 46.7% to 74.1% after treatment. Age-related loss of cohesin, the protein complex that normally holds chromosome halves together, can lead to eggs with abnormal chromosome counts and contribute to failed fertility treatment and pregnancy loss.

The human experiments demonstrated chromosome binding, not a reduction in errors or improved fertility. The researchers say further efficacy and safety studies are needed before clinical use; fertility specialist Dunja Baston-Büst said the approach is not readily compatible with standard in vitro fertilization (IVF) procedures.

title: Mouse study identifies mutation-specific metabolic targets in liver cancer
description:
Researchers identified mutation-linked metabolic weaknesses that could serve as treatment targets in six genetically distinct mouse models of liver cancer. The study, published in Science, found that tumor genetics shaped how cancer cells generated energy and evaded immune attack.

MYC-driven tumors relied on oxidative phosphorylation, while KRAS-driven tumors depended on creatine metabolism; disrupting either pathway slowed tumor growth in mice. In MYC tumors lacking the tumor-suppressor gene PTEN, blocking production of the membrane lipid phosphatidylethanolamine slowed tumor growth and extended survival, partly by helping immune cells attack the tumors.

title: Quantum studies show progress and limits in computing advantage
description:
Researchers demonstrated magic-state cultivation on a superconducting processor, using a protocol predicted to reduce the cost of a resource needed for fault-tolerant universal quantum computing. Separately, a team led by Google Quantum AI and Stanford reported a classical algorithm whose runtime nearly matches that of quantum simulation for certain sparse random Hamiltonians.

A third study, which analyzed quantum linear solvers for neural-network training, found that realistic end-to-end speedups emerge only under highly restrictive conditions. Gradient preparation scales with the number of model parameters and can erase gains from the quantum solver itself. The study estimated that crossover scenarios would require models exceeding 10^20 parameters and computation times above 10^19 seconds.

title: French institute plans AI farm adviser as Deere expands data tool
description:
France’s public agricultural research institute INRAE plans to build an AI assistant using verified scientific data to help farmers respond to climate change and other pressures. The project awaits approval for €1.2 million in France 2030 funding, with a first version planned for farmer testing within 18 months. Separately, John Deere expanded access to its free JD assistant on Nov. 16, linking it to the company’s Operations Center farm-management platform.

INRAE’s proposed assistant would tailor guidance to a farm’s location, practices, soil, expected water resources and finances, while Deere’s tool searches and analyzes information already recorded about a user’s fields, machinery and farm operations. INRAE says the project has demonstrated answers to simple queries and aims to handle more complex questions; farmer testing depends on the funding decision.

title: Senegal lawmakers condemn Faye's decree enacting rejected 2026 budget
description:
Senegal’s National Assembly voted 128 to 9, with two abstentions, on Nov. 25 to adopt a resolution condemning President Bassirou Diomaye Faye’s decree enacting a revised 2026 budget that lawmakers had rejected. The resolution also called for the decree’s immediate withdrawal and warned public officials they could be held responsible for implementing it.

A proposed $2.2 billion International Monetary Fund program, agreed in principle in September, still awaits approval from the fund’s executive board. Faye said he acted to keep state institutions operating normally, while the Assembly, led by the Pastef party, says the government did not provide enough information on public finances and debt assumptions.

title: Kenyan court halts US-backed Ebola centre, orders deal disclosure
description:
Kenya’s High Court ruled on Nov. 26 that the government violated constitutional requirements by allowing construction of a U.S.-backed Ebola quarantine facility without public participation. Justice Patricia Nyaundi barred further construction and operations at the 50-bed site inside Laikipia Air Base and ordered the government to disclose its agreements with Washington within 45 days. The facility cannot proceed until the court verifies compliance.

The planned centre near Nanyuki was intended to quarantine people exposed to Ebola, including U.S. citizens. Residents protested over the risk of infection and the lack of information, and people died during the demonstrations. Kenya recorded nine cases in its October outbreak, including two deaths. The last patient was discharged on Nov. 11, starting a 42-day countdown before the outbreak can be declared over. The court’s disclosure order covers the bilateral agreement and information on safety assessments, regulatory approvals and patient protocols.

title: Clonezilla Live 3.3.5-3 adds experimental ZFS cloning support
description:
Clonezilla Live 3.3.5-3, the Debian-based disk-imaging system, was released Nov. 26 with Linux kernel 7.3.6 and experimental support for saving, restoring and cloning ZFS filesystems. The update includes Partclone 0.3.54, which adds the ZFS capability, and fixes bugs that could wipe an LVM thin pool, destroy a source disk or erase a parent disk’s partition table during cloning.

The release also adds local disk-to-disk cloning for Linux software RAID arrays and improves LVM cloning. It tunes NVMe block queues before imaging and cloning to improve performance and prioritizes in-kernel NTFS drivers, with NTFS-3G as a fallback. Clonezilla Live 3.3.5-3 is available for download from the project website.

title: Researchers identify possible largest known scorpion, over one meter long
description:
Researchers have identified Praearcturus gigas, a scorpion known from a fossil found in the United Kingdom dating to about 415 million years ago, as a candidate for the largest known scorpion. They estimated that the animal exceeded one meter in length. A new analysis combining CT scans with traditional fossil tracings resolved decades of uncertainty over its classification.

Paleontologist Richie Howard and colleagues infer that it hunted both on land and in water; terrestrial ecosystems were still developing at the time. The researchers suggest that the absence of other large predators may have enabled its large size, while later competition may have contributed to its decline.

title: PipeWire 1.6.12 fixes Linux audio crashes and camera capture issues
description:
The Nov. 26 release of PipeWire 1.6.12, a maintenance update to the Linux audio and video system, fixes JACK shutdown and threading problems linked to crashes in Wine clients, as well as deadlocks in GStreamer integrations. The release remains API- and ABI-compatible with earlier 1.6.x versions, so existing clients do not need to be rebuilt.

The update also improves camera compatibility and fixes issues across audio components. Users can download the source code, though most should wait for their Linux distribution to package the update. Availability will depend on each distribution’s release schedule.

title: White House reorganizes cyber teams as FinCEN filing outage persists
description:
The White House said Wednesday it will reorganize its cyber policy and operations teams under the National Security Council and Homeland Security Council as the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) responds to an intrusion that disrupted filing services. FinCEN took some systems offline after unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. It has not identified the affected systems or the attacker, or said whether anyone accessed data.

The Bank Secrecy Act e-filing portal remains available, but some services are disrupted. Filing providers reported problems with automated batch submissions starting Nov. 18. FinCEN’s relief order gives eligible filers with deadlines from Nov. 18 through Dec. 29 until Dec. 30 to submit their filings. The White House said the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added more than 200 staff and expects over 400 more. It also said the Justice Department and FBI will announce a cyber defense initiative next week.

title: How job hunting became an expensive cash suck
description:
There’s an expense that’s easy to overlook when talking about the cost of living: getting and keeping a job. 

We tend to think of work as the thing that pays the bills, but commuting and the other costs associated with it come with a price tag of their own. In a recent TikTok video posted in October, content creator Char shared that she had just had to quit her job because she could no longer afford the commute. 

Char, who lives in the UK, said the amount of money she used to spend on a full tank of fuel now only filled her car halfway. And with fuel prices showing no sign of easing, she said, the commute was only going to get more expensive.

“I can’t afford to keep driving to work,” Char said. “I can’t afford to live. Something has to give.” 

And right now, she decided, that something was her job. She would have to search for a position closer to home. 

In the comments, people shared they had been in a similar position recently, also highlighting how everything else had hit them financially, such as grocery prices and rent.

Commuting costs are also affecting people looking for work. Some job seekers have shared online how the expense of traveling to interviews is becoming difficult to manage. One creator said in a recent TikTok that she can no longer afford the job hunt.

“Assuming you get past the 12,000 rounds of phone screens and Zooms, and you are invited to an on-site interview, what if you don’t have the money to commute?” she said.


Compound that with the fact many are interviewing at several different companies at once, she said, and the costs quickly rack up. 

The costs aren’t necessarily limited to getting from A to B. Job seekers may also need to pay for childcare, buy appropriate clothes, or cover other expenses associated with making a good impression. For those who have been unemployed for some time, and have to interview in person several times, they can easily end up hundreds of dollars out of pocket.

An Indeed/Harris Poll survey found that 84% of job seekers had spent money attending an in-person interview. Of those who had spent money, 30% said they spent at least $100 on their most recent interview.

Meanwhile, a 2026 Monster survey of 1,005 employed US adults found that 49% of workers had turned down a job opportunity because of commuting costs or the length of the journey. More than three-quarters (76%) said current gas prices increased their financial stress, and 68% believed employers should help with commuting expenses when employees are required to work on-site.

Commuting costs highlight a widening inequality between people who can afford to look for work and those who can’t. For example, job seekers with savings or financial support from their families may be better positioned to travel to interviews, pursue roles further afield, or absorb the costs of a lengthy search. For others, the price of getting to work limits the opportunities they can realistically pursue.

Work is supposed to be the most obvious way of providing financial security, but that isn’t necessarily the case anymore. For some, even getting their foot in the door is becoming something they have to budget for.

title: 1Password lengthens recovery codes as breach investigation continues
description:
Password manager 1Password has lengthened verification codes used for account invitations and recovery from six digits to 10 alphanumeric characters after an intruder accessed its software build-and-deployment system. The attacker used a compromised employee GitHub account to access private source code, insert malicious code into backend services and download customer administrative records; the company says the attacker did not access encrypted vaults or the keys protecting them.

The intrusion also reached 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) system, which can contain credentials used to operate company infrastructure. 1Password says it rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials, disabled the employee’s account, revoked a stolen token and restored clean versions of affected services.

The company has not disclosed how many customers’ records were copied or how the employee’s GitHub account was first compromised. It directly notified a small number of users with active invitation or recovery tokens. 1Password says it has found no evidence of account takeovers, and its investigation with independent cybersecurity experts continues.

The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

title: TEPCO reviews security facility schedules; restarted Unit 6 faces April 2031 deadline
description:
Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings (TEPCO) is reviewing schedules for required security facilities at Japan’s Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant, where Unit 7’s restart has been delayed. Unit 6 has already restarted but also lacks its facility and cannot continue operating unless it is completed by April 2031. The facility is designed to support reactor response if a deliberate aircraft crash or similar event disables equipment across a wide area.

TEPCO said on Nov. 26 that it was reviewing construction schedules for facilities at Units 6 and 7 after the contractor sought an extension and the company found uneven concrete finishing in part of a structure. Plant head Takeyuki Inagaki said TEPCO would aim to complete Unit 7’s facility in April 2031, but the company has not set a revised timetable. That target is more than a year later than the previous goal of August 2029.

title: Google speeds up Gemini commands in the smart home by up to 20 percent
description:
Gemini for Home, Google's AI assistant for Home and Nest devices, has been answering everyday smart home commands up to 20 percent faster since November 17, according to the company. Google has now fully rolled out the speed improvement. The new features complement the Google Home app update released on November 25.

Among other things, the update fixes issues with follow-up commands and stopping media. A faster version of Gemini Live conversation mode is due to arrive on speakers and displays in the coming weeks. Users will then also be able to set timers and switch lights on and off during a conversation. Google still hasn't given a firm launch date and hasn't said whether the new version will be available in German at the same time.

title: GreenIT starts construction of 131 MW solar plant in Sicily
description:
Italian renewable-energy joint venture GreenIT began building a 131-megawatt solar plant near Assoro in Sicily on Nov. 26. The project is its largest solar facility in Italy, and Circet Italia is the builder. GreenIT expects the plant to begin operating by the end of 2028 and produce about 210 gigawatt-hours of electricity annually.

The facility will use about 205,000 bifacial photovoltaic modules on fixed-tilt structures. GreenIT, owned 51% by Plenitude and 49% by CDP Equity, is pursuing a 1-gigawatt renewables target. Its deadline for reaching that target has shifted from 2025 to 2027 and then to 2030.

title: Battery maker Fluence posts $274 million loss as backlog surges
description:
U.S. battery-storage company Fluence reported a record $8.9 billion order backlog at the end of its fiscal year on Sept. 30, 2026, and a net loss of $273.9 million. Annual revenue rose 3.1% to $2.33 billion. Delays in increasing production at a contract manufacturing facility in Houston held back project shipments; Fluence incurred about $90 million in related penalties and $85 million in manufacturing and equipment cost overruns.

Fluence said Houston output had risen from about three units a day in early September to 10 units a day, and that most planned automation improvements were in place. The company deferred its fiscal 2027 financial guidance until its first-quarter earnings call in February 2027, as management works on production planning, pricing and costs.

title: Norse Atlantic suspends flights, warns of bankruptcy without urgent financing
description:
Norwegian low-cost long-haul carrier Norse Atlantic suspended all scheduled flights on Thursday, Nov. 26, and said its board intends to file for bankruptcy unless it urgently secures short-term financing. The airline is also discussing a possible takeover with investors but said it could not guarantee a viable solution. Its shares fell 85% on Wednesday.

Jet-fuel costs that rose sharply during the war involving Iran have intensified the cash crunch. Norse does not hedge fuel purchases and reported a $94.6 million loss in the first half of 2026. The suspension also disrupted Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) flights operated with Norse aircraft and crews. PIA said it would use its own fleet for UK services.

title: Can potential clients find you using AI?
description:
A few months ago, I got a DM on LinkedIn from someone wanting to interview me for a feature she was writing. At the end of the interview, I asked her how she found me. She replied, “ChatGPT.” 

If you’re running a solo business, you’ve probably thought about how people find you online. Maybe you even track the information by asking or through a “How did you find me?” question on your website.

Many people now ask an AI chatbot for a recommendation, the same way they’ve typed questions into Google for years. No matter how you feel about using AI tools personally, AI search is something that may have more and more of an impact on your business over time.

AI as the new recommendation engine

For a long time, getting found online meant search engine optimization (SEO), or showing up in Google results by publishing content like a blog. The newer version is AEO (answer engine optimization) or GEO (generative engine optimization). The idea is that AI tools might “find” you the way Google once did.

AEO and SEO share the same fundamentals. AI tools pull from publicly available information on the Internet, so the more you put out there, the easier you are to find. 

In BrightLocal’s 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey, 45% of consumers said they used ChatGPT or another AI tool to get recommendations for local businesses. A year earlier, it was 6%. That’s a big jump in a single year. The survey looked at local businesses, so it may not line up exactly with the work you do, but directionally it suggests that more and more people are turning to AI search to find what they’re looking for.

Make sure you have a consistent online presence

Like Google, AI tools look for an authoritative answer to whatever question someone asks. SEO has long focused on ranking in Google by following a set of “rules.” To me, AEO feels more like a wide-open, unclaimed field. No one quite understands it yet, though many people are trying to influence the AI search results.

You can’t control the algorithms or LLMs, but you can control some of the narrative when Google Search or AI search finds you. AI tools piece together a description of you from all of these sources. 

Your website

Your website is an obvious source for who you are and what you do. Your About and Products/ Services pages are good places to start. Make sure they’re up to date with the information you’d want someone to know or find.

From there, you might add content that answers the questions potential clients are likely to ask. My website includes an FAQs section to help the algorithms and LLMs understand me better.

Content also increases the likelihood that you’ll appear in search results, AI or otherwise. A blog works, and so does a publicly available newsletter. Case studies and testimonials help too, especially when they include client names and outcomes (with permission, of course).

Your content on other sites

Content on other sites gives AI tools something to cite when it answers someone’s question. It might be a podcast episode where you were a guest, or an article you wrote for someone else’s website. YouTube videos and social media posts count as well.

Claim your business profile

Google Business Profile is the original way to claim your business and correct its information. It’s worth setting up if you serve a local area, but for many online service providers (like me) it wasn’t necessary.

In November 2026, OpenAI launched a beta of Businesses in ChatGPT, which lets a business claim and manage its listing. It’s in beta and open to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S. Once your business is verified, you can update its details. You’ll even be able to see how often ChatGPT mentions your business in its answers and how many people click through to your website.

A LinkedIn Company Page works for a one-person business, too. I have one, and it shows up when people search on LinkedIn.

AI is one more way people ask for information

I’ll admit: I immediately claimed my business profile in ChatGPT when I heard it was available. It only took a few minutes to verify my website and identity, and then I could see what ChatGPT “knows” about me. I also plan to track how many times ChatGPT mentions me (currently sitting at 19).

Word of mouth still keeps my pipeline full, because people know the type of work I do. But I can’t ignore that people are also turning to AI chatbots for recommendations.

title: Floodwaters peak along parts of B.C. coast; central Island remains under warning
description:
Floodwaters have peaked across much of Vancouver Island and British Columbia’s south coast, but river levels remain a serious concern on central Vancouver Island after days of rain, high tides and storm surge. The provincial River Forecast Centre issued a flood warning for central Island waterways, where rivers had reached their banks or were expected to overflow soon. Officials said eastern Vancouver Island remained under a flood watch and coastal flood warnings continued in many areas.

Courtenay declared a local emergency and ordered evacuations from several low-lying properties, including the Maple Pool campground, while the Regional District of Nanaimo ordered some Cedar residents to leave homes along the Nanaimo River. Rain and wind warnings for the South Coast were lifted Thursday, but officials said rivers would need time to recede before advisories could be withdrawn. The Effingham Island weather station recorded 469 millimetres of rain in just over two days.

title: Iraqi court sentences eight French ISIS members to life in prison
description:
An Iraqi court sentenced eight French nationals to life in prison and two others to 15 years on Thursday for membership in the Islamic State (ISIS), bringing the number convicted to 26 among 47 French nationals transferred from northeastern Syria to Iraq last year. The Karkh Criminal Court postponed rulings for 10 other defendants, including Adrien Guihal, who voiced ISIS’s claim of responsibility for the 2016 Nice attack that killed 86 people.

Iraq is prosecuting the men under its anti-terrorism law for joining ISIS, including those whose alleged activity took place in Syria. Presiding judge Mohammed Salman said the court found that they had joined and supported the group after it seized territory in Iraq and Syria. In Iraq, a life sentence in this case means 20 years in prison.

Iraq is also prosecuting thousands of suspected ISIS members transferred from Syrian detention facilities. It received 5,704 detainees from 61 nationalities in an operation earlier this year. Hearings for that group began on Nov. 22 with Syrian defendants.

title: Global temperatures exceed pre-industrial average by 2°C for a week as El Niño intensifies
description:
Preliminary data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate-monitoring service, show global temperatures stayed more than 2°C above the 1850–1900 average for seven consecutive days, reaching 2.25°C above that baseline on Monday. These daily readings do not establish that the Paris Agreement’s temperature limit has been breached: that target is assessed over at least 20 years. Scientists attribute the spike to long-term human-caused warming combined with a strong El Niño.

The record run coincided with COP31 climate negotiations in Turkey, where nearly 200 countries failed to agree on language about moving away from fossil fuels. The UK Met Office forecasts an unusually sharp rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide in 2027 as drought weakens natural carbon sinks; one estimate puts the year-to-year increase at about 3.5 parts per million. The current El Niño began in June and is expected to continue until at least March.

title: South African opposition parties weigh appeals after Ramaphosa impeachment ruling
description:
South African opposition parties said they may challenge a court ruling that voided the parliamentary process to impeach President Cyril Ramaphosa over the 2020 theft of cash from his Phala Phala farm. The African Transformation Movement (ATM), which initiated the impeachment motion, is consulting lawyers and said it may appeal and seek a new panel. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) said it was likely to appeal, while ActionSA criticized the judgment and said the matter was not over.

The Western Cape High Court ruled on Nov. 25 that the independent panel’s report and Parliament’s subsequent steps were unlawful because the panel made legal errors. The judgment did not decide whether Ramaphosa committed misconduct. The African National Congress (ANC) welcomed the decision and said it put the matter to rest, while the Democratic Alliance said it would study the ruling and defend Parliament’s oversight role.

title: Data centres face power-management challenges as grid capacity tightens
description:
Cloud infrastructure operators face challenges beyond securing electricity: local grids and facility systems must manage rapidly changing data-centre loads while projects compete for power, water and land. In Jakarta, utility PLN says it serves 50 data-centre customers drawing 515.6 megavolt-amperes (MVA), with another 150 MVA of potential demand.

Grid work for NextDC’s West Footscray campus in Australia is on hold until at least February 2027. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie tracks more than 100 disclosed US data-centre sites with around-the-meter generation configurations, while a German analysis describes batteries and flexible workloads as potential tools for managing power alongside grid supply.

RMIT researchers in Victoria say construction is outpacing independent evidence on electricity prices, water and security; the state government says its action plan could unlock up to A$25 billion in further investment. Separately, businesses considering server replacements are weighing the use of supported older hardware as memory-component costs rise.

title: European farmers protest subsidy cuts as EU budget summit fails
description:
European farmers protested in Brussels on Nov. 26 against proposed cuts to the European Union’s Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) as leaders debated the bloc’s 2028-34 budget. The European Council summit ended without agreement, and its planned second day was canceled. Talks are due to resume at a Dec. 17-18 summit.

Farm groups say the latest budget plans could cut CAP funding by more than 20% after inflation. They also oppose folding agricultural and regional support into broader national plans, which they fear would give governments greater discretion over allocations. European Council President António Costa’s Nov. 21 compromise proposal put the overall EU budget at €1.582 trillion, below the European Commission’s original €1.76 trillion plan. Farmers’ organizations estimate the CAP reduction at about 15% in nominal terms and more after inflation.

CAP funding supports farm income, rural development and environmental measures. Spain’s COAG farm organization estimates the proposed changes could reduce Spanish farm income by €877.5 million annually, while Dutch agriculture organization LTO says the plans put nearly a quarter of the Netherlands’ CAP allocation at risk. Farm group Copa-Cogeca has called farmers back to Brussels on Dec. 17 for a larger tractor-led demonstration alongside the next budget summit.

title: Doctors warn Wainwright fire injuries may require years of recovery
description:
Nearly six weeks after a wind-driven grass fire burned soldiers during a training exercise at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, doctors say some face months or years of physical and psychological recovery. Five soldiers have died; as of Thursday, 19 injured soldiers remained in Alberta hospitals, seven in critical condition, while the military said 22 were still hospitalized across Canada.

Burn specialist Dr. Josh Wong said treatment for severe burns can involve repeated surgeries, rehabilitation and ongoing psychological support. The fire overwhelmed the Edmonton burn unit, and three investigations are examining how it started and why live-fire training continued as strong winds pushed flames across the base. Health officials say they will review the emergency response after addressing immediate treatment needs.

title: Architecture as a Measured Intervention: Inside the Work of Atelier Guo
description: An architectural intervention is not simply a question of how much or how little to introduce, but of understanding precisely where and how to act. This precision begins with a careful reading of the existing context, including the recognition of the spatial, material, and environmental conditions that shape a place. It extends into the process of design and construction, where complex considerations are distilled into deliberate, coherent decisions. Rather than pursuing formal complexity or reduction for its own sake, a measured intervention seeks to establish a meaningful relationship between what already exists and what architecture can contribute.

title: EU Parliament approves drug reforms to curb shortages and boost production
description:
The European Parliament gave final approval on Nov. 25 to an overhaul of European Union pharmaceutical rules and a separate Critical Medicines Act, aiming to prevent medicine shortages, speed patient access to medicines and expand production in Europe. The overhaul, the first major revision in more than 20 years, allows governments to require drugmakers to supply enough medicine to meet patient needs and requires shortage-prevention plans for certain medicines.

The rules also allow generic and biosimilar manufacturers to prepare applications before a branded medicine’s protection expires, while new medicines can receive up to 11 years of combined regulatory protection. Companies developing priority antibiotics may earn a transferable one-year exclusivity voucher, and all antimicrobials will require a prescription.

The Critical Medicines Act passed by 592 votes to 35, with 30 abstentions. It sets criteria for EU-based production projects and allows groups of at least five member states to make joint purchases. The pharmaceutical package must be signed and published before most provisions take effect, generally after a 24-month transition; the Critical Medicines Act still requires formal Council approval.

title: EU leaders confront deeper cuts as farmers, regions defend funding
description:
European Union leaders began two days of budget talks in Brussels on Thursday, with national governments disputing how much to spend and whether to shift money from farm subsidies and poorer regions to defence and competitiveness. European Council President António Costa’s revised 2028-2034 plan cuts €204 billion from the European Commission’s original proposal, bringing the proposed budget to about €1.582 trillion; roughly €740 billion would support farmers and poorer regions. The negotiations also cover a proposed €45 billion Ukraine loan, which German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants all 27 member states to support as a condition for a wider budget deal.

Net contributors including Germany want a smaller overall package, while the 17-member Friends of Cohesion group opposes further cuts to regional funding. France is pressing to preserve farm income support, while Greece has said it will not accept further cuts to cohesion and Common Agricultural Policy funding. Costa’s proposal would raise new EU revenue, including through a digital tax, but new revenue sources require unanimous approval.

Leaders are expected to use the Brussels meeting to clarify positions rather than settle the budget. A final deal requires unanimity, and a further summit is scheduled for Dec. 17-18; France has warned that negotiations should not run beyond December, ahead of elections in 2027.

title: South Korea raises key rate to 3.25% as AI exports lift outlook
description:
South Korea’s central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.25% on Thursday, its third increase since July and the highest level in two years, as inflation remained above target and strong semiconductor exports prompted higher growth forecasts. The Bank of Korea lifted its 2026 growth estimate to 3.9% from 3.3% and its 2027 forecast to 4.1% from 2.9%, citing robust demand for AI-related chips.

Consumer prices rose 2.8% in October, compared with the central bank’s 2% target. The bank said higher energy costs and strengthening demand could keep inflation above target for a considerable time. It also warned that rising property prices and household borrowing pose risks to financial stability, while consumer spending remains constrained by prices, stagnant wages and debt payments.

The decision followed rate increases in July and August and a pause in October. Five of seven policy-board members backed the move, while two favored holding rates at 3%; the bank’s next scheduled meeting is Jan. 14.

title: Economists warn AI spending bust could slow U.S. growth
description:
Economists warn that a sharp pullback in artificial-intelligence spending could weaken U.S. growth. AI investment accounted for an estimated 25% of economic growth over the past year, according to Barclays. Recent stock-market swings and turmoil at Nvidia have drawn attention to the risk, but the warnings concern a potential downturn, not a sector collapse already underway.

A fall in AI-linked shares could curb spending by households whose wealth is increasingly tied to stocks, while cancelled data-center projects could hit construction and suppliers. Economists disagree on whether that would cause a U.S. recession. They also point to less room for a federal response than before the 2008 financial crisis, with public debt now above 100% of GDP, compared with about 35% then.

title: AI may not be a bubble. But the way we’re financing it might be
description:
Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. On November 23, the semiconductor giant reinstated its cofounder as president and CEO, less than two weeks after his abrupt resignation threw the company into a leadership crisis.

Investors may be relieved to have Huang back. But the events of the past two weeks have shown just how much Nvidia—and the wider AI industry—still depends on one man. The board said it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before reinstating Huang and concluded that his return posed no national security risk. Its investigation remains open, however, and Nvidia has announced additional measures to address national security and compliance concerns.

Huang’s departure also raised questions about Nvidia’s maturity as a corporate institution. In an analysis published shortly after Huang’s resignation, Andy Thurai, founder and principal analyst at The Field CTO, pointed to companies like Apple and IBM that spend years preparing their next generation of leaders. “That separates a mature corporate entity from a founder-led juggernaut,” he wrote. Huang is back, but Nvidia still needs to prepare for a future without him.

Meanwhile, another major artificial intelligence company was making history on Wall Street. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, went public on November 19, pricing its shares at $83 in one of the largest initial public offerings in history. At that price, every one of an estimated 96% of the company’s employees held equity worth more than $1 million, according to data from Hill.com reported by CNN.

The stock opened at $111.50 before closing its first trading day at $97.17. Investors who bought at the IPO price made money, but those who bought when trading opened were already sitting on losses.

Both developments come at a pivotal moment for the AI industry. Billions of dollars continue to pour into the sector, but how much money are the companies receiving those investments actually making? And how long will investors be willing to wait?

Judah Taub, managing partner at Hetz Ventures, thinks investors need to separate their excitement about AI from their assessment of the businesses behind it.

“AI isn’t a bubble. But the way we’re financing AI might be,” he tells Fast Company. “The internet wasn’t a bubble, but many internet companies were. AI will be exactly the same.”

AI could transform entire industries and create enormous economic value. But there’s no guarantee that the companies spending billions to make that transformation possible will benefit most from it. Much of that value could instead go to businesses that find the most profitable ways to use the technology.

THE MONEY BEHIND THE AI BOOM

Anthropic’s IPO illustrates the extraordinary sums flowing into the AI industry. The company closed the offering on November 20, raising approximately $93.5 billion, including proceeds from shares sold by existing shareholders. Of that, $91.6 billion went to Anthropic before fees and expenses. The company also secured a separate $26 billion investment from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, and an affiliate of TSMC, the Taiwan-based chipmaker.

Notably, several of those investors also supply the computing power and infrastructure Anthropic needs to operate. AI developers need vast amounts of computing power, while chipmakers and cloud providers need customers willing to pay for it. Both sides benefit. But if a supplier gives its customer the money to buy its products, how do investors know how much of that demand would have existed otherwise?

Such circular financing deals linking AI developers, chipmakers, and infrastructure providers have become increasingly common among the industry’s biggest players.

“Nvidia has been selling the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush,” Taub says. “But when the shovel manufacturer starts financing the gold miners, investors should ask whether they’re measuring demand for shovels or demand for financing.”

Isabelle O’Keeffe, a London-based deep tech investor, worries that the infrastructure buildout could outpace demand for AI products.

“The circular financing works as long as real customer demand is pulling it through,” she says. “The risk is when the infrastructure gets built faster than end customers are paying for it.”

That could leave cloud providers servicing debt on underused data centers and model developers struggling to meet their spending commitments. Anthropic’s IPO filings detail approximately $900.9 billion in compute and related commitments extending over many years. Though some arrangements are conditional and the money isn’t due all at once, the figure illustrates how much future demand the company is betting on.

In a recent analysis for Fast Company, Mark Sullivan showed how Anthropic is pursuing more efficient computing techniques and developing infrastructure that could reduce its dependence on outside cloud providers. The company also needs to attract more customers, expand beyond its strength in coding, and find profitable ways to serve users as its models become more sophisticated—all of which could become increasingly difficult if competitors offer similar capabilities at lower prices.

Complicating matters is that some of Anthropic’s competitors also control much of the infrastructure it needs to grow. “The hyperscalers sit on both ends of Anthropic’s supply chain: They control the route to market, and they ration the physical compute required to serve it,” Thurai wrote in his analysis of the company’s IPO filing.

“The revenue growth is real, but so are the costs,” O’Keeffe says.

She isn’t particularly alarmed by Anthropic’s first day on Wall Street, interpreting the stock’s retreat from its opening price as a sign that investors are becoming more discerning.

“I’d read it as selectivity, not rejection,” she says.

For other AI companies considering an IPO, O’Keeffe believes the lesson is to price their stock sensibly, demonstrate improving margins, and avoid relying on overly optimistic revenue projections to justify their valuations.

Now that Anthropic is public, investors will gain regular insight into the financial performance of one of the world’s leading AI developers. Other AI companies looking to raise money may find their prospects increasingly tied to Anthropic’s performance.

THE BILL IS COMING DUE

Investors aren’t the only ones scrutinizing AI spending. So are the businesses buying the technology.

Kevin Kiley, CEO of the enterprise AI management company Airia, says businesses are changing how they evaluate the technology. A year or two ago, executives faced pressure from boards and investors to adopt AI more quickly. Some companies celebrated employee usage figures without assessing whether the tools actually improved their work. Many bought AI tools before figuring out what they needed them for or how much money they could save.

“The bills are coming in, and executives are asking more pointed questions,” Kiley says. “Are we improving productivity? Are we reducing operating costs and risk? How is this investment contributing to revenue and the bottom line? The focus is shifting from input to output.”

Businesses are becoming more selective about the applications they fund, and executives want to understand which departments are consuming AI resources and what they’re getting in return. The difficulty is that measuring AI returns remains a challenge. Employee usage can increase even as savings or productivity gains remain elusive.

Kiley says some companies are spending more on AI even as models become cheaper to use. As organizations expand their deployments, AI agents take on more work, call additional services, and process more information. What looks like a simple request to an employee could involve dozens of separate model calls, each potentially incurring a cost.

Some of that expense could be avoided. Kiley notes that organizations frequently use powerful, expensive models for routine tasks that smaller systems could handle. Airia’s internal data suggests that 89% of common enterprise AI tasks don’t require the capabilities of frontier models, though that estimate hasn’t been independently verified.

The company has also encountered agents that process more information than necessary, repeatedly call external tools, or get stuck performing the same actions. For an enterprise with thousands of employees using AI daily, even small amounts of unnecessary computing can quickly become expensive.

Airia says its testing has produced cost reductions exceeding 50% through better model selection and workflow design, without sacrificing quality. Actual savings will vary by workload. But identifying those opportunities requires companies to understand where their AI spending goes—something Kiley believes many organizations still struggle with.

“Making a model 20% smarter doesn’t necessarily make an employee 20% more productive,” he tells Fast Company.

This could become a problem for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. If smaller, cheaper models can perform a growing share of everyday business tasks, how much more will customers be willing to pay for each new generation of frontier models?

Companies that help businesses deploy, manage, and integrate AI could capture more of the economic value. Airia operates in that market, so Kiley has a commercial interest in that outcome. He also expects demand for AI governance, security, and cost management to grow.

“I expect a more selective but healthier market, where organizations focus their resources on AI applications delivering measurable returns and scale back those that aren’t.”

WHO GETS THE VALUE?

Some of the biggest winners of the AI boom may turn out to be companies that have no intention of selling AI software.

Michael Heltzen, CEO of the biotechnology company eXoZymes, sees opportunities in pharmaceuticals, materials, energy, and manufacturing, where AI could help develop products that are difficult or expensive to produce through conventional methods.

“There’s a fundamental difference between generating financial activity and excitement around future potential, including hype-driven sales, and creating genuine, lasting economic value for shareholders,” he says. “The AI industry is doing plenty of the former. Now it needs to prove the latter.”

His company combines AI with laboratory experimentation to develop enzymes for manufacturing valuable molecules. While its commercial ambitions still need to be judged against measurable results, the approach illustrates how businesses could use AI to create entirely new products rather than simply making existing operations more efficient.

“Our measure of value is simple,” Heltzen says. “Can we make something highly valuable that only we can make?”

Taub at Hetz Ventures argues that investors would benefit from distinguishing between three markets within the AI economy: compute, or spending on the infrastructure needed to develop and operate AI; intelligence, or what customers will pay to use AI models; and outcomes, or the economic value created when AI performs useful work.

“These markets are connected, but they are not interchangeable,” he says.

Consider a data center that generates billions of dollars in equipment sales and construction spending before anyone knows whether its computing capacity will generate enough revenue to justify the investment. Equipment suppliers may have already made money, while the data center operator still has years of expenses to recover. Further down the chain, the companies paying for that computing power have their own investments to justify.

For Matt Calkins, CEO of the AI automation company Appian, creating more value from AI will require making the technology dependable enough for businesses to use in their most important operations.

“The top job of the AI industry today is not to drive blockbuster IPOs but to do the hard work of making AI useful in the biggest organizations for the biggest jobs. The AI value proposition isn’t complete. We need to focus more on safety and reliability,” he says in written commentary.

A tool that saves employees hours of work during a demonstration may prove less economical once the costs of checking its output, correcting mistakes, and maintaining the system are factored in. We’re already seeing a version of this with AI-generated software. Developers can produce code faster than before, but companies still need people and systems to maintain it, investigate failures, and keep applications running.

And even if AI companies get pricing and reliability right, they still need to build products people want.

During a conversation at Dubai Future Week last week, Pat Pataranutaporn, an assistant professor at MIT, described what he called “the bubble of people creating technology.”

He argued that AI developers can become disconnected from public concerns and the ways people experience their products. That presents a business risk, too. Companies could spend billions developing capabilities that impress researchers and investors but have limited appeal to the customers expected to pay for them.

WHAT A CORRECTION COULD CHANGE

A slowdown in AI funding could be good news for startups that have learned to do more with less computing power. Those struggling to retain customers or generate healthy margins, meanwhile, could find it increasingly difficult to raise money.

O’Keeffe, the deep tech investor, believes such a shift could benefit companies building applications on top of existing AI models.

“For the application layer, a reset would be healthy,” she says. “It clears out the me-too products and makes everyone focus on efficiency and real customer ROI.”

But there’s a potential downside. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous capital, often years before a company can expect meaningful returns. If investors become reluctant to finance those efforts, the advantage could shift further toward tech giants with the cash and infrastructure to fund research themselves.

Ironically, greater financial discipline could give the biggest technology companies even more control over the AI industry. Businesses might have thousands of AI applications to choose from, yet many could depend on models developed by the same handful of companies.

Still, history offers some reassurance that a financial correction need not spell disaster for AI itself. Taub points to railroads, electricity, and the internet, each of which attracted extraordinary investment. Many of the businesses financing those technologies failed or disappointed their shareholders, but the infrastructure they built supported economic activity long afterward.

AI may produce a similar outcome, creating opportunities for businesses that don’t even exist today while leaving some early investors with substantial losses.

“We should be careful not to confuse a correction in AI valuations with a correction in AI’s potential,” Taub warns.

Huang’s return may restore some confidence in Nvidia’s leadership, and Anthropic’s IPO has provided the company with a huge infusion of capital. Over the coming quarters, Anthropic’s earnings, the performance of infrastructure investments, and the AI contracts businesses choose to renew could tell us much more about where the industry is headed.

For much of the boom, the industry has measured its ambition in chips purchased, data centers announced, and billions raised. The challenge now is turning those investments into enough paying customers, useful work, and profits to sustain the businesses behind them.

Some of the companies spending the most today may discover that they financed the future without securing much of its rewards.

title: Why Does the Same Floor Plan Get Drawn So Many Times?
description: A floor plan arrives as a PDF. It shows the existing layout of a small store slated for renovation, and the client has sent it over the day before the first meeting. Before anyone can begin sketching a proposal, someone has to redraw the plan, line by line, in CAD. Once the ideas begin to take shape, the same space is modeled again in another program, this time in 3D, to produce images and renderings. The furniture list goes into a spreadsheet, the presentation comes together in a third program, and the client's comments arrive by email, text, and voice message, often with screenshots marked up in red, several steps removed from the drawing they refer to. If a wall moves after that, someone has to make the same change in each file.

title: Loud Clattering/Clicking,
description:
Hello,

This is the response from Bambu Lab Support.

Dear Customer,

Thank you for your reply.

We’ve reviewed your video, and there’s nothing obviously abnormal during the manual movement. The sound isn’t coming from the idler pulley.

The sound you hear while printing is most likely caused by the toolhead starting and stopping quickly over short distances, which produces a mechanical sound as the motion absorbs the impact. This is normal and won’t affect the printer’s performance.

Because the H3C prints with higher speed and acceleration than our other models, this sound tends to be more noticeable on the H3C.

If the sound bothers you and you’d like to reduce it, there are two things you can try: 1. Turn on Silent Mode. You can switch it on directly in “Settings” on the printer’s screen, and it can effectively reduce operating noise. 2. Adjust the slicer settings. In your slicer (such as Bambu Studio), lower the maximum acceleration a little, then re-slice and print again. This can also noticeably reduce the sound.

If you still have any issues after making these adjustments, please don’t hesitate to contact us.

Best regards,
Bambu Lab Customer Support

The support team’s response isn’t entirely satisfactory, but it makes sense. The print quality is good. The only real downside: Compared to the H2C, it’s significantly louder.

title: Colombia withdraws from joining the BRICS bank and will seek other sources of financing
description:
The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that it would not continue the process of Colombia joining the BRICS group or the New Development Bank (NDB), the bloc’s financial institution. The Foreign Ministry said it would seek resources and technical assistance from other multilateral organizations for the priorities of the 2026–2030 National Development Plan, but did not explain the reasons for the decision.

Former president Gustavo Petro initiated the process in 2025 to access financing for, among other areas, infrastructure, renewable energy, and health. Although the bank approved the application, accession required a law passed by the Colombian Congress; the bill introduced in November 2025 never came to a vote. The government said it would continue working with other international partners and reiterated its commitment to multilateralism.
