title: Spain election puts banks, utilities and EU policy at stake
description:
Spain’s Nov. 29 election could shift the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy toward a more conservative policy agenda, with banks and utilities among the sectors investors are watching. The conservative People’s Party (PP), led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, is expected to need support from the far-right Vox party to govern, while Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is seeking another term.

The result could affect proposed corporate tax cuts, the banking levy and regulation of utilities, although analysts cited by Reuters expect Spain’s public finances to remain broadly stable under either outcome. Spain’s economy grew 2.6% last year, twice the eurozone average, and its 10-year bond spread over German debt was 60 basis points, compared with 150 for French debt.

A change of government would replace one of only three social-democratic leaders among the 27 national leaders attending European Union (EU) summits, according to reporting by Sweden’s public broadcaster. Polls close Sunday at 8 p.m. local time, with official results expected to begin appearing at 9 p.m.; the newly elected chambers are scheduled to convene on Dec. 23.

description: In the center of Bucharest, about a kilometer and a half from the Old Town, stands the world's heaviest building. The Palace of Parliament, the seat of Romania's legislature, occupies Dealul Arsenalului, a hill at the western end of Bulevardul Unirii. This straight avenue crosses the city centre from east to west for roughly three kilometers, passing through Piața Unirii, before ending in front of the palace's main façade, which rises 84 metres in stepped tiers of stone.

title: French drug regulator warns of eight AI-linked medication errors
description:
France’s National Agency for the Safety of Medicines (ANSM) warned on Nov. 25 that artificial-intelligence advice about medicines can lead to harmful dosing and treatment errors, after eight cases were reported in France between 2024 and 2026. One person was hospitalized, and the agency said cases may be underreported.

The reports included overdoses and incorrect translations of medicine names in medical documents that led to the wrong drug being dispensed. ANSM deputy director Alexandre de La Volpilière urged patients not to change or stop prescribed treatment based solely on an AI response and to consult a health professional.

title: Shanghai leaders back probe of party chief Chen Jining before 2027 reshuffle
description:
Shanghai’s senior Communist Party leaders publicly backed the central investigation into party chief Chen Jining at a meeting late on Nov. 24, the day authorities announced the probe into suspected “severe violations of discipline and laws.” Officials have not specified the allegations, and Chen remains a member of the Politburo during the investigation.

Chen, 62, is the fourth member of the 24-member Politburo selected in 2022 to face investigation since 2025. The earlier cases involved former military leaders He Weidong and Zhang Youxia and former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, all of whom were expelled. Chen rose from academic posts at Tsinghua University to environment minister, Beijing mayor and Shanghai party secretary, a job often held by officials later promoted to national leadership.

title: November supermoon coincided with record California tides, flooding waterfronts
description:
The Nov. 24 Beaver supermoon coincided with record-high tides along parts of California’s coast, where flooding affected low-lying waterfront communities in the San Francisco Bay Area and heavy surf destroyed a popular pier. The moon was full near its closest point to Earth in its monthly orbit, adding to the gravitational effects that produce higher high tides and lower low tides when the sun, Earth and moon align.

When a full moon’s alignment with the sun and Earth occurs near lunar perigee, spring tides can be amplified; these tides are often called king tides. The report links the coastal impacts to the timing of the lunar event but does not identify the pier or give a flooding total.

WRAL lists two International Space Station (ISS) viewing opportunities: a pass on Nov. 29 from about 6:55 to 6:58 p.m., and a longer pass on Nov. 30 beginning around 6:05 p.m.. During the later pass, the station is expected to remain visible for about six minutes as it travels from northwest to southeast.

title: US tariff proposal targets imports but shields energy, food and chips
description:
The Trump administration’s proposed import duties could raise costs for businesses bringing covered goods into the United States, while exemptions and existing trade deals would limit the impact across products and trading partners. The proposal follows a U.S. investigation into alleged industrial overcapacity and would generally replace duties imposed in July rather than add to them. China is the exception, with a proposed 20% tariff added to existing duties.

The administration says the targeted levies would protect U.S. manufacturers from subsidized foreign production. Economists warn that businesses may pass higher import costs on to consumers. The proposal exempts energy, some foods that cannot be grown domestically, certain semiconductor chips and pharmaceuticals. The new duties would not apply on top of existing sector-specific duties, including those on autos, steel and aluminum.

The duties are not final. Written comments are due by Jan. 5, 2027, and hearings are scheduled to begin Jan. 25. The U.S. Trade Representative’s office has not set an implementation date.

title: Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant switches to diesel after grid line cut
description:
A Russian attack knocked out the 330-kilovolt Ferrosplavna-1 line at 4:28 a.m. on Nov. 25, cutting external power to the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant and leaving its essential systems reliant on backup diesel generators, Ukraine’s state nuclear operator Energoatom said. The line was cut after an attack on the right bank of the Dnipro River, about 13 kilometers from the Ferrosplavna substation.

The International Atomic Energy Agency said it was the plant’s 28th loss of all external power since Russia’s full-scale invasion began; Ukraine’s energy ministry counted it as the 17th such outage this year. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said agency experts at the plant were investigating where and why the line disconnected. Energoatom warned that repeated damage near the facility increases the risk of a nuclear accident.

title: Neolithic tomb pots point to fermented milk offerings in Denmark
description:
Researchers studying 330 Neolithic pots from western Zealand, Denmark, found corrosion on 31; 29 came from passage tombs. In experiments with reconstructed vessels, fresh, unpasteurized milk produced damage resembling the marks on ancient pottery, while beer and mead did not. The findings, published in Antiquity, suggest fermented dairy may have been placed with the dead, although corrosion alone cannot identify the contents with certainty.

The results challenge an earlier interpretation that the corroded pots held beer, an idea based partly on evidence from brewing communities elsewhere. Fermentation makes milk more acidic, and the researchers say fermented dairy products could also have been easier to digest and lasted longer. Lead author Lone Claudi-Hansen, an archaeologist, said she hopes to examine pottery from other parts of Denmark to see whether the same pattern appears elsewhere.

title: Exercise linked to measurable gains across stroke, heart and lung care
description:
Exercise-based rehabilitation was associated with better quality of life after stroke or transient ischemic attack, greater exercise capacity in heart failure, and measurable changes in small-airway function in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), according to a systematic review, a clinical review and a 62-person study. The evidence differs by condition: the stroke analysis pooled 38 randomized trials, while the COPD study followed participants through a 12-week program combining aerobic and strength exercises.

The COPD researchers found clearer changes with impulse oscillometry than with standard spirometry. The heart-failure review said evidence supports fewer short-term hospital admissions from all causes, but effects on heart-failure admissions and mortality remain uncertain. The review also reports that 2026 European Society of Cardiology guidelines recommend cardiac rehabilitation for chronic heart failure with either preserved or reduced ejection fraction.

title: California king tides flood coastal homes as warming raises water levels
description:
Unusually warm Pacific waters and a strong El Niño raised coastal water levels as November king tides flooded California homes and streets, damaged seawalls and contributed to the collapse of part of Pacifica’s pier. Los Angeles, Santa Barbara and La Jolla set or matched tide records, while floodwaters in Pacifica overwhelmed pumps despite sandbags and other preparations.

Ocean warming expands seawater, while human-caused sea-level rise raises the starting point for each tide. In San Francisco, sea level rose about 9.7 inches from 1900 to 2025, with 6.1 inches attributed to human-caused warming, Yale Climate Connections reported.

California officials and coastal researchers warned that temporary barriers cannot manage repeated flooding as sea levels continue to rise. Another Pacific storm could bring heavy rain and strong winds to central California around Dec. 1, and forecasters expect further king tides in December and January.

title: Scandinavian study finds no increased developmental risk from prenatal ADHD drugs
description:
A study of more than 3.6 million children born in Denmark, Norway and Sweden found no increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders associated with mothers’ use of ADHD medication during pregnancy. Researchers tracked the children for about a decade; 7,595 had prenatal exposure, including 2,389 exposed in the second or third trimester.

The researchers said the findings do not support stopping medication solely over concerns about children’s future neurodevelopment, but stressed that treatment decisions should be made individually with a health professional. The study was observational. The authors said unmeasured factors, such as maternal ADHD severity and genetics, and the relatively small exposed group limit conclusions about some specific conditions.

title: Are AI companies ‘glosslighting’ you with misleading jargon? This report says yes
description:
Ever describe an AI agent’s error as a “hallucination”? Fret over the threat of “superintelligence”? How about call an AI assistant your “co-pilot”? Beware: you may have been glosslit by the AI industry.

“Glosslighting” combines “glossary” and “gaslighting.” It’s for situations where industries develop lingo that intentionally misleads consumers to shape public perception—something that researchers at Simon Fraser University think the AI industry is doing in spades.

Every industry has its own specialized vocab, and there’s nothing inherently wrong with insider lingo. But with an industry like AI, where development is hotly debated and potential controversy lies around every corner, word choice around the industry takes on extra weight.

What is glosslighting?

For the study, researchers analyzed 30 of the AI industry’s biggest buzzwords, breaking down the ways that common language around the technology can control public opinion.

The study’s authors emphasize that while AI terms have been looked at in isolation, they’re more interested in AI’s “interlocking vocabulary” and the way it protects AI companies from taking accountability for the dark sides of their technology. 

“Behind the language of seamless intelligence are workers who classify traumatic content for low wages, communities whose water is consumed by server farms, and individuals whose lives are determined by probabilistic decision tools sometimes named, reassuringly, as ‘solutions,'” the authors write.

How AI jargon causes harm

The study’s authors group the terms by the way they cause harm, the truth about AI they obscure, and the questions they deflect. Those groupings include the following:

  • “Hallucination,” “co-pilot,” “robot rights,” and “agentic AI” humanize the technology, diverting attention from the people and companies making the decisions around them
  • “The cloud,” “data mining,” “scaling,” and “human-in-the-loop” hide the environmental and social costs of AI development
  • “Superintelligence,” “frontier AI,” “AGI,” “existential risk,” “smart city,” “AI superpower,” and “race to AI” shift focus to the future of AI, limiting attention on present-day concerns
  • “Democratizing AI,” “open AI,” “responsible AI,” “ethical AI,” “collaborative AI,” and “human-centric AI” let AI companies frame themselves as trustworthy
  • “Bias,” “ex-ante risk regulation,” “deep learning,” and “data subjects” paint some problems as technological or too complex for laymen to understand, shutting down debates about their usage before they begin

The study’s authors go on to recommend alternatives for many of these terms that either simplify communication, demystify confusing terms, or go more in-depth to provide greater accuracy to AI’s impact.

One author, assistant professor of computing science Nicholas Vincent, told Tech Xplore that “issues where there’s real complexity mean there’s a responsibility to do more to help people understand.”

“Everyone exposed to AI deserves accurate descriptions of what it is and how it’s used,” Vincent said. “As consumers get a little bit pickier, there’s going to be more demand for specifics. That is, ‘If you want me to buy your expensive AI product, you better have a pretty clear sales pitch for what it actually is.’”

title: Senate panel adds privacy safeguards to Canada’s lawful-access bill
description:
A Canadian Senate committee has amended the Liberal government’s lawful-access bill, Bill C-22, which would require electronic service providers to help police and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service obtain information for investigations. Senators say the changes clarify protections against cybersecurity risks, but the bill would still require providers to retain metadata for up to six months.

The committee’s amendments include a process for seeking technical advice on whether ministerial directives could create security vulnerabilities. Senators will vote on the amended bill. If approved, it returns to the House of Commons, where MPs can accept, reject or change the Senate’s version.

title: U.S.-backed consortium agrees to acquire Lukoil’s foreign energy network
description:
A U.S.-led consortium agreed to acquire Lukoil’s non-Russian energy business, including oil and gas fields and three European refineries, under a deal announced Nov. 25. The portfolio’s oil and gas operations produce about 350,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day, and its refineries have a combined capacity of roughly 350,000 barrels a day.

The consortium, led by Eldridge and including the U.S. International Development Finance Corp. (DFC), agreed to acquire Lukoil International through a restricted-share swap rather than a direct cash payment to Russia. The deal still needs approval from the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Eldridge said the assets would be separated from Lukoil’s Russian parent when the transaction closes.

Eldridge said the consortium would prioritize stabilizing operations and restoring full refinery capacity, while Todd Boehly said closing could take up to a year. The Romanian Petrotel refinery restarted on Nov. 23 after more than a year offline.

title: U.S. access curbs spur resale offers for thousands of Nvidia AI chips
description:
Sellers are seeking buyers for an unusually large volume of Nvidia graphics processors after new U.S. rules restricted Chinese companies’ remote access to advanced AI computing in overseas data centers. Offers include thousands of B300 chips, but no completed transactions were reported. The rule took effect Nov. 19 after the Commerce Department announced it on Nov. 16.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to the company after an 11-day absence as scrutiny of Chinese access to its chips continued. Lenders are also reassessing or delaying data-center financing in Southeast Asia, where facilities serve Chinese technology customers.

The reported resale offers involve hardware originally intended for data centers renting computing capacity to Chinese clients. Nvidia declined to comment on the offers, and the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to CNBC. Existing data-center services covered by the rule have a 90-day window to seek required licenses.

title: North Korean leader Kim expands tactical nuclear focus as Seoul vows deterrence
description:
South Korea’s Defense Ministry said its military would strengthen deterrence through consultations with the United States and improve its response to nuclear threats after North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for wider use of tactical weapons. Seoul also urged Pyongyang to stop justifying its nuclear development and comply with U.N. Security Council resolutions.

Kim made the remarks during a Nov. 25 tour of nuclear-material and weapons-research facilities, including a nuclear-powered equipment production base whose location state media did not disclose. He said North Korea was systematically expanding nuclear-material output and should use tactical weapons for different missions across multiple domains, citing the border with South Korea.

Analysts cited by The Straits Times said the equipment base may be producing submarine reactors and parts, potentially for a nuclear-powered submarine planned for 2027. South Korean experts said Kim’s position appeared aimed at making future U.S.-North Korea talks focus on arms control between nuclear-armed states rather than denuclearization.

title: Colombian police put the number of hostages in Cartagena at 76
description:
Colombian police reported that 76 people were held during the assault on a supermarket in Cartagena, more than double the roughly 30 mentioned initially. All were freed after a 17-hour hostage standoff in which one kidnapper was killed. The incident began when armed men took refuge in the Éxito store and took customers and employees hostage after unsuccessfully attempting to rob an armored cash-in-transit vehicle. Ten people had left before special forces entered.

Carlos Tapia, one of the hostages, said the men drank whisky and beer and played music, and that they beat and tied up some of those held. Retired Colonel Gustavo Camargo, a crisis negotiation expert who advised those handling the emergency, said keeping the talks open allowed them to gain time as long as no one was injured.

The identity of the man killed during the operation remained unclear: the family of Jailer Humberto Muñetón Zapata, a missing shopkeeper, said he had gone to the supermarket to shop and denied that he was one of the kidnappers.

title: 1Password Security Breach: What Was Accessed and What Wasn't
description:
Popular password management app 1Password today said it experienced a security breach earlier this month. 1Password says some customer names and email addresses were accessed, but no customer vault contents were compromised.


On November 19, 1Password saw indications that an employee's GitHub account had been breached and began investigating. The company says the breached GitHub account was used to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, with the code downloading some customer data. Here's a list of what the hacker was able to get:

  • Names and email addresses customers use to sign into 1Password

  • Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

  • Public keys

  • Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (1Password says this can't be used for account access)

  • Tokens in emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery

  • Other non-secret account data related to 1Password's internal architecture, like version numeric identifiers and file numeric identifiers

  • 1Password source code, which 1Password says does not include customer data or user secrets

  • Access to 1Password's CI/CD system, which it says has infrastructure-related secrets for the service to work


According to 1Password, there is no impact to its services, availability, or product security. Customer vaults and the items in them were not accessed, nor were the keys that protect vaults. The hacker did not have access to account recovery keys or 1Password apps and browser extensions. 1Password vaults are encrypted and protected by keys on the user end, so content is not accessible to 1Password or anyone who hacks the 1Password servers.

The biggest risk comes from the token breach. Tokens can be used for account recovery, but they only work when paired with an SSO sign-in or a six-digit code sent to a user's email address. Codes have now been changed from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them more difficult to brute force.

The affected GitHub account has been disabled, and the attacker's token was revoked. Internal credentials that may have been exposed have been revoked. Internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls have been "tightened," with new detection methods for similar attacks. The company found no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using the exposed account provisioning tokens, and it has hired independent cybersecurity experts to validate its response.

1Password users who had a token accessed were notified, but it is unclear if 1Password has sent notices about the breach to all users. While the blog post is titled as "update on" a security incident, it does not seem that the breach was disclosed when 1Password first learned of it six days ago.

1Password will not contact users to ask for an account password or Secret Key, and the information should be entered only in the official 1Password app or official website. It recommends all users be cautious about phishing attempts like emails, texts, and calls that mention 1Password or account recovery.

Users do not need to update or change anything in their 1Password accounts.
Tag: 1Password

title: Trump renovation account receives unexplained $300 million deposit
description:
A National Park Service account President Donald Trump has used for Washington renovation projects received about $300 million from an undisclosed source in September. Government records do not identify the donor or the project the money will fund. The White House declined to answer questions about the deposit, which raised concerns about whether donors might seek benefits from the administration.

The account, originally set up to collect donations for national parks, has taken in about $790 million since Trump returned to office, compared with annual receipts of less than $100 million before his second term, according to government records. The administration has used it for projects including a White House ballroom and work at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool; the New York Times estimates the broader building program will cost more than $1 billion. Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January say they will try to stop taxpayer funding for the projects.

title: Signal adds default screen protections to limit AI access to chats
description:
Signal has introduced default protections to prevent AI assistants from capturing conversations displayed in its messaging app, after tests found Meta’s Muse agent could read Signal messages using device permissions without connecting directly to the app. The tests found Muse used notification access on Android and accessibility and screenshot capabilities on macOS; they did not reproduce the behavior on iPhone. The issue does not involve breaking Signal’s encryption: agents can access content after a device decrypts it for display.

Signal’s screen protections do not block every form of access, including access to files already stored on a device. Apple is revising macOS permission controls to give users more specific choices. Separately, South Korea’s privacy and science ministries are preparing guidance on AI agents, and Anthropic has opened a beta monitoring system designed to detect misuse while keeping conversation data in customer-controlled cloud storage.

title: Investigators suspect AI tool in breach of three US spy agencies
description:
U.S. investigators suspect hackers used Artex, an AI-enabled penetration-testing framework, to breach an unclassified intelligence-analysis system used by the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA). Early indicators point to China, but no attacker has been publicly identified. The network processes open-source intelligence, and officials have said classified information was not compromised.

The network combines publicly available material with commercially sourced datasets, social-media content and satellite imagery. Investigators have not specified what records were accessed or when the breach occurred. An ODNI official said critical capabilities and classified systems were not disrupted, and a person familiar with the incident told The Associated Press the issue had been resolved.

Separately, the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. The agency took some systems offline as a precaution, directed banks to use its Financial Institutions Hotline for reports, and said the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and outside forensic examiners were assessing the incident.

title: Fed survey finds cost pressures squeezing U.S. firms’ margins
description:
A Federal Reserve survey found that businesses across the United States faced persistent increases in energy, transportation, health care, insurance and tariff-related costs, while competition and price-sensitive customers limited their ability to pass those expenses on. The gap between rising input costs and selling prices is squeezing company margins, the Fed said in its Beige Book, based on interviews conducted through Nov. 16.

Conditions varied by region: eight of the Fed’s 12 districts reported slight to moderate growth in recent weeks, while four saw no change. The survey also described consumers shifting toward cheaper goods and cited a Michigan commercial-furniture seller whose customers increasingly sought lower-priced items.

Separately, the Commerce Department reported that October inflation, measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, was 3.8% year over year, with core inflation at 3.3%. Its revised estimate put third-quarter growth at a 4.3% annual rate. The Fed’s next policy meeting is scheduled for Dec. 8-9.

title: Phoronix compares Pop!_OS 26.04 and 24.04 performance
description:
Phoronix published a performance comparison of Pop!_OS 26.04 and 24.04, the latest and previous long-term-support versions of System76’s Ubuntu-based Linux distribution. The tests ran on a System76 Thelio Prime with an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor, 32GB of memory, a 1TB Samsung NVMe drive and an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 Ti graphics card.

Phoronix compared Pop!_OS 26.04 with a clean installation of Pop!_OS 24.04 that included all available updates. Both test systems ran Linux kernel 7.2, Nvidia driver 595.104.02 and the COSMIC 1.11 desktop. Pop!_OS 26.04 includes newer default system packages, including GCC 15.2 instead of 13.2 and Python 3.14 instead of 3.12. Phoronix said it was still preparing a separate comparison with other Linux distributions.

title: Health Canada warns Ozempic users of very rare vision-loss risk
description:
Health Canada warned Wednesday that semaglutide, the ingredient in Ozempic, Wegovy and other prescription drugs, may carry a “very rare” risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), which can cause sudden, permanent vision loss. The department is working with manufacturers to add the risk to Canadian product information and is assessing whether other drugs in the GLP-1 class carry a similar risk.

People taking semaglutide should seek urgent medical attention for sudden or rapidly worsening vision changes; Health Canada says to stop the drug if NAION is confirmed. The regulator reviewed 23 reported cases and 10 scientific studies, but the reason for any link remains unclear.

title: The most dangerous election disinformation campaigns
description:
You scrolled through your feed, and a video clip of a candidate’s speech popped up. It doesn’t matter who you planned to vote for, the video struck an emotional—and negative—response. The clip was not AI-generated; the candidate really uttered the words you found upsetting. But the story the video told was fundamentally false. That was the 2026 midterms.

Candidates and their supporters spent a whopping $80 million to make AI-generated ads, as part of what AdImpact projected will be the most expensive election cycle on record. This is one attempt to capture eyeballs and sway voters. Another is through foreign interference. In just one example, researchers tracking a Russian influence operation recently found a fake video masquerading as a Mother Jones report that captured over 11 million views.

But disinformation is not stopping at deepfakes. Authentic videos that are repurposed and stripped of context represent a new frontier. I am not talking about a mere twisting of words. What we’re seeing is next level.

THE NEW LOOK OF DISINFORMATION

Think about the recent catastrophic flooding in Nepal and India. Some footage released within hours of the floods, intended to showcase the magnitude of the disaster, turned out to be from entirely different events. The footage was authentic. It just happened to be from a glacial flood in Alaska, a landslide in Japan, or a flood that occurred years before. These videos racked up millions of views. They also caused panic among friends and relatives trying to find information about their missing loved ones, and they potentially hindered rescue efforts by confusing the locations where help was needed.

Now, consider the same tactic applied in the political sphere—real speeches and words taken drastically out of context, coming from events that could have happened years earlier. 

One of the most notable examples involved Michigan’s recently elected Democratic Senator Abdul El-Sayed. In August, he was eviscerated by Republicans for apparently calling for Sharia law to take over in America. Social media went crazy. Was the clip real? Yes, it was from a speech he gave in 2022. But the meaning was quite different when you look at its entirety in context. So different that Politifact gave it a “pants on fire” rating for its meaning being distorted. 

In Georgia’s hotly contested Senate race, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff ran an ad of Republican Mike Collins urging Americans to get off Social Security and return to work. But that’s not exactly how it went down. The audio came from a broader conversation about tax policy, government revenue, and workforce participation. Collins was not saying retirees should get back into the workforce and lose their benefits (Politifact rated this one as “mostly false”).

In both cases, the recordings were authentic. The misleading impressions came from stripping away the information necessary to understand what was being said, not from manipulating the original material. You may believe that this is just par for the course in a political campaign, but just because something is common does not make it safe, normal, or acceptable. 

THE IMPORTANCE OF CONTEXTUAL UNDERSTANDING

This tactic is becoming effective for two main reasons. Video is now our most prominent data source. Everything is recorded, so if someone is looking for a soundbite to make someone look bad, there is plenty of material available, if they’re willing to dig for it. The second issue is more technical. Deepfake detectors look for signs of manipulation. Authentic videos pass that test. Determining whether a clip is deliberately misleading requires a new set of inquiries, identifying when and where the video took place, what was happening around it, and what the broader context revealed.

Making such determinations traditionally has taken a lot of people a lot of time to dig through archives. Even with the deep war chests candidates possess, they’re not going to devote the human resources needed to debunk every false video, at least not in time for that work to make a dent in the video’s impact. So, campaigns take hits, and candidates can spend considerable time and energy trying to explain past comments and rebuild trust. 

WHAT’S THE FIX?

In 2026, voters and media companies are learning that two things can simultaneously be true: A clip can be legitimate while what it depicts is inaccurate. 

Voters are overwhelmed with election messages. Expecting them to research every clip they see is highly unlikely. Candidates and their backers count on this. Media companies and social platforms bear a greater responsibility, however. Fact-checking and moderation capabilities are essential to reduce the rapid spread of disinformation. Interestingly, while generative AI can be used to create convincing fakes, a different application of AI can be a powerful tool for identifying misleading content and stopping its spread.

As good as AI is getting at generating realistic videos, it’s also getting good at understanding them. Solutions that can read a video and its contextual clues can be indispensable in determining whether an authentic video is being misrepresented online. Imagine an instant army of agent fact-checkers. When AI understands video the way a human does, it recognizes not only what is said and who’s speaking, but what else is on the screen and what the setting looks like. It can also search massive archives to see if that moment has appeared anywhere else. And, at the agent layer, tech can flag suspicious content, assembling supporting evidence and escalating cases to human reviewers in minutes.

The technology that helps media companies and platforms find original footage, restore full context, and flag misleading claims will enable a faster response, not just to political ads but any sort of controversial content that might catch fire. Stopping the spread of disinformation is a perpetual problem. Thankfully, we are now building intelligent tools that can help.

Jae Lee is CEO and cofounder of TwelveLabs.

title: Inverting process dynamics in knowledge production
description:
Boozhoo News River Readers,

Today’s edition of the news features an article about lived experience, relationality and community in the process of knowledge generation. It reminds me of one of our most popular stories our readers clicked from last month on indigenous jurisprudence. Together they might make a great pair to contemplate  with a warm cup of tea.  

Here’s the rest of this weeks news…

In the age of AI, Indigenous ways of knowing remind us why lived experience matters

The Big Picture: Universities, long entrusted with teaching, research and knowledge production, are confronting one of their most significant challenges: The rising use of artificial intelligence. As UNESCO has acknowledged, generative AI raises questions about the importance of human participation in knowledge production. For universities, these developments invite an uncomfortable question: If AI can produce knowledge more efficiently, what makes human contributions to knowledge production valuable?

Why lived experience matters: Knowledge is not necessarily confined to information that can be collected, analyzed and reproduced. It can also emerge from the meanings people develop through participation in the world. This distinction is especially important when considering Onkwehón:we (Indigenous) understandings of knowledge.

Indigenous ways of knowing: Although Onkwehón:we knowledge traditions are diverse, many emphasize that knowledge emerges through relationships among people, communities and the natural world. Onkwehón:we scholarship on relationality demonstrates how knowledge and relationships are inseparable from the people and communities in which they are developed.

Read the full article here. 

More curated reads

Utah Has a New Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives Database

A Native-led organization in Utah has unveiled a new database dedicated to Missing and Murdered Indigenous Relatives (MMIR). The database, dubbed Traces, was launched Monday by MMIR Utah, a nonprofit that advocates for MMIR victims and families. The group’s co-founder and executive director, Tammy Dee Platero (Diné), said Traces aims to be a balm against the lack of media attention Native victims receive, compared to non-Native victims. Platero, who co-founded MMIR Utah after the MMIR Task Force was disbanded in 2024, said the database was inspired by the movement for Indigenous data sovereignty and the OCAP framework — ownership, control, access and possession — created by the First Nations Governance Center to determine how data about Native people is collected and used. It’s by this model that the database allows families to submit information at their discretion, whether it be a full case entry or simply a photo of a loved one. And it remains private, accessible only to MMIR Utah staff, and information is shared with law enforcement only at a family’s request.

To do better research with Indigenous communities, share the driver’s seat

The partnership model IIF developed was a deliberate departure from how academic research typically works. Often, universities set the questions, communities provide access or data and outcomes circulate within institutions the communities rarely encounter. IIF inverted this. Community members developed their own future imaginaries, with IIF providing support and encouragement, and research questions were developed in response. That inversion took shape through four interconnected pillars: workshops that built technical capacity; residencies supporting artists’ deep engagement with the technology, along with commissions to help populate the future with Indigenous images; symposia and lecture series that circulated these methods more widely; and preservation of digital media artworks for future generations. 

UNBC researchers secure $800K to study potential impacts of proposed NeToo Hydropower Project

An extensive research project out of the University of Northern British Columbia (UNBC) has secured funding for its fourth phase of research involving the Nechako River Basin, this time to examine the potential impacts of the proposed NeToo Hydropower Project at the site of the existing Kenney Dam. “The overarching goal of the research is to collect baseline data and information on the Nechako Canyon for integrative responses to climate, water and community connections in the Nechako Watershed,” Martins said. “Water stewardship is strongest when it reflects local knowledge, priorities and lived experience,” said Garcia-Becerra. According to UNBC, partners include the Lheidli T’enneh First Nation, Nulki-Tachick Lakes Stewardship Society, Yinka Dene (Nechako First Nations), Nechako Environment and Water Stewardship Society and Nechako Watershed Roundtable. The project also includes other UNBC researchers, researchers from the University of British Columbia and BC Hydro.

Camosun opens applications for tuition-free Indigenous technology program

A tuition-free, 12-week program at Camosun College is giving Indigenous learners an opportunity to explore careers in technology and engineering, with no previous experience required. The province-funded Indigenous Peoples in Technology Pathways (InTech) program begins its next cohort on Jan. 11, 2027, at the college’s Interurban Campus. It is open to Indigenous Canadian citizens and permanent residents, with no age restrictions or academic prerequisites. “Indigenous learners bring knowledge, experiences, and perspectives that our technology industries need,” said Olga Gould, Camosun’s program co-ordinator for Technology Pathways.

Community collaboration preserves Indigenous history online

For more than a decade, Rudy De La Cruz Jr., director of the Texas Heritage Project (THP), an initiative of American Indians in Texas at the Spanish Colonial Missions (AIT-SCM), has worked to preserve the histories of Indigenous families in South Texas and connect students with that history beyond the classroom. De La Cruz has built a collection of more than 30,000 digital assets, including family photographs, genealogical records, and historical documents. Making those materials accessible to researchers, educators and the public while respecting the families who entrusted their histories to the THP presented a challenge. As the collection grew, so did the need for a digital archive. That’s when UT San Antonio Libraries’ Community Engaged Digital Scholarship Hub (CEDISH) stepped in. Through the Preserving Archives of Texas Heritage (PATH) program, launched in 2025, CEDISH provided technical expertise, student support and resources to help the THP develop a digital archive.

SFU and Tsawwassen First Nation collaborate on Indigenous-led greenhouse project

While modern greenhouse operations typically rely on private software, automated sensors, AI and predictive algorithms to maximize harvests, an emerging research partnership in Delta is taking a different approach to agricultural technology. Backed by seed funding from SFU’s Climate Innovation Amplification Grant, researchers and Tsawwassen First Nation (TFN) lead a plan to turn an existing community greenhouse into a living laboratory. The project will address four elements rarely combined in agricultural research: upholding Indigenous governance, knowledge authority and data sovereignty; developing low-carbon, climate-resilient greenhouse systems; adopting locally repairable agritech with transparent operation and safe manual fallbacks; and creating viable community operations along with training and career pathways for local youth. Crucially, the framework centres on Indigenous governance and data sovereignty. Too often, technological ventures collect operational data that remains locked behind corporate firewalls or academic databases.

title: Wyoming lawmakers seek limits on license-plate surveillance cameras
description:
A Wyoming legislative committee has advanced a bill that would sharply restrict automated license-plate readers, including Flock cameras. The measure is set for consideration when the Legislature convenes Jan. 12, 2027. Police could use the systems for specified purposes, but would have to permanently delete unmatched scan data within three minutes. The bill would also bar selling or broadly sharing the information.

At a Nov. 18 town hall in Lakeport, California, residents questioned data security and access to Flock images. Lake County officials said the cameras have aided investigations, while the contracts grant Flock the right to use captured material at its discretion.

title: UK discounter Poundland enters administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk
description:
Poundland, the UK’s first and largest nationwide single-price retailer, entered administration on Wednesday after its U.S. owner, Gordon Brothers, failed to agree on a solvent sale, putting about 11,000 jobs and roughly 600 stores in the UK and Ireland at risk. AlixPartners, the restructuring consultancy appointed as administrator, said stores and distribution centres would continue operating while it pursued a sale of the company or its assets, in whole or in parts.

The collapse followed worsening access to working capital before Christmas, which Poundland managing director Barry Williams said had left the business unable to operate as a going concern. Gordon Brothers disputed claims that it had cut off funding and said it had released cash when requested.

Gordon Brothers said it had provided £85 million in financing and backed £100 million in cost savings, but maintained that Poundland remained vulnerable to inflation and weaker sales or margins. The UK Parliament’s Business and Trade Committee has recalled Gordon Brothers’ regional managing director, Mark Newton-Jones, for public questioning as administrators continue seeking buyers.

title: U.S. intelligence agencies split over Nvidia spy probe as chip scrutiny widens
description:
U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staffers that investigators have found no evidence Beijing ordered businesswoman Alice Huang to spy on Jensen Huang, chief executive of U.S. AI-chip maker Nvidia. Accounts of the classified briefing describe disagreement within the government over whether she was recruited. The FBI reportedly sees no proof she acted as an agent, while other officials believe she may have been recruited. Officials also said China’s Ministry of State Security had contacted her, but that there was no indication she passed on significant intelligence. The briefing also identified Alice Huang’s husband, businessman Kang Wei, as having deeper ties to the Chinese intelligence service.

Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Nov. 23, 11 days after stepping down. President Donald Trump said he had persuaded the board to bring him back, while Nvidia said its board’s security and export-control committee would continue reviewing the matter. Separately, U.S. investigators are examining whether advanced Nvidia chips reached China through intermediaries. The Commerce Department added Singapore-based data-center company Megaspeed International to a trade blacklist on Nov. 23; Megaspeed denies wrongdoing.

A CBS News investigation also found that two California companies with Chinese ownership obtained advanced Nvidia hardware, with some servers later leased or sold to companies in Southeast Asia. Nvidia’s CEO is scheduled to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

title: Suzlon begins construction of ₹2 billion blade factory in Tamil Nadu
description:
Suzlon Energy has begun building a ₹2 billion ($21.55 million) wind-turbine blade factory in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, designed to produce enough blades annually for 1 gigawatt of turbine capacity. The company expects to add the plant’s manufacturing capacity within about 12 months and says it will make blades up to 95 meters long for its S175 5-megawatt turbine.

The facility is one of three planned blade factories powered by artificial intelligence, with the other sites in Gujarat and Karnataka. The factories are intended to expand supply for Suzlon’s roughly 6-GW order book. Suzlon will fund the project with internal cash, without borrowing or a capital increase, according to the company’s filing. Suzlon expects the plant to create more than 1,000 skilled jobs, with at least 80% of workers coming from rural areas, Power Technology reported.

title: Ozempic is changing the way Americans shop and eat, even if they’ve never taken it
description:
The new class of drugs led by Ozempic and Wegovy don’t just have transformative effects on the people who take them – they’re reshaping the lives around them too.

Patients prescribed GLP-1s are eating less and drinking less, but those behavioral shifts are trickling down to people in their life who aren’t taking the medications themselves. Nearly one in four U.S. consumers have adjusted the way that they shop, eat, and drink based on knowing other people who take GLP-1s, according to a new survey from market research firm Escalent. 

The survey homed in on a group that the market research group calls “echo consumers,” which refers to people who don’t take a GLP-1 themselves but are changing their habits based on others in their social circles who do. The survey included data from 315 U.S. and 335 U.K. respondents who haven’t taken a GLP-1 drug but know someone who does and report changes to their own behavior based on those social connections.

“Much of the attention surrounding GLP-1 medications has focused on the people taking them, and those living in their households,” Escalent Europe Managing Director Melissa Bane wrote. “… For retailers, food and beverage brands and restaurants, that’s a significant consumer group whose changing habits have gone largely unnoticed.”

Among the echo consumers, 42% reported exercising more, 36% said they consume more wellness products, and 27% are drinking less. When eating out, 49% said they are ordering less at restaurants when eating with someone taking a GLP-1, while 21% are opting for alternative activities instead of socializing while eating and drinking. Almost one in five say they have picked different gifts for GLP-1 users they’ve shopped for, and many say they are buying different food and drinks to bring along to social gatherings in light of smaller appetites and friends and family who aren’t drinking as much.

Industry-shifting numbers

While the new survey only offers a small snapshot of consumer behavior, GLP-1 medications are clearly causing some seismic cultural shifts that we’re only beginning to understand. In the U.S., a massive 11% of the population are currently prescribed GLP-1s and 15% say they have tried them for weight loss before. That huge swath of Americans is already walking, running, and cycling more, buying fewer sweet treats, spending less on groceries, and drinking less alcohol.

Habit shifts among GLP-1 users alone already represent a massive amount of change for industries to adapt to across just a few short years. Beyond those consumers, Escalent’s survey suggests that there are 1.7 times as many people shifting their behavior in light of the widespread use of weight management drugs than there are GLP-1 users. If similar numbers play out in future research, that’s an even more massive chunk of the population suddenly eating, drinking, and buying differently than they did prior to the advent of drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound.

“For Echo Consumers, a box of chocolates or a bottle of wine may no longer be the gift of choice, and social occasions could increasingly revolve around activities rather than going out for food and drink,” Bane said, calling the changes a “major shift” that will be even more evident during the holiday season. 

“Brands, retailers and hospitality businesses will need to find ways to adapt their offerings to reflect changing demand as these habits continue to spread through social networks.”

title: Jerusalem judges cite witness problems in Netanyahu bribery case
description:
Jerusalem District Court judges said evidentiary problems, including difficulty drawing factual conclusions from key witness Shlomo Filber’s testimony, weakened the bribery case against caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. They urged prosecutors to drop Case 4000, reconsider Case 2000 and seek an agreement in Case 1000, while stressing that their comments were preliminary and not a verdict.

Case 4000 alleges Netanyahu granted regulatory benefits to telecommunications company Bezeq in exchange for favorable coverage on the Walla news site, then controlled by Bezeq shareholder Shaul Elovitch. Netanyahu and Elovitch deny wrongdoing.

Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, summoned to the hearing, said she would review the judges’ recommendations and that the trial should end with either a verdict or an appropriate plea agreement. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot was seeking to form a government after an inconclusive election, with coalition talks still unsettled.

title: Password manager 1Password discloses customer-data breach; says vaults remain secure
description:
Password manager 1Password disclosed on Nov. 25 that an attacker accessed internal systems and copied account information for some customers. The company says the attacker did not access stored password vaults or the keys protecting them. The company has not said how many users were affected.

1Password said it began investigating Nov. 19 after detecting unauthorized access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker used that access to reach private source code, insert malicious code into backend services and download customer records. The intruder also accessed the company’s software build-and-deployment system, which contains infrastructure credentials.

The copied records included names, sign-in email addresses, account identifiers and sign-in timestamps, along with certain invitation and recovery-link tokens. 1Password says it disabled the compromised account, removed the attacker’s access, rotated potentially exposed credentials and brought in independent cybersecurity experts. It reports no evidence of customer account takeovers and says users do not need to change their account passwords, but warns them to watch for targeted phishing messages.
summary: Password manager 1Password disclosed on Nov. 25 that an attacker accessed internal systems and copied account information for some customers. The company says the attacker did not access stored password vaults or the keys protecting them. The company has not said how many users were affected.

title: Digital Duty of Care Act passes in Australia. Opposition say the law is ‘authoritarian’
description:
Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.

The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.

The Digital Duty of Care Act requires Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.

Australian online law falls in line with EU and British legislation

The legislation is similar to the European Union’s Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom’s Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The legislation became law in the House of Representatives, where the center-left Labor Party government commands a majority, by 97 votes to 43.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told Parliament the law would stand as a “powerful instrument to protect our children and our society from online harms by placing the onus on the tech platforms to ensure a safer online environment.”

“This is a victory for our children and young people. The dangers were unforeseen when the digital world was young,” Albanese said. “But now that the digital world has matured, they can be easily recognized and they can be remedied.”

Opposition leader vows to repeal ‘authoritarian’ law

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told Parliament he would repeal the legislation if his conservative Liberal Party wins elections in 2028. Taylor described the legislation as “authoritarian.”

“This bill is a blank check for political censorship,” Taylor told Parliament. “The bill is an attack on free speech that is absolutely central to our democracy.”

The government struck a deal with the minor Greens party on Tuesday to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

“Today, the safety and wellbeing of Australians and their children have finally been put ahead of Big Tech’s bottom line,” Greens chief negotiator Sarah Hanson-Young said in a statement after the bill passed the Senate by 36 votes to 23.

“My message to Big Tech companies is, it’s time to make your platforms safe or we will see you in court,” she added.

The Australian legislation sets minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

The Greens’ amendments include increasing maximum penalties for breaches from 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), as the government originally proposed, to 5% of a tech company’s global revenue.

U.S. Ambassador to Australia David Brat said on Tuesday the then-proposed laws would “impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”

“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media.

—Rod Mcguirk, Associated Press
summary: Australia’s Parliament on Wednesday passed online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms . The United States and the Australian opposition party warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech .

title: EU and UK fine fragrance makers €570 million for cartel
description:
The European Union and United Kingdom fined fragrance suppliers Firmenich, Givaudan and International Flavors & Fragrances (IFF) a total of more than €570 million on Nov. 25, 2026, for exchanging commercially sensitive information and coordinating aspects of their business from March 2019 to March 2023. The European Commission imposed €471.9 million in penalties, while Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) fined them £85 million.

The Commission said the exchanges covered prices, costs and dealings with Unilever, the world’s largest buyer of consumer fragrances. The three suppliers account for about half of a European fragrance market worth more than €4 billion, and their ingredients go into products including cosmetics, detergents and cleaning supplies. EU competition chief Teresa Ribera said the conduct likely increased costs for customers and may have raised shoppers’ bills.

The companies admitted participating in the cartel and cooperated with regulators, reducing their fines. Firmenich said its role was limited to information exchanges concerning one customer and denied that the conduct involved a price-fixing agreement. The Commission formally opened its investigation in November 2025, following surprise inspections in March 2023.

title: Anthropic lets Claude users install AI-built apps on Mac and Windows
description:
Anthropic has begun beta testing a feature that turns interactive tools made with its Claude AI assistant, known as artifacts, into desktop apps for Mac and Windows with their own icons and windows. Users can share the apps, and edits to an underlying tool update its installed app. The feature is rolling out across Claude plans but requires the desktop app, an internet connection and a signed-in Claude account.

The apps can use Claude and connected services, with requests counting against a user’s plan limits. Permissions range from browser-like access to the ability to run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time. Anthropic says it does not review apps before installation and warns users to grant full access only to apps whose creators they trust.

Users can open installed tools without finding them in old chats, but the apps require an internet connection and are unavailable on Linux, the web and mobile devices. Anthropic says the feature is unavailable to HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments; Enterprise administrators must enable it.

title: Black Sea shipping risks lift European wheat prices as exports shift
description:
Renewed attacks around the Black Sea and the absence of a new grain-shipping agreement have pushed European wheat and corn prices higher as buyers turn to European suppliers while Russian and Ukrainian exports face constraints. On the Euronext exchange, December wheat traded at 242.25 euros a tonne on Nov. 25, up from 233 euros a week earlier; March corn reached 267.75 euros a tonne, up from 259 euros.

French ports were preparing to load nearly 1.5 million tonnes of wheat in November, an unusually large volume for the season, including shipments to Morocco, China and Djibouti. U.S. wheat and corn prices fell as export sales lagged, with a strong dollar and competition from Europe, Australia and Argentina weighing on demand.

Ukraine says its September agricultural exports totaled 2.4 million tonnes, 46% of the volume it needs to ship; alternative routes cost an additional 50 to 80 euros per tonne. The Ukrainian agriculture ministry warned that more than 30 million tonnes could remain unexported by the end of the marketing season in June 2027 if maritime restrictions persist.

title: Lunar craters could shield habitats from reactor radiation
description:
Researchers studying a proposed lunar nuclear power system say crater walls and other natural terrain could block reactor radiation from reaching a future base, reducing the need to transport heavy shielding from Earth. NASA’s planned 40-kilowatt reactor faces a design constraint: the full system must weigh less than 6,000 kilograms for transport by rover.

The findings are based on computer simulations, not a physical test. The researchers also warn that the area around an operating reactor would remain dangerous, and reflected neutrons could require a no-fly zone over the site.

South pole site: The team modeled Connecting Ridge near Shackleton Crater, where some terrain receives sunlight 80%–90% of the time and lies beside permanently shadowed ice-bearing regions (universetoday.com, phys.org). Rover limits: The terrain model accounted for a rover limit that rules out slopes steeper than 18 degrees, with the reactor positioned 1.5 meters above ground (phys.org, aroundprague.cz).

title: Swiss agency confirms four successful AI-agent hacks, including attacks on critical-infrastructure operators
description:
Switzerland’s National Cyber Security Centre says attackers using AI agents breached systems in four of five cases reported in the country, including attacks on three critical-infrastructure operators. The cases are part of a rise in campaigns using AI frameworks to automate reconnaissance and exploit security weaknesses. The Swiss agency has not identified the attackers, and officials reported no major outages.

Italy’s incident response team says it observed campaigns in which multiple agents worked in parallel to compromise exposed systems. Canada’s cyber centre says automated tools have shortened some reconnaissance and exploitation from days or weeks to minutes. Amazon separately described agents that found and exploited an unpatched flaw on a university server in about 11 minutes.

Swiss authorities advise organizations to reduce the number of internet-facing systems and install critical updates within 24 hours of release. Italy also urged operators to restrict remote-management access and monitor unusual authentication and network activity.

title: Four Guangxi fossil teeth point to Denisovans and another ancient lineage
description:
Researchers analyzing four fossil teeth from two caves in China’s Guangxi region identified Denisovan-related remains and evidence of a potentially distinct ancient human lineage, according to a study published in Nature on Nov. 25. The two Longchuandong teeth align with Denisovans, while two teeth from Chuanshandong—at least 100,800 years old—have traits that do not readily match any known East Asian Homo group.

The findings suggest different archaic human populations lived in southern China during overlapping periods, but researchers cannot yet confidently assign the Chuanshandong teeth to a named group. Warm, humid conditions in the region hinder ancient DNA preservation, so researchers analyzed tooth shape and proteins. They say more fossils and molecular evidence are needed to establish the teeth’s evolutionary relationships.

title: Romania signs sheep export certificates, but restrictions still block trade
description:
Romania’s National Veterinary and Food Safety Authority and Jordan signed health certificates on Nov. 25 for exports of live sheep and sheep carcasses, setting conditions for entry into Jordan’s market. The certificates do not lift the restrictions blocking shipments; exports can resume only after those restrictions are lifted, and no restart date was announced.

The agreement followed visits by Jordanian officials to farms and processing businesses in Constanța and Tulcea, where they assessed biosecurity, processing and veterinary controls. The Romanian authority said vaccination of sheep and goats supports, rather than blocks, export access.

title: Italy awards 16 GWh of battery storage at lower auction prices
description:
Italy’s grid operator Terna awarded 16 GWh of battery-storage capacity in its second MACSE procurement auction on Nov. 24, at a weighted-average premium of €11,382 per megawatt-hour-year. The premium was 12% below the first auction’s level, while bids totaled about 43 GWh for the 16 GWh sought. The winning projects must provide the contracted capacity for 15 years and are scheduled to begin operating in 2029.

The auction covered southern Italy and its islands, where Terna is buying storage to shift renewable electricity to periods of demand and reduce reliance on gas-fired generation. Terna said it set the procurement volume so storage costs would be lower than the savings from reduced gas use. Developers that missed out can pursue merchant-market revenues, tolling agreements or Italy’s capacity market, though revised capacity-rating coefficients affect projects in some southern zones.

title: Cyber officials urge outage drills as supply-chain weaknesses spread
description:
Cybersecurity experts and officials are urging organizations to rehearse responses to service outages and prepare fallback plans as cloud disruptions and supplier weaknesses expose risks that can spread across businesses. The World Economic Forum’s 2026 cybersecurity outlook found small organizations were twice as likely as large ones to report inadequate cyber resilience; 65% of large companies identified third-party and supply-chain vulnerabilities as their biggest challenge, up from 54% in 2025.

New Zealand’s National Cyber Security Centre recorded 1,694 incident reports in July-September, 50% more than the previous quarter; reported financial losses rose 115% to NZ$5.9 million. In Mississippi, a lawmaker says a bill planned for the next legislative session would consolidate state cybersecurity resources under one department and support local governments.

excerpt: Cybersecurity experts and officials are urging organizations to rehearse responses to service outages and prepare fallback plans as cloud disruptions and supplier weaknesses expose risks that can spread across businesses (tweakers.net, techtarget.com). In Mississippi, a lawmaker says a bill planned for the next legislative session would consolidate state cybersecurity resources under one department and support local governments (oxfordeagle.com). Skills gap: The World Economic Forum report found 46% of small organizations cited a shortage of cybersecurity skills, compared with 29% of large organizations (techtarget.com). Basic safeguards: For smaller suppliers, experts recommend phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, tested offline backups and written incident-response plans, rather than costly security operations platforms (techtarget.com). Scam pattern: Phishing and credential harvesting were New Zealand’s most common incident types; the country’s cyber chief said she clicked through a convincing Dropbox link but could not proceed because she had forgotten her password (interest.co.nz). title: Why isn’t AI changing career advice?
description:
Ask a 17-year-old where their career plan came from and the answer is usually someone at the kitchen table. A parent, maybe an uncle. These are people who love them and want the best for them. They are also, in most cases, working from a job market map that is 20 or 30 years out of date.

The school counselor rarely enters the picture. Most U.S. school counselors spend no more than 20% of their time on career counseling while serving hundreds of students. The available capacity works out to well under an hour per student per year, even before accounting for group programming and administrative responsibilities.

Meanwhile, nearly the entire AI and jobs conversation is about what this technology will take away from young workers. That concern is fair. I’ve argued here before that AI will reduce the need for some entry-level white-collar roles, and employers need to plan for that now.

But we have become so focused on what AI will do to young workers that we have stopped asking what it can do for them. And there is an irony sitting right in front of us. One of the hardest problems in workforce development is getting accurate, real-time labor market information to the people who need it most. That happens to be the kind of problem AI is unusually good at.

THE DATA EXISTS BUT FEW CAN READ IT

Labor market data is not scarce. Governments, job boards, and industry groups publish enormous amounts of it every month. The trouble is that it is dense, scattered, and close to illegible for anyone without a statistics background. A 16-year-old is not going to read a state workforce projection. Neither is her dad.

So young people make one of the biggest decisions of their lives with the least information. We are preparing them for yesterday’s jobs while tomorrow’s technology sits on the phone in their pocket.

They know the system is failing them. In the Broken Marketplace, a Schultz Family Foundation and HarrisX survey of more than 5,700 young Americans ages 16 to 24, more than four in 10 said the education system and the employment resources available to them are broken. Seven in 10 said they learn about career pathways on social media.

We know that young people are already asking algorithms for career advice. They are just asking the wrong ones.

WHAT A GOOD AI COUNSELOR SOUNDS LIKE

At the International Youth Foundation, we’ve been testing this idea with a chatbot called Clara, a partnership we have with the Salesforce Foundation. The premise is straightforward: Take labor market data that would make most people’s eyes glaze over and turn it into a conversation.

Picture a young woman who has just finished a technical program and doesn’t know where to apply. Instead of a spreadsheet, she gets something closer to a knowledgeable friend. A chat that says, “Did you know they’re hiring electricians a few miles from you? A couple of things in your background could make you competitive. Let me ask you some questions and see whether it’s worth pursuing.”

From there, the tool can explain what training she would need, how long it takes, and whether that field is growing where she lives. That is the guidance a great counselor gives. But most students never get it. Nearly half of career and technical educators say their school’s counselors spend less time on career pathways than on college prep.

AI can close that gap at a scale no hiring plan ever could. Big data sets, updated in real time, delivered to one person at a time in plain language. That is what these models do best.

THE RISK AND FIX ARE REAL

To be clear, this is not without risk. General-purpose AI models can sound authoritative while missing the details that matter. When researchers at Renaissance Philanthropy tested leading models on thousands of real career questions from young people, most would have earned a C-minus. For a young person making a first career decision, a confident wrong answer can cost years.

That is a reason to build these tools carefully, and to build them now. If AI makes the labor market more volatile, good information becomes increasingly valuable. The work of measuring whether AI gives young people good career advice has barely started, and it deserves far more investment than it is getting.

The AI labs should be paying attention, too. Millions of young people are already typing some version of “what job should I go for?” into their products. Making sure those answers are accurate and grounded in real local demand would cost a fraction of what is being spent on the next generation of models.

AI can’t save every job. But it could help a young person find the next one. Employers, funders, and the companies building this technology spend a great deal of energy worrying about what AI will do to the next generation of workers. They should spend at least as much making sure it works for them.

Christina Sass is president and CEO of the International Youth Foundation.

title: Euclid survey identifies ancient quasar, Webb measures black-hole mass
description:
The European Space Agency’s (ESA) Euclid space telescope found quasar J1504+6252 in a search of millions of sources in its wide-area survey. Nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, the object is seen as it was about 630 million years after the Big Bang; the James Webb Space Telescope measured its central black hole’s mass at an estimated 360 million solar masses.

Euclid identified the faint source but could not confirm it with its own instrument, so Keck Observatory, Hubble, the Large Binocular Telescope and Webb conducted follow-up observations. Euclid primarily surveys galaxies to investigate cosmic structure, dark matter and dark energy. Researchers plan further observations with Euclid and Webb to test whether other early quasars show a similar pattern. The study appeared Nov. 24 in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

title: Israeli lawmakers advance October 7 inquiry bill despite Netanyahu opposition
description:
Israel’s Knesset gave preliminary approval on Nov. 25 to a bill establishing a state commission to investigate security failures before Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 attack and the war that followed. The measure, sponsored by Yashar lawmaker Orit Farkash-Hacohen, passed 65-50. Yashar is led by Gadi Eisenkot. The bill must clear three further readings to become law.

The proposed five-member commission would examine events from the end of Israel’s 2014 Gaza war through the return of the last hostage’s body on Jan. 26, 2026. It would issue an interim report within a year of its establishment and receive an initial allocation of 7 million shekels, about $2 million.

Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu opposes an independent state inquiry and has advocated a politically appointed alternative. His opponents support an independent investigation. The bill now moves to committee deliberations before three further Knesset votes. Eisenkot, who is trying to form a government after the Oct. 27 election, has until Dec. 6 to secure a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension.

title: Eisenkot advances Israeli coalition talks as ultra-Orthodox draft dispute persists
description:
Negotiations between Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party have advanced, but the parties remain divided over military service for ultra-Orthodox men. The party wants legislation on draft evasion passed before a new government takes office; Eisenkot favors a cabinet decision after the government is sworn in, Israeli broadcaster KAN reported. United Torah Judaism’s rabbis have approved continued talks, and party chairman Yaakov Asher has met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as negotiations continue.

Eisenkot is seeking to replace Netanyahu after Israel’s Oct. 27 election left no bloc with a parliamentary majority. His Yashar party has agreed to a coalition pact with Yisrael Beiteinu, chaired by Avigdor Lieberman, while the left-leaning Democrats party has suspended talks over Yashar’s parallel discussions with Netanyahu’s Likud. Eisenkot is aiming for a vote in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, to install a government on Dec. 2, four days before his mandate expires.

Judges in Jerusalem urged Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara to consider dropping the bribery charge in Case 4000, one of the corruption cases against Netanyahu, the caretaker prime minister. The recommendation is not a final ruling; Baharav-Miara said she would review it with prosecutors.

title: Treasury intrusion leaves scope and data exposure unresolved as investigations continue
description:
The U.S. Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), which collects financial intelligence for criminal investigations, confirmed that an intruder accessed a limited subset of its systems. The agency has not identified the systems accessed, how the intruder gained access or whether information was viewed or taken. Authorities have not publicly attributed the intrusion or linked it to other recent federal breaches.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and outside forensic examiners are assessing the incident’s scope and impact. FinCEN said investigators had found no evidence that its Bank Secrecy Act or beneficial-ownership databases were breached. The review continues.

The incident follows a separately reported breach of an unclassified intelligence-analysis system used by the Central Intelligence Agency and other agencies. Officials have not publicly linked the cases. FinCEN says it is working to restore affected systems but has not set a date for full service.

title: EU quantum law targets industrial scale and tighter technology security
description:
The European Commission’s proposed Quantum Act would steer public contracts toward European Union-controlled suppliers and prepare public systems for quantum-era cyber risks. The proposal, presented in Strasbourg, would also coordinate EU and national research programmes, expand shared infrastructure and establish specialist hubs to help companies move technologies from laboratories into commercial use.

The draft law also provides the legal basis for a proposed Sovereign Tech Equity Fund and sets out a framework for quantum technologies across the bloc. The Commission says Europe has about one-third of the world’s quantum companies, but its startups secured €1.1 billion in private funding, compared with €7 billion in the United States.

EU member states and the European Parliament must now negotiate the proposal before it can become law.

title: AI toy tests find unsafe responses as New York enacts five-year ban
description:
A Common Sense Media assessment found that 27% of tested AI-toy responses were inappropriate for children. The group’s Youth AI Safety Institute tested five internet-connected toys with more than 600 prompts. Testers said the toys claimed to love children, promised to keep secrets and gave guidance on locating household hazards such as matches, knives and pills.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a five-year ban on manufacturing, distributing and selling toys with AI chatbots on Nov. 24. The measure covers toys designed for children 12 and younger and takes effect 90 days after signing. California has also adopted a moratorium on AI companion toys.

More than 155 child-safety groups and technology experts separately asked Amazon and eBay to stop selling AI toys. Testing has also prompted some major retailers to remove products from their listings. Amazon said it would restrict sales in jurisdictions where such toys are prohibited but did not detail how it would do so.
