title: Goldman Sachs sees 52 gigawatts of new U.S. data-center capacity in 2028
description:
Goldman Sachs expects U.S. data-center power capacity to keep growing through 2028, with an additional 52 gigawatts that could come online that year as artificial-intelligence companies build larger, more energy-intensive facilities. The bank says data-center power capacity and associated demand have risen nearly 30% year to date, accounting for more than one-third of the country’s total increase in electricity demand.

Goldman said the expansion could tighten U.S. electricity markets and increase natural-gas demand, supporting its outlook for higher Henry Hub gas prices between 2028 and 2030. It also warned that political scrutiny after November’s midterm elections could slow growth: Democratic victories in data-center hubs including Texas and Georgia may contribute to divided government and tighter oversight of development.

title: UN rights chief warns of growing atrocity risk in Gaza, West Bank
description:
United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Wednesday that Israeli actions and policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank point to a growing risk of further atrocity crimes, and called on all states to act immediately. Türk said senior Israeli officials had repeatedly set out policies of annexation, ethnic cleansing and collective punishment in the West Bank, and cited incitement to violations that could amount to war crimes, crimes against humanity or genocide.

The UN said nearly two million of Gaza’s 2.1 million residents have been forcibly displaced, often more than once, while most live in tents or makeshift shelters. Türk also cited the continuing destruction of civilian infrastructure, arbitrary detention and torture, and restrictions that deprive people of food, medicine and shelter.

Türk called for independent investigations, accountability and support for international courts, while reminding Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups of their duties to protect civilians and humanitarian operations. He said unlawful killings continued despite the ceasefire announced in October 2025; Palestinian and Israeli tallies cited by RTÉ put the death toll since the truce at at least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers.

title: Implementing OpenCart Browser & Server-Side Tracking with GTM, Stape & Cloudflare Workers
description:
This post is part of Web Tracking Series Earlier I shared how I implemented both browser and server side tracking on a Shopify store using GTM and direct CAPI implementation via a Custom Pixel. This time we are going to see how one can implement browser and server tracking on an OpenCart store. Read on! So, someone approached me to take care web tracking on their OpenCart store. I was like, why not! I had never worked with OpenCart before. Most of my ecommerce tracking work has been with Shopify or WooCommerce. I thought it would be an easy task: find a free plugin, install it, configure GTM, and move on. To my surprise, there are very few OpenCart extensions (the OpenCart version of plugins) for this. Secondly, pretty much everything I found was paid. The minimum was around $30, with some going close to $100. Initially, I thought of simply buying one. But there were no trial versions, and I wasn’t even sure whether they’d give me the flexibility I wanted. Then the developer in me whispered: “Hey, why don’t you make one?” Hmm… not a bad idea. Especially because I wanted control over exactly how the tracking data was generated. So I started exploring the OpenCart documentation and, with the help of docs + AI, started building my own extension. Instead of relying on DOM scraping or modifying the theme, the extension hooks into OpenCart’s built-in event architecture and generates the tracking data itself Implementation Extension Development and Browser Side Tracking We used OpenCart’s event hooks to run our custom PHP controller at key points in the storefront and checkout. For purchases, the controller pulled the order details, products, and totals from OpenCart, stored them in the session, and injected a dataLayer.push() call just before </body> on the order confirmation page. Below is the interface of the extension I made. Below is the screenshot of the fired events in the GTM interface. Meta Pixel viewer extension shows fired events And Meta’s event manager was also recording events Server side implementation via Stape and Cloudflare workers Unlike previous post in which we directly called CAPI APIs, we are going to rely on Stape. Stape is a server side tagging platform that helps us to create and manage server containers. When you signup you see an interface like below to create your first container: You select the location that is nearest to your visitors. Next, once the sGTM running you will see something like below: It will generate a tagging server URL like http://xxx.apd.stape.io/ for you that you could use for testing purpose. Next, we will be using this URL in the server container within GTM so that it can serve tags from the custom domain instead of GTM’s Now, let’s test it: Next, I am gonna Add Data Tag template by Stape in webGTM Set the server container URL and save tag: We don’t want to send hard-coded event names so we’d make it dynamic: We are gong to use the Event variable to use the info of the incoming event name. If all goes well, we’d see server GTM in action: Next, we need to configure Meta CAPI. We are going to add Facebook Conversion API template by Stape. We will be adding all required tags to interact with Meta servers. If all goes well you’d see something like: Similarly we’d be configuring other events as well. Custom domain configuration in Cloudflare We needed the tracking requests to be processed via the domain of the store itself so that the GTM Server Side configuration could have the same-origin endpoint and be able to create first-party cookies. We set up a custom tagging subdomain for our Stape-hosted server-side GTM container and configured its DNS records in Cloudflare. We also deployed a Cloudflare worker under a separate path of the OpenCart store domain which then stripped the path and forwarded the request to the Stape tagging subdomain. We made the necessary adjustments to the web GTM Data Tag and checked whether the endpoint is working correctly by sending an event through a product view page. Conclusion That’s how we set up browser and server-side tracking for the OpenCart store. I’ve kept this post focused on the implementation steps and left the code and configuration details for another time. Setting up server-side tracking for OpenCart with Stape takes some care. Once the OpenCart data layer, web GTM, and server container are wired together, you can test the full flow from the storefront to Meta Events Manager. If you run an OpenCart store and want to set up tracking or check whether your existing setup is working correctly, book a call with me. After this project, I also released a free GTM extension for OpenCart.

title: Stanford researchers find nanoscale niobium phosphide wires outperform copper
description:
Stanford University researchers reported that ultrathin niobium phosphide ribbons conduct electricity more efficiently than copper wires of comparable size, with resistivity falling as the ribbons narrow. The study, published in Nature, tested ribbons as small as 5–6 nanometers wide and about 1.5 nanometers thick.

Resistance in the tiny connections linking transistors can delay signals in advanced chips. Researchers disagree about whether the material’s topological properties explain the drop in resistivity. Outside scientists questioned whether a niobium surface layer influenced the measurements, and Stanford physicist and study leader Eric Pop acknowledged that other explanations remain possible.

excerpt: Stanford University researchers reported that ultrathin niobium phosphide ribbons conduct electricity more efficiently than copper wires of comparable size, with resistivity falling as the ribbons narrow. Outside scientists questioned whether a niobium surface layer influenced the measurements, and Stanford physicist and study leader Eric Pop acknowledged that other explanations remain possible (science.org). Chip bottleneck: Leading chips use copper interconnects about 15 nanometers wide, where resistance-related delays can last 20 times as long as it takes to switch a transistor (science.org). Manufacturing path: The team says it can make the ribbons using existing chip-fabrication techniques and that they conduct electricity at room temperature. It is continuing work on fabrication compatibility, endurance and temperature behavior (science.org, techxplore.com).

title: Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted Riemann claim prompts math departments to adapt
description:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says the company’s Claude assistant helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis, a longstanding mathematical claim about prime-number distribution. The claimed proof remains subject to human verification.

Johns Hopkins University’s mathematics department has issued guidance for Ph.D. applicants and job candidates, saying it expects transparency about AI use and will not give written work positive weight unless candidates demonstrate they understand it. Professor Yiannis Sakellaridis said the guidance was prompted by the risk that candidates could submit AI-generated proofs without learning the underlying mathematics, not by a specific applicant case.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei rejected the idea that people should hand governance to AI, while David Krueger, founder of the nonprofit Evitable, argued that concern about losing control calls for a halt to advanced AI development. Researchers and technology leaders have debated whether the mathematical advances signal progress toward systems that exceed human capabilities.

title: Anthropic details Claude Ship’s access limits and GitHub approval controls
description:
Anthropic’s Claude Ship, a GitHub workflow that reviews and repairs proposed code changes, lets teams define which changes its AI agents can approve and when a person must review them. Repository policies can require a separate check by the Code Review tool, while GitHub continues to enforce branch rules and mandatory human sign-offs.

The repository tools are available to Claude Team and Enterprise customers, while an individual `/ship` command is rolling out in Claude Code. Organizations using zero-data-retention or HIPAA configurations, or their own encryption keys, cannot use the repository workflow; FERPA and Access Transparency settings also rule out Claude Approvals. Charges are based on token use, and admins can set separate spending limits for Code Review and the repair agent PR Steward.

title: Israeli opposition leader Eisenkot wins first coalition pact, majority remains elusive
description:
Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief who leads the centre-right Yashar party, agreed to sign the first coalition pact since Israel’s Oct. 27 election with Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Israel Our Home party. The deal gives Eisenkot a partner but not a majority: his bloc holds 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, Israel’s parliament, while the alliance backing caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has 53. Parties representing Israel’s Arab minority hold 19 seats and could support Eisenkot, but Lieberman has opposed relying on them.

The parties remain divided over the makeup of a government. The left-wing Democrats party, led by Yair Golan, suspended talks with Yashar, citing progress in unity-government discussions between Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s Likud party and deadlock over forming a government without Netanyahu. Eisenkot could also seek support from ultra-Orthodox parties; negotiations with United Torah Judaism have focused on arrests for draft evasion and the enlistment of ultra-Orthodox men.

President Isaac Herzog gave Eisenkot a 28-day mandate to form a government, running through Dec. 6, with the possibility of a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu can try to form a government; if neither succeeds, Israel is expected to hold another election next year.

title: WHO warns drug-resistant Klebsiella threatens vulnerable hospital patients across Europe
description:
The World Health Organization warned that drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is spreading in Europe, putting hospitalized patients with existing health problems at greatest risk; the resistant strains circulate mainly in hospitals and clinics. Bloodstream infections caused by the strain increased 72% from 2019 to 2025, with reported fatality rates of 40% to 70%. WHO experts assess the risk of the strain becoming established across the European Union and European Economic Area as very high.

Jean-Pierre Njemazi, director of WHO's antimicrobial-resistance department, cited estimates that resistance could be directly linked to 39 million deaths over the next 25 years. Member states aim to cut deaths attributed to resistance by 10% by 2030, but Njemazi said current trends and action are not on course to meet that goal. Experts also point to antibiotic use in people and animal farming, and to resistant microbes moving through wastewater and the environment.

WHO experts assess the risk of the strain becoming established across the European Union and European Economic Area as very high (rambler.ru). Jean-Pierre Njemazi, director of WHO's antimicrobial-resistance department, cited estimates that resistance could be directly linked to 39 million deaths over the next 25 years. Member states aim to cut deaths attributed to resistance by 10% by 2030, but Njemazi said current trends and action are not on course to meet that goal (dw.com). Experts also point to antibiotic use in people and animal farming, and to resistant microbes moving through wastewater and the environment (dw.com). Resistance in South Africa: Gauteng officials warned that resistance could leave health workers with fewer treatment options for common infections and reverse decades of medical progress (timeslive.co.za). Prevention options: The Paul-Ehrlich-Institut says influenza vaccination can reduce antibiotic use by preventing flu and bacterial complications that might otherwise require antibiotics (pei.de).

title: B.C. premier directs cabinet to reverse Indigenous, climate and drug policies
description:
British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson has directed his new cabinet to reverse key policies on Indigenous rights, climate action and substance use, while pursuing tax relief and tighter government spending. The government released the mandate letters Tuesday, after Doerkson and his cabinet were sworn in on Friday.

The government says ministers must focus on affordability, economic growth, health care, community safety and provincial pride, and submit new funding requests to the Treasury Board for an affordability review. The letters also call for an independent review of provincial finances as the government pledges to address a record $13.8-billion deficit.

title: EU weighs €50 billion fund for AI and quantum firms
description:
The European Union is considering a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund that could mobilize up to €50 billion for European artificial intelligence and quantum computing companies as Brussels seeks to reduce reliance on U.S. and Chinese technology. The proposal, reported by the Financial Times citing two officials involved in the discussions, would make larger, riskier and longer-term investments than existing EU financing schemes. Reuters said it could not immediately verify the report.

The European Commission plans to use EU money as seed capital to attract private investment, aiming to mobilize as much as €6 for every euro committed. An independent manager would run the fund, while the precise financing arrangements remain under discussion. The European Investment Bank could provide financial expertise without taking on investment risk.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged an ambitious proposal for technology-sovereignty funding after EU leaders discussed artificial intelligence earlier this month. The Commission is expected to present details of how the fund would operate at EU leaders’ competitiveness retreat in Alden Biesen, Belgium, in February 2027.

title: Somalia orders UAE ambassador out within 72 hours in diplomatic rift
description:
Somalia’s government on Nov. 19 ordered the United Arab Emirates ambassador to leave within 72 hours and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi after President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud accused the UAE of interfering in Somali affairs, backing armed groups and making port deals with regional administrations without federal approval. The UAE rejected Mogadishu’s accusations, calling its approach “escalatory and hostile,” and said it had already closed its embassy and withdrawn its diplomats in January after Somalia canceled bilateral agreements.

The dispute involves UAE relations with Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland, as well as disagreements within Somalia over constitutional changes and election arrangements. Parliament amended the constitution in March to extend presidential and parliamentary terms from four years to five; regional administrations and opposition figures rejected the changes. Somalia’s Supreme Court later ruled that the current leaders’ terms had expired and set deadlines for an election framework and polls.

title: Car bomb in Villavicencio leaves more than 20 injured on anniversary of peace deal
description:
On November 24, Colombia commemorated the tenth anniversary of the peace deal signed in Bogotá between the government and the FARC guerrillas. The day before, a car bomb exploded in Villavicencio, leaving more than 20 people injured. President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed the attack on FARC dissidents and ruled out negotiating with armed groups. The agreement ended more than half a century of conflict between the government and the guerrillas; more than 13,600 combatants laid down their arms.

A decade later, the Kroc Institute estimates that 36% of the commitments have been fulfilled. The Office of the Ombudsman records 521 signatories killed, and the Armed Forces estimate that armed groups total around 29,000 members across 165 structures, compared with approximately 13,000 in 2022. After the FARC withdrew, the government failed to establish a sufficient presence in several areas, which were left vulnerable to disputes among other groups.

De la Espriella has cut the budget of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), the court created by the agreement, and ended talks with armed groups. Former president Juan Manuel Santos maintains that the problems stem from the failure to implement the agreement. At the request of the Colombian government and with the backing of the United States, the UN verification mission will stop monitoring rural reform; its overall mandate was renewed for one year.

title: Study links sperm mitochondrial DNA retention to lower pregnancy odds
description:
A study of 327 men with normal semen-test results found that higher levels of mitochondrial DNA retained in sperm were associated with lower monthly chances of pregnancy, researchers reported Nov. 24. The association remained after accounting for factors including both partners’ ages, body mass indexes and smoking status.

The study does not show that retained mitochondrial DNA causes infertility. Researchers said further work is needed to explain why some sperm retain it and whether it affects fertilization or embryo development.

title: From Policy to Pavement: Preparing Cities for El Niño in the Greater Horn of Africa
description: To limit the toll of El Niño's October-December rains, IGAD's specialized climate institution, the Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC), has released a practical guide with UN-Habitat for Horn of Africa cities. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) is a regional bloc in Eastern Africa of governments from the Greater Horn of Africa, and their High-Level Call to Action on El Niño Preparedness establishes a regional commitment to move from reactive disaster response to proactive action for long-term resilience. Emphasizing cross-border coordination and crediting local knowledge, the call states: "We recognize that climate and disaster risks do not respect national borders, and that no single country or institution can manage them alone."

title: Singapore says Megaspeed chips never entered country, seeks U.S. data
description:
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Nvidia chips bought by cloud company Megaspeed never physically entered Singapore. His government is seeking more information from the United States to identify the chips' end users and verify transaction documents. Singapore is investigating possible breaches of its own laws while working with Washington on checks to help the United States enforce its export controls.

Wong said the chips were routed to other countries, limiting what Singapore can investigate on its own. “We did ask for some information. Not all of it was forthcoming,” he said. The U.S. Commerce Department placed Megaspeed and six related companies in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand on its Entity List on Nov. 23, requiring licenses for U.S. exports. The department cited the risk of advanced computing technology reaching unauthorized users or uses.

Singapore's inquiry remains active, and Wong said companies found to have violated local law would face firm enforcement. During his visit to Canberra, Wong and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also signed an agreement to secure essential supplies, including food, pharmaceuticals and agricultural inputs.

title: U.S. survey: 44% of GLP-1 users who drank when starting treatment reported drinking less
description:
A survey of U.S. adults found that 44.2% of people who drank alcohol when they began taking GLP-1 medications reported drinking less during their first three months on the drugs. Researchers surveyed 2,009 adults in March and April 2026; 242 respondents said they drank when they started taking a GLP-1 medication.

The findings do not establish that the drugs caused the reported changes or are effective in treating alcohol use disorder, which the study did not assess. Participants recalled their drinking, and researchers did not measure how much consumption changed. Larger clinical trials are needed to test whether the medications reduce unhealthy alcohol use.

title: Researchers model helium bubbles to limit metal buildup in molten-salt reactors
description:
Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute used computer simulations to study how replenishing helium bubbles could prevent radioactive metal particles from accumulating in molten-salt reactor systems. The particles can coat heat exchangers, trapping heat and reducing reactor efficiency; the models indicate that adding fresh bubbles can sustain the bubbles’ ability to collect the metals.

The team combined experimental data from the 1960s and 1970s with Argonne’s SAM reactor-safety software to track tellurium-132 under different bubble-flow conditions. The study was published in the journal Nuclear Technology. Its findings are based on simulations, not experimental validation of the proposed operating approach.

title: Hackers breach U.S. spy analysis network, risking exposure of priorities
description:
Hackers breached an unclassified open-source intelligence analysis network used by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), exposing some information, according to people familiar with the incident. A source told The Associated Press that the breach had been resolved and involved no classified information.

The network processes publicly available and commercially sourced material, including social media, satellite imagery and paid data feeds. Investigators have not identified the attacker or specified which records were exposed. Reports also indicated that the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was affected and that information at other government agencies may have been exposed.

Access to analysts’ activity could reveal what U.S. intelligence agencies are tracking, even without access to classified files. Nextgov reported that investigators believe hackers used ARTEX, an AI-enabled intrusion tool, but U.S. officials have not publicly attributed the breach to a person, group or government.

title: B.C. towns issue evacuation alerts as storm tides threaten coast
description:
Squamish declared a local state of emergency as communities across British Columbia issued evacuation alerts and closed waterfront areas Tuesday amid coastal flooding risks from king tides, storm surge and heavy rain. Squamish said the declaration would allow it to carry out flood-mitigation work. Parksville and the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation warned shoreline residents to be ready to leave.

Environment Canada warned that tides could run 20 to 50 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides through Thursday. Forecasts called for up to 225 millimetres of rain on parts of Vancouver Island, wind gusts up to 90 km/h in Greater Victoria and rapidly rising rivers across Vancouver Island and the South Coast.

The alerts cover coastal areas from Metro Vancouver and Vancouver Island to Haida Gwaii and the central and Sunshine coasts. Victoria closed sections of its Dallas Road waterfront seawall, and Ucluelet closed beaches and trails. The province increased highway patrols and warned that debris or flooding could force sudden road closures.

title: Trump’s tariff plan could add 2% to 7.5% to import duties
description:
A new round of U.S. tariffs could add 2% to 7.5% to import duties if the administration uses the new levies to restore rates imposed before the Supreme Court struck them down, trade-policy expert Deborah Elms estimated. President Donald Trump’s administration is preparing country-specific duties on China, the European Union and 14 other economies following an investigation into industrial subsidies by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR); final rates and effective dates remain unsettled. The duties would focus largely on manufactured goods and could raise costs for importers and consumers. The July tariffs tied to forced-labor enforcement have already contributed to higher U.S. consumer-goods prices, the Associated Press reported.

The administration is expected to keep overall tariff rates within ceilings set by existing trade deals rather than apply a single blanket rate. The European Union, Japan and South Korea face ceilings of 15% or less, while China’s ceiling is expected to remain at 20% if its trade truce with Washington is extended.

The USTR is expected to release its findings shortly. Targeted economies can then seek changes through hearings, public comments and talks before rates are finalized. The administration could also reduce duties if countries take steps to address excess production capacity; the exact product list and start date remain unclear.

title: Argentina's recession hits employment and consumption ahead of the 2027 elections
description:
Between November 2023 and August 2026, Argentina lost 274,300 registered private-sector jobs, and real wages in the sector remained 2.3% below their November 2023 level. Economists estimate that economic activity fell 1.8% between July and September, after contracting 0.6% in the second quarter; the final quarterly figure will be released in December.

In September, ten of the 15 sectors surveyed posted year-on-year declines: fishing fell 48.6%, financial intermediation 11.5%, and manufacturing 1.8%. Mining grew 11.1%; consultancy ACM attributes nearly all of the year's accumulated growth to agriculture and mining.

The government has not confirmed a recession ahead of the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INDEC) publishing third-quarter GDP, scheduled for December 16. Finance Secretary Federico Furiase attributed the July decline to temporary factors and said August and September showed a recovery. Analysts warn that a possible interest-rate hike to contain currency-market pressure would make credit more expensive and hinder the recovery of consumption and investment.

title: Australia’s inflation hits 4.9%, complicating rate and budget decisions
description:
Australia’s annual consumer inflation rate climbed to 4.9% in October from 4.3% in September, while the Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred underlying measure rose to 3.8%, above forecasts of 3.6%. Inflation remains above the central bank’s 2%-3% target, while unemployment has risen and economic activity shows signs of slowing.

Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation. Electricity prices rose 25.2% over the year as government rebates ended, and new-home costs also increased. The Reserve Bank’s next rate decision is due Dec. 8; economists differ on whether rates will stay on hold or rise again. Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government will set out substantial savings in its mid-year budget update, due before Christmas.

title: Judge lets Epstein survivors’ privacy claim over file disclosures proceed
description:
A federal judge in San Jose on Tuesday allowed five Jeffrey Epstein survivors to pursue a Privacy Act claim against the U.S. government, rejecting its bid to dismiss the case. The plaintiffs allege that the Justice Department’s release of investigative files in late 2025 and early 2026 exposed personal information identifying about 100 victims without their consent.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi said the allegations plausibly supported a claim of intentional or willful disclosure but did not rule that the department broke the law. The government cited the 30-day release mandate and acknowledged mistakes, arguing that the plaintiffs had not shown deliberate conduct. The claim can proceed; separate claims against Google and X.AI over AI services that allegedly republished the information remain under challenge.

excerpt: A federal judge in San Jose on Tuesday allowed five Jeffrey Epstein survivors to pursue a Privacy Act claim against the U.S. government, rejecting its bid to dismiss the case. The plaintiffs allege that the Justice Department’s release of investigative files in late 2025 and early 2026 exposed personal information identifying about 100 victims without their consent (courthousenews.com, reason.com). U.S. Magistrate Judge Virginia DeMarchi said the allegations plausibly supported a claim of intentional or willful disclosure but did not rule that the department broke the law. The claim can proceed; separate claims against Google and X.AI over AI services that allegedly republished the information remain under challenge (courthousenews.com, law360.com, reason.com). Proposed class: The proposed class would cover Epstein victims whose names, images, phone numbers, email addresses or residential details appeared in unredacted government documents. A subclass seeks removal of information still accessible through government, Google or X.AI services (reason.com). Legal threshold: A Privacy Act disclosure claim requires allegations that the information was contained in a system of records, was improperly disclosed, caused an adverse effect and resulted in actual damages. The agency must also have acted willfully or intentionally; the motion addressed that element (reason.com). Government response: The Justice Department said it created a confidential website for victims to request additional redactions after acknowledging inadvertent disclosures (courthousenews.com, reason.com).

title: Microsoft launches Code Red after outage, sets one-hour recovery goal
description:
Microsoft has launched an internal “Code Red” overhaul after a Nov. 12-13 failure disrupted Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services for about 24 hours. The company aims to resolve future global incidents within one hour. Microsoft attributed the outage to a Windows scalability defect introduced in July and said neither cyber activity nor AI agents caused it. The disruption affected government agencies, trading firms and airline communications across several countries.

The company’s review found that diagnostic information scattered across internal systems hampered its response: engineers exchanged more than 11,000 messages in 11 Teams chats without maintaining a single shared view of the incident. Microsoft plans to limit system load, separate traffic by region and speed recovery, with AI agents intended to help engineers interpret system-health data.

The company has not said when it expects to meet the one-hour target. Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team and weekly reviews. In a separate recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days to reach users worldwide.

The company’s review found that diagnostic information scattered across internal systems hampered its response: engineers exchanged more than 11,000 messages in 11 Teams chats without maintaining a single shared view of the incident (reuters.com, firstpost.com). Microsoft plans to limit system load, separate traffic by region and speed recovery, with AI agents intended to help engineers interpret system-health data (reuters.com). The company has not said when it expects to meet the one-hour target. Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team and weekly reviews. In a separate recent incident, an urgent fix took five to six days to reach users worldwide (reuters.com, arstechnica.com). Failure history: Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said the affected component had accumulated “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to a memo by Amanda Silver (reuters.com). Patch goal: Jason Henderson said Microsoft wants its most urgent security fixes safely deployed worldwide within an hour of detection (reuters.com, koreatimes.co.kr).

title: More than 120 climate scientists urge House to reject energy permitting bill
description:
More than 120 climate scientists urged the U.S. House to reject a sweeping energy permitting bill that the Senate passed 62-33 on Nov. 19, warning it could lock in fossil-fuel projects while weakening environmental safeguards. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten federal reviews and make it harder to challenge some projects in court; its supporters say faster approvals could help connect clean power and lower electricity costs.

The House is expected to take up the measure after the Thanksgiving recess, but no vote date has been announced. Lawmakers also face year-end legislation, including government funding due by Dec. 11. If the House passes it, the bill would go to President Donald Trump, whose administration has endorsed it.

title: Dell raises fiscal 2027 outlook as AI-server orders hit $132 billion
description:
Dell Technologies raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to $202 billion from $192 billion after third-quarter revenue more than doubled to $54.94 billion, beating analysts’ estimates. Adjusted earnings reached $9.45 per share, and Dell lifted its forecast for AI-optimized server revenue to $78 billion. Its AI-server backlog reached a record $132.3 billion after $60.2 billion in orders during the quarter.

The infrastructure business drove the gains, while Dell’s PC revenue rose 3% and fell short of forecasts. The company also authorized another $25 billion in share repurchases. For the current quarter, Dell forecast revenue of $56.3 billion and adjusted earnings of $8.40 per share. It expects memory-chip supply constraints to continue into 2027 and said its infrastructure operating margin could dip below 15% as lower-margin AI servers account for more sales.

title: Tiny solar tracker records hummingbird’s 4,055-mile migration to Alaska
description:
Researchers used miniature solar-powered transmitters to track a male Rufous hummingbird from Alabama to Alaska, recording a 4,055-mile journey in 38 days—the longest hummingbird migration documented to date. They tagged the bird in Lillian, Alabama, on March 27, 2025, and it reached Juneau on May 3.

The team fitted 11 hummingbirds with the devices in coastal Alabama and Florida in spring 2025 to track their movements across North America. The study authors said Rufous and ruby-throated hummingbird populations have recently declined; further research is needed to assess any long-term effects of wearing the transmitters.

Earlier record: The previous documented record was about 3,500 miles, set by a female Rufous banded in Florida in 2010 and later found in Alaska (gizmodo.com).

title: EFPIA says faster EU trial approvals won't fix hospital delays
description:
A study commissioned by the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) says a proposed European Union Biotech Act could shorten regulatory approval times for clinical trials but would not, by itself, eliminate delays before hospitals open trial sites. Under the proposal, approvals would take 75 days, or 47 days if regulators request no additional information; patients in Europe would still face an estimated wait of 294 to 339 days before a trial site opens.

The study compares Europe’s projected timelines with 168 to 276 days in the United States and 126 to 291 days in China, while cautioning that international comparisons have limits. EFPIA says hospitals need more staff, funding and research infrastructure alongside streamlined approvals. The proposed law remains under legislative negotiation.

excerpt: Conservative candidate Kristina Loewen won the Kelowna Centre riding by 132 votes on election night, Oct. 24, 2026. Conservative Party of BC candidate Kristina Loewen has won Kelowna Centre following a judicial recount, widening her margin over the BC NDP’s Loyal Wooldridge, to 46 votes. In a Facebook post, Loewen announced that the recount was complete. Elections BC posted the results on its website Tuesday (Nov. 23) afternoon, confirming the totals. “The Kelowna Centre recount is done!!! I’ve now won with a margin of 46 votes (up from 43)!!!!” Loewen wrote on Facebook. “I’m ready to be able to fully move forward in my role as an MLA representing Kelowna Centre – as well as in my new role as Minister of Children and Family Development.” Loewen also thanked Wooldridge and OneBC candidate Bill Desrossier for contesting the seat. Following election night on Oct. 24, Loewen held a lead of 132 to 137 votes over Wooldridge before mail-in, absentee, and telephone ballots were counted during Elections BC’s final count between Nov. 6-8. Once those ballots were factored in, Loewen’s advantage narrowed to 43 votes—11,689 votes to Wooldridge’s 11,646 votes. Because the margin fell below Election BC’s automatic judicial recount threshold of one-500th of total ballots cast (48 votes in Kelowna Centre), the riding headed back to a judicial recount which started Nov. 23. The finish echoed the 2024 provincial election where Loewen and Wooldridge also battled down to the wire, and a judicial recount was also needed.

title: Utah seeks to drop Kalshi charges after platform halts trading
description:
Utah has asked a state court to dismiss 14 criminal charges against prediction-market operator Kalshi and co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara after the company stopped accepting new trades from Utah residents. The charges alleged illegal gambling. The state seeks dismissal without prejudice, allowing prosecutors to refile if Kalshi returns. A judge must still approve the request. The executives had been scheduled to appear in court on Dec. 4.

Kalshi halted new trading after a federal judge declined to block Utah’s enforcement of its gambling laws while a federal case over regulatory authority proceeds. Kalshi and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission argue that the platform’s event contracts fall under federal commodities law, while Utah and other states say sports-related contracts constitute gambling subject to state law. Utah’s separate civil case seeking Kalshi’s profits continues, and the company says it will continue challenging the state’s authority.

title: Canada puts 100,000 temporary-worker residency slots under provincial control
description:
Canada’s immigration minister, Lena Metlege Diab, says provinces and territories will decide whether to nominate up to 100,000 temporary workers for permanent residency under a one-time 2027 measure; unused places will not be filled. The government’s regular target is 380,000 permanent residents, while one-time measures could bring total admissions to as many as 662,000 next year.

Diab says most people counted are already in Canada and changing status, while Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argues the plan could add pressure to housing, jobs and public services. The House of Commons debated a Conservative motion to block the plan; the Bloc Québécois says it will support the motion, which needs backing from some Liberal MPs to pass.

title: Bank of Canada warns oil costs may prolong inflation
description:
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said Tuesday that inflation pressures could persist even as global energy prices ease because businesses may pass earlier increases in production and transport costs on to consumers. He said the bank’s inflation forecast was somewhat lower than its October projection of 3.5% at year-end.

Businesses have so far absorbed much of the cost increases, but Macklem said surveys and historical lags point to further price increases in the year ahead. The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by a quarter-point to 2.5% in October; before its Dec. 9 decision, it will assess third-quarter gross domestic product and November employment data.

title: ESA's Euclid telescope finds record quasar beyond its survey reach
description:
The European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope identified a quasar candidate in its wide-area survey data, beyond the distance the mission was designed to map; ground- and space-based observatories then confirmed it. European Southern Observatory astronomer Julien Wolf led the discovery.

The object, J1504+6252, was seen as it existed about 630 million years after the Big Bang. Follow-up observations with the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes, among other observatories, established its record distance. Euclid launched in 2023 to survey galaxies and help investigate dark matter and dark energy; the team published its findings in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

title: Missouri court approves Bayer's $7.25 billion Roundup settlement
description:
A Missouri state court approved a class settlement worth up to $7.25 billion to resolve current and future claims that Bayer-owned Monsanto’s glyphosate-based herbicide Roundup caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The agreement calls for declining annual payments over as long as 21 years; an appeal could delay payments until the challenge is resolved.

The deal follows a June 2026 U.S. Supreme Court ruling barring state failure-to-warn claims that federal pesticide law pre-empts. The settlement remains subject to appeal, and people who opt out may pursue individual cases on other legal grounds.

title: IAEA moves to appoint sanctioned Russian regulator as deputy chief despite Ukraine’s protest
description:
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is preparing to appoint Alexey Ferapontov, a sanctioned Russian nuclear regulator, as a deputy director general. A senior diplomat said he is expected to take up the post in January 2027. Ukraine’s foreign and energy ministries demanded that the appointment be canceled, saying Ferapontov was involved in efforts to legitimize Russian regulatory control over the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant. Ukraine sanctioned him in February 2023.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi defended the choice as a staffing decision based on professional qualifications, not nationality or geopolitics. Ferapontov is also expected to head the agency’s Department of Nuclear Energy, which oversees programs on nuclear power development, fuel cycles and technical cooperation. Ukraine has urged IAEA member states, especially the Board of Governors, to use the agency’s statutory procedures to review the decision; preparations for the January appointment are continuing.

title: Archaeological studies trace ancient diets and Roman Britain’s diversity
description:
Three separate archaeological studies offer new evidence about past diets and migration. A study of “Rodhals Man,” excavated in 1956, describes him as a rare source of evidence about the shift toward farming. Research at two sites in Western Australia challenges the idea that ancient people widened their diets only when preferred foods became scarce.

A study of cremated remains from Colchester, Britain’s first Roman capital, found that some residents had origins in the Mediterranean, including Italy, Spain and Lebanon. The researchers used strontium and lead isotope ratios in dense skull bone to trace the origins of people whose cremated remains would otherwise be difficult to study.

title: Norway’s Equinor signs 18-year gas deal to supply Germany through 2044
description:
Norwegian energy company Equinor signed an 18-year contract with German gas importer VNG on Nov. 24 to supply up to 15.3 terawatt-hours, or about 1.4 billion cubic meters, of natural gas annually. Deliveries to Germany’s Trading Hub Europe market area are scheduled to start Jan. 1, 2027, and run through the end of 2044. Prices will reflect market terms; the companies kept other commercial details confidential.

The agreement is Equinor’s longest Norwegian gas sales contract since the 1986 Troll agreements. Norway supplied 44% of Germany’s gas in 2025, becoming its largest supplier after Russian deliveries fell following Moscow’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. VNG said the deal would diversify its supply portfolio and help it plan customer deliveries.

The contract follows a separate 15-year Equinor agreement with German utility Uniper to supply about 30 terawatt-hours annually from 2027 to 2041. VNG and Equinor have worked together for decades: Norwegian gas first reached eastern Germany in 1996. Deliveries under the new agreement do not begin until Jan. 1, 2027.

title: Valve releases Proton 11.0-3, adding support for 15 games and fixing regressions
description:
Valve released Proton 11.0-3 on Nov. 24, adding support for 15 Windows games on Linux and SteamOS and introducing experimental support for 32-bit OpenXR applications. Proton is Valve’s compatibility layer for running Windows games on Linux through Steam without requiring native Linux versions.

The update also fixes 19 regressions in the Proton 11 line, along with graphics, audio, controller and game-launch problems. Valve updated underlying components, including DXVK and VKD3D-Proton, which handle graphics compatibility, as well as Wine Mono, Xalia and FEX. Steam distributes the stable release through its client; users can also select a different Proton version for an individual game.

title: DR Congo suspends cobalt exports again as prices fall
description:
The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will suspend all cobalt exports from Nov. 30 until further notice, its strategic minerals regulator, ARECOMS, announced on Nov. 23. The government says it is responding to falling prices, weak global consumption and rising inventories. The DRC supplies nearly three-quarters of the world’s cobalt, used in batteries for electric vehicles and consumer electronics.

The suspension is due for review four months after it takes effect. Kinshasa previously replaced an export halt with quotas. Industry participants warn that restricting shipments may not clear the glut if copper mining continues to produce cobalt as a byproduct while demand remains weak.

title: China and India set Russian oil import records as demand shifts
description:
China and India are on track for record seaborne Russian oil imports averaging 3.4 million barrels per day in 2026, based on figures through mid-November, about 530,000 barrels per day more than a year earlier. The Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, while temporary U.S. sanctions waivers eased purchases and Ukrainian drone attacks reduced Russian refining capacity, leaving more crude available for export.

Traders and analysts expect purchases to ease in 2027 if Middle Eastern supply recovers. China’s Russian oil imports averaged 2.34 million barrels per day in January-October, while India’s averaged 1.87 million barrels per day over the same period.

title: Japan plans medical AI study as countries weigh oversight rules
description:
Japan’s health ministry plans to study the use of artificial intelligence in diagnosis and treatment next fiscal year, assess its accuracy and patients’ views, and examine who bears legal responsibility. The ministry has requested 120 million yen for the study and will use the findings to convene experts and consider changes to existing rules.

The Czech Republic has introduced a strategy through 2029 covering safety, reimbursement, data protection and clinician training, while Poland has begun offering hospitals a public platform with certified AI tools for imaging. Health-system leaders are calling for ongoing performance checks and clear clinical accountability.

Adoption levels: In 2025, 77% of U.S. hospitals used generative AI, surpassing the 69% using predictive AI for the first time (beckershospitalreview.com).

title: Salvadoran tribunal registers Bukele to seek a third term
description:
El Salvador’s Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) officially registered the candidacy of President Nayib Bukele and Vice President Félix Ulloa, of the Nuevas Ideas party, on November 23 for the elections on February 28, 2027. Bukele will thus seek a third consecutive term.

The candidacy is possible thanks to the constitutional reform approved by the Legislative Assembly in July 2025, which enabled indefinite reelection, extended presidential terms from five to six years, and eliminated the runoff. The TSE said the other presidential tickets had pending documentation and gave them three days from notification to submit it; afterward, it will decide which ones are definitively registered.

title: Battery storage projects expand across Spain, Cyprus, US and China
description:
Spanish developers Sungrow Renewables and Actuate Energy have agreed to build a seven-project battery storage portfolio totaling 380 megawatts and 1.5 gigawatt-hours. The projects are expected to begin operating from 2027 through the first half of 2028, and some are already under construction. Cyprus plans more than 300 MW of batteries to reduce solar power curtailment.

Energy research firm Enverus forecasts 376 GW of new U.S. battery storage capacity through 2050, the largest addition among the technologies it assessed, ahead of solar at 241 GW. Chinese manufacturer Chint Power plans an uninterruptible power supply factory with annual capacity of 2 GWh for data centers, while a separate Chinese company shifted funding from a battery project to AI data-center power systems.

title: Broadcom patches 23 VMware flaws, including critical vCenter bypass
description:
Broadcom released patches Nov. 24 for 23 vulnerabilities across VMware products, including a flaw with a severity score of 9.8 that could let an attacker with network access to vCenter bypass authentication. Two other critical flaws in the ESX I/O filter service could allow remote code execution on affected hosts.

The new vCenter bug, CVE-2026-123903, is separate from another vCenter authentication bypass, CVE-2026-123890, which Broadcom patched days earlier. Rapid7 said attackers had exploited the earlier flaw as a zero-day. Broadcom did not report any exploitation of the newly disclosed flaws in the wild. Fixed versions include vCenter 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 and 8.0 U3m; administrators must check the relevant builds for ESX and other products separately.

title: AI investment drives U.S. growth, complicating Fed's inflation choices
description:
Artificial intelligence investment has become a major contributor to U.S. economic growth through spending on data centers, chips, computing equipment, power systems and cooling. It has also boosted activity among businesses serving construction projects. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has called AI central to U.S. leadership, while the central bank faces strong inflation data and financial markets signaling weaker inflation expectations.

Hotels near data centers have reported revenue growth, and snowmobile maker Polaris has reported demand from contractors building data centers. Evercore ISI Vice President Krishna Guha, a former Federal Reserve Bank of New York official, said the Fed must avoid both undermining its inflation credibility and being seen as having halted the AI boom. Separately, Seeking Alpha analyst Nicolas Bolsinger argues that rapid capital spending and credit links among AI infrastructure firms could spread financial stress if growth falters. His assessment is based on his own credit-risk model, not an official forecast.

description:
North West businessman Brown Mogotsi appeared in Pretoria Magistrate’s Court on Nov. 24 on a perjury charge over statements to the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry that he was a Crime Intelligence contact agent. The allegations concern his affidavit and oral testimony in November 2025; the South African Police Service says he was never a contact agent.

Mogotsi has been in custody since May 2026 in a separate case involving an alleged staged assassination attempt, and a Johannesburg court denied him bail in June. The National Prosecuting Authority’s Gauteng spokesperson, Lumka Mahanjana, said the new case was postponed to Dec. 1 for bail investigations and the state intends to oppose his release.

title: England's 5,258 heat deaths spur calls for climate adaptation
description:
An estimated 5,258 heat-associated deaths in England in summer 2026, a record, have intensified calls to prepare homes, health services and public infrastructure for rising temperatures. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) warned that climate change will make extreme heat longer, more frequent and more intense. The estimate covers May to September and remains provisional because death-registration data are incomplete.

The summer was also dry: drought was declared across Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires damaged parts of the country. The agency said heat protection should start early in the season because people and public services may be less prepared for heat episodes in May and June. It also urged longer-term adaptation alongside emissions cuts.

title: Canada-U.S. tariff deal nears, but auto duties and China divide negotiators
description:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington and Ottawa are fairly close to a tariff-relief agreement, but Canada’s trade relationship with China and tariffs on autos remain sticking points. Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the talks had made progress but cautioned that Canada was not about to sign. The two governments have not published proposed terms or a list of tariff changes.

The talks resumed after negotiations collapsed in August and President Donald Trump imposed tariffs of up to 50% on about $28 billion of Canadian goods under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. Ottawa’s counter-tariffs and U.S. duties on vehicles and industrial goods remain in dispute. Canadian automakers are seeking an interim arrangement to narrow the tariff gap between plants on either side of the border. Auto industry representatives say the terms must preserve production in Canada, while Greer has criticized Ottawa’s recent trade agreements with China.

title: NASA opens lunar reactor competition, requiring nonnuclear ground tests first
description:
NASA has opened its formal competition for Lunar Reactor-1, a proposed 20-kilowatt fission system intended to power a future Moon base. The initial contract work focuses on design and ground testing, not building a flight reactor. Industry proposals are due Dec. 21, and NASA is targeting a launch-ready system by 2030.

The first phase calls for refining the flight design and demonstrating a nonnuclear engineering test unit that uses electrical heaters in place of nuclear fuel. NASA’s plan includes component radiation testing and an integrated demonstration of heat transport, power conversion, heat rejection and power management in a thermal-vacuum environment simulating lunar conditions. Selected contractors would have 18 months to complete that work.

NASA describes the current effort as technology development, testing and flight design; any later flight-system work would require further procurement. The reactor is intended to provide electricity through lunar nights lasting about two weeks, when solar generation is unavailable. NASA says the solicitation may also support other space-nuclear projects through additional task orders.

title: EU seeks climate summit rule changes after COP31 deadlock
description:
The European Commission plans to propose changes to the United Nations climate summit process after the COP31 summit ended in Antalya without a political agreement. The European Union wants to revisit the consensus rule that lets any country block a decision. EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said Brussels also wants more transparency and a greater focus on carrying out existing commitments.

Climate-vulnerable countries say they need financing and practical ways to identify where adaptation is most urgent. COP31 backed work on adaptation indicators adopted at the previous summit and asked countries to improve and test them nationally. Brazilian climate and environmental justice adviser Thaynah Gutierrez said breaking down data by race, gender and age could help identify vulnerable communities, but funding remains necessary.

South Korea’s climate ministry said it will convene about 80 experts on Nov. 26 to discuss COP31, the Paris Agreement, carbon budgets and national emissions-reduction pathways. The European Commission says it will develop its proposals in consultation with EU member states.

title: ESA revises BepiColombo maneuvers after Mercury insertion software fault
description:
The European Space Agency (ESA) has revised BepiColombo’s remaining maneuvers after a software fault cut short the joint European-Japanese mission’s Mercury orbit-insertion burn. ESA says the revised sequence can correct the spacecraft’s trajectory without additional thruster burns, keeping the separation of its two science orbiters and the start of science operations on schedule.

The fault involved attitude guidance and thruster control, and the spacecraft entered a protective safe mode when the burn stopped. The spacecraft reached a stable Mercury orbit; ESA and its partners continue to investigate the software problem.

The European Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Japan’s Mio orbiter remain joined and are scheduled to separate on Dec. 9–10, with routine science operations planned for April 2027. The European orbiter is expected to reach its final orbit in March, while Mio will investigate Mercury’s magnetosphere.

title: Australia awards top science prize to melanoma oncologist and physicist
description:
Australia jointly awarded its 2026 Prime Minister’s Prize for Science to oncologist Professor Georgina Long and physicist Professor Anthony Thomas at a ceremony in Canberra on Tuesday night. Long’s research led to effective melanoma drug therapies, while Thomas was recognized for work on protons, neutron stars and dark matter.

Among other recipients, Professor Asha Bowen received the life scientist award for research that helped deliver the first significant reduction in skin infections among Aboriginal children in 50 years. Professor Mark Smythe won the innovation prize for turning Australian research into medicines approved to treat conditions including psoriasis and a blood cancer.

title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

title: UK seafood groups welcome EU trade deal, seek transition clarity
description:
UK seafood and agricultural trade groups have welcomed the UK-EU sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, intended to reduce food-trade paperwork and routine checks, while seeking clarity on the transition. The agreement is due to take effect on March 1, 2028, but still requires formal approval. Until then, exporters and producers must follow existing requirements.

The Shellfish Association of Great Britain said the agreement could restore access for some shellfish from Class-B waters, which EU rules have barred unless the catch is purified. Scottish seafood representatives said removing paperwork and checks could reduce costs and help smaller producers return to European markets, but stressed that businesses need time to comply with the aligned rules. The German agricultural trade association has also sought clear provisions for transition periods and existing stocks.

title: EU sets hybrid import limits as European carmakers lose market share
description:
European carmakers are losing ground in their home market as hybrid demand grows. German manufacturers’ European Union sales fell 5.7% in October, and their market share dropped from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to figures cited by DW. On Nov. 24, the European Commission published temporary import quotas for hybrids from China and other exporters after its investigation found an imminent threat of serious injury to EU producers.

The limits cover imports from major suppliers including Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the United Kingdom. The Commission said the restrictions are tightest for China, while most other countries’ allocations exceed recent shipments. German automakers have announced widespread layoffs as their market shares shrink. The Commission has linked import growth to global production overcapacity and trade barriers in other markets.

The provisional measures run for up to 200 days, through June 18, 2027, while the Commission continues its investigation. Any longer-term measures would require backing from EU member states.

title: Scottish floating wind project reserves 28 Siemens Gamesa turbines
description:
Green Volt, a planned floating offshore wind farm off Peterhead, Scotland, has reserved manufacturing capacity for 28 Siemens Gamesa turbines rated at more than 15 megawatts each. The project has consent for up to 560 megawatts and would supply electricity to the UK grid. The reservation is a procurement step, not a final turbine supply contract, and Siemens Gamesa says further milestones remain.

Green Volt’s developers also signed a letter of intent with the Port of Aberdeen for anchor and mooring operations at Aberdeen South Harbour, supporting a proposed £15 million package for infrastructure and supply-chain work. The project secured key consents and a 400-megawatt UK government Contract for Difference in 2024, but still needs further contracts and investment before construction.

title: AI-assisted Riemann proof fuels debate over understanding and value
description:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge’s claim to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with AI has prompted debate over whether a machine-checked result can advance mathematics when researchers cannot yet explain its reasoning. Alpöge said he developed the proof with Anthropic’s Claude model and released it as about 17 million lines of Lean code. The Lean and Mathlib organizations expressed confidence in its correctness, while the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved pending publication and broad acceptance.

Researchers are trying to extract an intelligible argument from the formal code. More than 60 people on the Principia Math platform are using AI agents to translate sections and have completed work on more than 3,000 pieces. The platform’s chief executive, Anton Shakov, told WIRED that a conceptual account could take months. Mathematicians say they need to understand the reasoning—not just confirm its formal validity—to build on the result.

The Association for Human Mathematics criticized the announcement’s lack of accountability and accessibility, while Google DeepMind researcher Seb Krier said a pure-math result does not immediately improve Anthropic’s operating margins. Cybersecurity specialists say the result itself does not weaken RSA encryption, though they argue AI’s growing ability to explore and verify mathematics warrants renewed attention to cryptographic readiness.

But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

title: Ottawa seeks faster land seizures for Toronto-Quebec City rail line
description:
Canada’s federal government has proposed giving Alto, the Crown corporation developing a high-speed rail line between Toronto and Quebec City, expanded powers to acquire land through expropriation without public hearings and transfer property directly to a private consortium. Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the measures would prevent land acquisition disputes from delaying the project for years and argued they do not remove due process.

The proposals, included in a Budget 2026 motion published Nov. 20, would exempt Alto from the federal Expropriation Act and parts of several rail and environmental laws. The project is expected to cost $60 billion to $90 billion; construction of its first phase, between Montreal and Ottawa, is scheduled to begin in 2029 or 2030. Farmers, opposition politicians and municipal representatives have raised concerns about property rights, farmland and consultation, while Alto says it will pay fair compensation and limit the impacts.

title: Battery developers expand four-hour storage as power markets shift
description:
Battery developers are planning longer-duration projects as solar growth and rising electricity demand increase the need to shift power into evening peaks. In France, BW ESS and local developer Wattmen plan to develop about 500 megawatts of battery projects over three years, with at least four hours of storage per site. In the United States, utility-scale battery capacity reached nearly 52 gigawatts by June 2026.

U.S. developers are competing with gas peaker plants, while French batteries could earn revenue from wholesale power, balancing services and capacity markets. Japan’s storage market faces uncertainty over whether strong early revenues from ancillary services can sustain projects over their 20-year lifetimes, Umer Sadiq said.

title: Iraq orders federal takeover of Kurdish oilfields and border crossings
description:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal agencies to take over the Kurdistan Region’s border crossings and manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahaddin and Nineveh provinces. He also barred the regional government from approving oil exports outside the federal Oil Ministry. The directives followed an investigation into suspected oil smuggling involving the state-run North Oil Company and are part of al-Zaidi’s campaign to assert state authority over oil and border security.

The measures also direct security forces to close unofficial crossings and routes, station federal personnel at checkpoints and monitor fields and pipelines. Baghdad dismissed the head of its border authority and Kirkuk security commanders and suspended North Oil Company executives pending investigations. The government has not specified when or how it will carry out the takeovers.

Kurdish leaders, including Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, reject the orders as unilateral and unconstitutional but say they remain open to dialogue based on Iraq’s Constitution. The two main Kurdish parties, the Kurdistan Democratic Party and Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, issued a joint statement opposing the measures. The dispute is also complicating negotiations over Iraq’s 2027 budget and oil-revenue arrangements.

title: Does Your Building Work or Does It Just Photograph Well? What Neuroscience and Use Data Could Teach Architects
description: Architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each new medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

title: EU probes European Coca-Cola bottler over suspected limits on Spanish imports
description:
The European Commission is investigating whether Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP), a UK-headquartered bottler, offered retailers incentives to restrict soft-drink imports into Spain and used country-specific packaging to impede cross-border sales. The formal investigation concerns suspected barriers to trade between EU countries and restrictions on wholesale buyers’ ability to negotiate purchases across several markets; the Commission has not established that CCEP broke the law.

CCEP is the largest supplier of carbonated soft drinks in eight member states: Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. The case concerns wholesale supply to supermarkets and other retailers, rather than sales to restaurants, hotels and cafes. The Commission says the suspected practices could limit retailers’ access to lower-cost supplies from other countries and reduce consumer choice.

The Commission is also consulting on possible tools to address territorial supply restrictions that competition law may not cover. A separate EU initiative on those restrictions is expected around spring 2027 and could take the form of legislation or a voluntary code of conduct.

title: Trump, Xi and Putin end Shenzhen summit without concrete agreements
description:
U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held talks on Nov. 19 in Shenzhen during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit but reached no concrete agreements. Their joint statement called for United Nations reform, increased oil-product supplies and talks to reduce nuclear risks, while omitting the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

Some analysts described the meeting as largely symbolic, while a Chinese foreign-policy expert said he expected U.S.-China relations to remain broadly stable in 2027 even as tensions rise. Da Wei, director of Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said future stability would depend partly on whether Washington recognizes the two powers’ “mutual vulnerability”.

title: Chinese maker brings foldable off-grid solar EV charger to Australia
description:

The company says the battery buffers solar input and supplies regulated alternating-current power to a vehicle. The unit can also provide backup power during mains outages. Gaotu offers the system to Australian distributors and says it can customize versions for local partners.

title: COP31 in Antalya: What the Climate Summit Means for Buildings and Cities
description: The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

title: BepiColombo adjusts Mercury orbit plan after software glitch
description:
The European Space Agency (ESA) says it has revised BepiColombo’s remaining maneuvers after a software problem cut short the spacecraft’s Mercury orbit-insertion burn. The joint ESA and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency mission to study Mercury remains in a stable orbit. The revised plan is expected to correct its trajectory without additional thruster burns.

ESA’s analysis points to a software problem involving attitude and thruster control, though the precise cause remains under investigation. The revised sequence is intended to maintain the mission’s schedule: the orbiters are still due to separate in December, with routine science operations planned for April 2027.

title: Smart Heating and Saving Electricity: Comparing Tariffs, Storage, and Thermostats
description:

title: UK-EU food deal would remove checks from 2028, pending ratification
description:
The United Kingdom and European Union have concluded negotiations on a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement intended to reduce routine certification, inspections and other barriers to trade in food, farm products, animals and plants. Britain would align its rules with EU requirements in covered areas, including future updates, and have a role in discussions on new rules. The agreement is scheduled to take effect on March 1, 2028. Customs procedures and rules of origin would remain in place.

The agreement still requires signing and ratification, and businesses must follow current rules until it takes effect. The UK government says the arrangements could reduce exporters' costs and ease trade, but some British farmers question having to follow EU standards for production for the domestic market. Animal-welfare groups warn the deal could complicate planned reforms. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said legislation to implement the summit agreements would be introduced to Parliament on November 26.

title: Singapore and Malaysia tighten checks on AI chip routes
description:
Malaysia will tell data-centre operators not to host, rent space to or provide services to seven companies placed on a U.S. trade blacklist, including Singapore-based Megaspeed and two firms it identifies as Malaysian entities, Speedmatrix and MSFusion. Malaysia’s trade ministry said another listed company, PT Megaspeed International, is neither registered in Malaysia nor operating there as a data-centre operator or tenant.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said during a visit to Canberra that Singapore is investigating whether Megaspeed breached local laws and is working with Washington to share information and develop a mechanism for U.S. authorities to enforce their own chip controls. He said tracking chips’ eventual destinations is complex and that the U.S. had not provided all the information Singapore requested.

The U.S. Commerce Department added seven companies across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand to its Entity List on Nov. 23, citing diversion risks; future licence applications face a presumption of denial. Malaysia accounts for more than half of Southeast Asia’s data-centre capacity under construction.

title: NASA seeks partners for 20-kilowatt Moon reactor by 2030
description:
NASA has opened a competition for industry partners to design, build and test Lunar Reactor-1, a 20-kilowatt fission system intended to be ready for launch by 2030 and operate on the Moon for at least five years. Proposals are due Dec. 21, and the reactor must meet U.S. Department of Energy safety standards for nuclear operations.

The system is designed to provide continuous electricity for future lunar habitats, communications, rovers and scientific equipment, including through lunar nights that last about two weeks. NASA revised its solicitation after releasing a draft in August and holding an industry day in September; the agency says it may also commission additional work on other space nuclear power systems.

title: Macron weighs January vote on French constitutional budget rule
description:
President Emmanuel Macron is weighing whether to revive a 2011 constitutional budget amendment and convene France’s lawmakers in Congress in January to reassure investors over borrowing costs and a deficit the government has struggled to reduce. Macron told Le Figaro he would explore the proposal if market volatility persisted into January; he is also watching whether lawmakers pass the 2027 budget by year-end. France expects a 2026 deficit of 5.4% of gross domestic product, while public debt is about 119% of GDP.

The proposal would require multi-year plans to restore balance rather than impose an immediate numerical deficit ceiling. Both houses approved the 2011 text, but it never went to a final vote in Congress. Adoption at Versailles would require three-fifths support from lawmakers.

Even if the constitutional change passes, lawmakers would need to adopt an organic law defining how the framework works, followed by a first budget framework law. Macron’s January decision remains conditional on market volatility and the budget debate; lawmakers would still need to establish the measure’s implementing rules.

title: Bird flu outbreaks prompt poultry culls in France and Delaware
description:
France reported a highly pathogenic H5N1 outbreak at a poultry farm in Pas-de-Calais, where the virus killed 80 of 4,300 birds and authorities culled the remaining flock. Delaware separately announced a presumptive positive H5 test result in a commercial flock in Sussex County; officials quarantined the farm and began culling its birds, which will not enter the food supply.

Authorities detected the French outbreak as bird flu cases rose seasonally in Europe. France had raised its national risk level to high. Researchers also reported that mammary tissue in several livestock species contains receptors that influenza viruses can use, while noting that infections in those species have been reported only sporadically. French authorities suspect contact between farmed poultry and wild birds in the Pas-de-Calais case.
